completion of Bharatmala Pariyojana Phase -I was 2021 -22, only 168 km o f the port 
connectivity roads have been awarded while the rest of the 2,105 kms are in various 
stages of DPR preparation. The Committee is of the considered view that lack of robust 
road connectivity to ports is one of the major bottlenecks faced by the Sh ipping sector 
in India. The Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry should take a serious 
look at the various factors impeding the award of these road projects and take urgent 
steps and undertake dedicated efforts to iron out the same to bolster th e growth of the 
Shipping sector in the country.  
(Para 5.2) 
 

75 
 
 
CENTRAL SECTOR SCHEMES/PROJECTS 
Recommendation/Observation 
The Committee desires to know the reasoning provided, if any, for allocation of only Rs. 
9,870.89 crores under the Revenue section at B.E. 2021 -22 stage, as against the 
projected requirement of Rs. 14,557.60 crore. The Committee notes that several 
critically important schemes of the Ministry are funded by the allocation made under 
the Revenue section and therefore, it must pursue the Min istry of Finance for allocation 
of higher funds under the Revenue head in future.  
(Para 6.2) 
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS AUTHORITY OF INDIA 
Monetization of National Highways 
The Committee notes that the reply furnished by the Ministry does not provide any 
details regarding the Initial Estimated Concession Value (IECV) amount in case of TOT 
Bundle 2 and the amounts quoted by the bidders for Bundle 2. In case the bids received 
from the bidders have been lower than the IECV, the Ministry may apprise the 
Committee regarding possible reasons for the same.  
(Para 7.3) 
The Committee takes note of the positive impact made by the Data Lake software on the 
decision making process of NHAI. The Committee is of the considered view that the 
Ministry/NHAI should take necessary ste ps to onboard State PWDs on the Data Lake 
platform so as to improve the decision making process of the State PWDs as well, not 
just for National Highways projects, but for the State Highways and other roads as well.  
(Para 8.4) 
Quality Inspection 
The Committee notes that the reply of the Ministry does not furnish any information 
regarding the action taken by it to ensure disciplinary action against the 
person/agencies involved in preparing DPR, the concessionaire as well as the approving 
official, in case discrepancies/ deficiencies are found in the compliance of guidelines for 

76 
 
road construction and material quality. The Committee would like to be apprised 
regarding the steps taken by the Ministry in this regard.  
(Para 9.2) 
Vacancies and Staffing in NHAI 
The Committee notes the various hindrances being faced in the filling up of vacancies in 
NHAI and the remedial measures undertaken to overcome the same. The Committee, 
however, is distressed to note that the total manpower working in NHAI, includin g both 
regular officials and those on deputation, as on 31.03.2021 is just 1122 out of the total 
sanctioned strength of 1892. The Committee is of the strong view that given the huge 
financial allocation made to NHAI each year, it is pertinent to ensure tha t sufficient 
manpower is in place so as to make optimal utilization of the available funds. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the ongoing comprehensive review of existing 
Recruitment Rules of NHAI may be finalized at the earliest and sincere effort s may be 
made to ensure that the vacancies presently lying unfilled in NHAI are filled up at the 
earliest.  
(Para 10.4) 
EXTERNALLY AIDED PROJECTS 
The Committee may be apprised of the action taken by the Ministry for analyzing the 
possibility of periodically sharing a part of the revenue generated from road 
infrastructure projects with those whose land was acquired and the possible effects of 
the same on the land acquisition process.  
(Para 11.2) 
SCHEMES OF UTs FINANCED FROM CRIF 
The Committee takes note of the details of funds released to the various UTs during the 
year 2020-21. The Committee is concerned to note that the amount of funds released i.e. 
Rs. 96.95 crores to the UT of Ladakh is less than even 40 percent of the budgetary 
provisions available for the UT during the year 2020 -21. Given the strategic location of 
the UT of Ladakh and the pressing need for development of a robust road network in 
the region, the Committee recommends that the Ministry may proactively reach out to 
the UT Department concerned and try to iron out any technical difficulties being faced 
in the execution of projects, if need be, so that the budgetary provisions made for the 
UT of Ladakh can be utilized optimally.  

77 
 
(Para 12.4) 
DEVELOPMENT, PLANNING, QUALITY ASSURANCE, RESEARCH AND TRAINING 
– FINANCED FROM CRIF 
The Committee is not satisfied with the reasons furnished by the Ministry for managing 
to spend a mere Rs. 34.36 crores under Highway Research as against the RE allocation 
of Rs. 79.00 crores. The Committee strong ly recommends that the Ministry should take 
up more schemes under this head and urgently look into the reasons behind low 
sanction of R&D schemes in the road sector.  
(Para 13.2) 
The Committee would like to be apprised about the action taken by the Ministr y in 
order to initiate and fund researches to gain insights into various issues pertaining to 
road transport sector.  
(Para 14.2) 
RESEARCH, TRAINING, STUDIES AND OTHER ROAD SAFETY SCHEMES 
The Committee feels that the role played by Indian Roads Congress in  carrying out 
research programmes pertaining to road construction is of immense value and that the 
Ministry should ensure that budgetary constraints are not faced by IRC since the 
guidelines issued by it are followed across the country and have enormous im plications 
on the quality of roads in India. In this light, the Committee reiterates its 
recommendation that the Ministry should provide adequate budgetary support needed 
by IRC to carry out research programmes in collaboration with the leading 
Universities/ Research Institutions in the country.  
(Para 15.2) 
The Committee desires to be apprised of the actions taken by the Ministry in this 
regard.  
(Para 16.2) 
Road Safety 
The Ministry takes note of the data furnished by the Ministry with regard to black spots 
across the country. The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the Ministry may 
analyze the data pertaining to the existing black spots in order to gain actionab le 

78 
 
insights into prevention of creation of such accident -prone black spots in the upcoming 
road projects of the Ministry. The Committee further recommends that the rectification 
of black spots across the country should be given topmost priority and the Ministry may 
review the existing framework in place to ensure the same.  
(Para 17.4) 
The Committee appreciates that a scheme for cashless treatment of road accident 
victims is under consultation with the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, National 
Health Au thority and other Stakeholders. The Committee recommends that the same 
may be finalized within a fixed timeline so as to save precious lives in road accidents. 
The Committee further desires to be kept apprised about the progress made in this 
regard.  
(Para 18.2) 
The Committee takes note of the various measures taken by the Ministry for 
rectification of black spots and recommends that a mechanism may be put in place to 
ensure that periodical monitoring and maintenance of measures such as amber beacons, 
crash barriers, signages etc. is carried out on National Highways across the country. 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry must bring out strict guidelines 
specifying that long-lasting rust-free materials are used for signages and that the shrubs 
and trees on the Highways are trimmed regularly so as to ensure that signages installed 
on the Highways remain clearly visible to the drivers at all seasons. The Committee 
hopes that the Ministry would be able to succeed in its efforts to rectify all identified 
Black spots by September, 2021. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry 
may consider reviewing the definition of Black spots scientifically following the 
international standards, once all the presently identified Black spots have been rectified.  
(Para 19.8) 
The Committee, after going through the installed A.C. (Asbestos Cement) Road 
Reflector in various Municipalities and PWDs like MCGM (Mumbai), Uttarakhand etc. 
used under Road Safety & Road Furniture Division as a Road/ Highway Divider & 
Crash B arrier in place of Metallic Crash Barrier, found that it is a cheaper, green 
product having more strength and durability which can take the strength of the vehicle 
in case of an accident, avoiding any extreme fatal  damages, in comparison to the 
metallic and other alternatives. The A.C. Road Reflector/ Crash Barrier installed are 
rust and theft proof as its components have Asbestos and Cement which are not prone 

79 
 
to rust and have no resale value, resulting in no theft, this unique feature can help save 
large exchequer amount and simultaneously give higher road safety while beautifying 
the roads. The Committee was informed that the product comes with a seven year 
guarantee, though its life span is estimated to be more than two decades. The 
Committee, therefore , recommends that the Ministry may explore the possibility of 
using A.C. Road Reflector/ Delineator/ Crash Barrier in the highway projects as an 
alternative to metallic crash barrier.  
(Para 19.9) 
The Committee takes note of the efforts made by the Ministry to ensure that the 
meetings of District Road Safety Committees. The Committee, however, is disheartened 
to note that details of only 7 meetings of District Road Safety Committees have been 
uploaded by 4 States/ UTs and feels that the same might be a reflection of the number of 
meetings of the District Road Safety Committees actually being held across the country. 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry may further pursue the matter with the 
Chief Secretaries of the various States in order to increase the frequency of the meetings 
of the District Road Safety Committees and look into other possible measures that can 
be taken to this end. The Committee further notes that the reply of the Ministry does 
not address the recommendation made by the Commi ttee for constitution of a Road 
Safety Committee at the State level. The Committee desires to be apprised of the action 
taken by the Ministry in this regard.  
(Para 20.5) 
Core Group on Safety and Security

(Para 21.2)

Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee observes that excluding the budgetary allocation for Air India Asset 
Holding Limited (SPV) in 2021-22, the projected requirement of the Ministry for all the other 
Schemes under Revenue Section is ₹1358.85 crore, against which BE allocation of  ₹915.16 
crore only has been made. The Committee, therefore, is apprehensive that the budgetary 
allocation made to the Ministry is not in sync with the actual budgetary requirements of the 
Ministry. The Civil Aviation sector has been dealt a huge blow by t he Coronavirus pandemic 
and there is a need for huge intervention to save this sector, in this hour of crisis. The 
Committee notes that it is unreasonable that instead of giving an enhanced budgetary 
allocation, there has been a significant shortfall in the BE 2021-22 allocation of the Ministry. 
This surely is a matter of grave concern. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a 
higher fund allocation should be provided at the RE 2021 -22 stage, to the Ministry, so that 
the Ministry can fulfill its mandate and bolster the growth of Civil Aviation sector in the right 
direction.

requirement of funds under Revenue Section, the Ministry of Finance will be approached for 
allocation of additional budget at RE stage for FY 2021-22.

on particular routes submit their proposals at the time of bidding under RCS - UDAN from 
time to time.

feasibility of operation on a particular route and bid under the scheme  from time to time. 
Selection of airlines is done through a transparent bidding process.

19. On recommendations of the Committee, a Core Group has been constituted under the

implemented in the operations of helicopter ambulances.

Aviation.

in the respective fields, with requisite global exposure and good reputation for the services

Public Private Partnership of Airports 
Recommendation/Observation  
14. The Committee underlines the need for a comprehensive negotiation and guidelines, 
in the award of airports under PPP model. The Committee urges the Ministry to take note of 
the management model of Kochi International Airport at Nedumbassery, and analyze the 
advantages and liabilities of such a model. The Ministry, may, after such analysis, adopt such 
a concept, if the advantages outweigh the liabilities. The Committee, further, stresses upon 
the need to make sure that the guidelines regarding operationalizing the new airports are 
unbiased, so that all parts of India are benefitted by the same. 
 (Para 19.3) 
Reply of the Ministry 
14.1 Airport Sector  is one of the Sectors where Public Private Partnership (PPP) was 
implemented first in the country. PPP at airports has evolved with the time and with the 
different models of execution. Cochin International Airport (“CIAL”)  was established as  a 
Greenfield airport way back in 1999 and  is being  managed by Cochin International Airport 
Limited (“CIAL”). Currently, CIAL is having equity participation from the Government of 
Kerala   (32.42%), NRIs (32.49%), Industrialists, Financial Institutions an d Airport   Service 
Providers, with around 18,000 shareholders from 29 countries. When the Cochin airport was 
conceived, the Indian economy had just opened up for the private sector and therefore, there 
were not many takers of the airport projects. And the refore, the State Government of Kerala 
itself executed the project at an estimated project cost of Rs. 200cr. by arranging the 
funds through joint financial   participation of airport users (mainly non -resident Indians), 
Airport Service Providers and the Government.  
14.2 Thus, the current ownership model of   CIAL is the result of financial paucity 
prevailed at that period to fund the   project and the requirement to mobilize fund by alternate 
method and it is a fact that the management of the airport still remains with  the State 
Government which is at the center of the project. 
14.3 Whereas, the concept of PPP at airports has shifted from Government centric to 
Private centric. The efforts of Government of India has been that the airports are substanti ally 
financed by the private investors and management remains with them till the lease period. 
The idea behind this has been that AAI is relieved from running the airports with financially 
sound background and strong passenger throughput which is not the c ase with CIAL. AAI 
gets the revenue share or Concession Fee from these airports which is utilized for 
development of smaller and unviable airports.   Unlike CIAL, there is no financial crunch for 
the   development, modernization, upgrading of PPP brownfield  airports by the   private 
players. Even Greenfield airports like Jewar, MOPA, Bhogapuram, Navi   Mumbai are being 
developed by private players with huge capital expenditure. 

27 
 
14.4 The financial difficulties faced   by State of Kerala during the project fun ding of 
CIAL during the nineties,  which necessitated funding from NRIs and Financial Institutions, 
is not  the case presently and private players are willing to fund  both Brownfield and 
Greenfield airport   projects. 
14.5 Further, if the   companies, which develop, operate and manage the brownfield and 
greenfield   airports offload the shares in future to general public, the shareholding of   these 
companies will be akin to CIAL. 
14.6 As regards Committee's recommendations for unbiased development of   Greenfield 
airports, it is stated that Government of India has notified the Greenfield Airports Policy in 
2008 according to which AAI,  State Government or any other airport developer can develop 
a Greenfield airport in the country with the prior approval of th e Government of India. The 
Policy document is applicable to all parts of the country uniformly and does not discriminate 
against any region/part.

Operationalization of Defence airports for Civil Aviation 
Recommendation/Observation  
40. The Committee desires that the Ministry may submit a detailed note, after due study, 
on the difference between a Greenfield project, a brownfield project and a defence 
brownfield project (civil enclave). All advantages and disadvantages of each category of 
project should be spelt out comprehensively so that State Governments which are willing to 
undertake expansion of civil aviation activities may avail the note for sound decision making. 
 (Para 57) 

46 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
40.1 A Greenfield project means a work which is started from scratch on the unused lands 
where there is no need to remodel or demolish an existing structure. A greenfield airport is an 
aviation facility with greenfield project characteristics. The designation reflects certain 
environmental qualities (using previously undeveloped or empty greenfield land, for 
example) and commissioning, planning and construction processes that are generally carrie d 
out from scratch. While a green field in nature is defined as a wide expanse of natural land 
(meadow, prairie, grassland), here greenfield denotes that a project lacks any constraints 
imposed upon it by prior work or existing infrastructure. As per the G overnment of India's 
Policy, no Greenfield airport will normally be allowed within a distance of 150 kms from the 
nearest existing airport. 
40.2 A brownfield, on the other hand, remodels or improves upon existing facilities. 
Brownfield projects are built o ver Brownfield land or Brownfield site. A Brownfield land or 
Brownfield site means a land which was operational in the past but now is in idle condition. 
Hence, a brownfield airport project is one which develops on the existing facilities.  
40.3 A civil enclave is an area at a military air base allotted for the usage of civil aviation. 
AAI establishes a civil enclave at the existing defence airfield instead of developing a new 
airport. A civil enclave is basically a joint user airport, where the time -slot for civilian and 
defence flights are allotted by coordination between AAI and Defence authorities.  
40.4 The establishment of Greenfield, Brownfield or Civil Enclave depends upon the 
existing circumstances, availability of resources including land, viability of commercial flight 
operations etc. 
Recommendation/Observation

Airports Authority of India, Air Traffic Control and cargo operators including the DGCA, 
state administration and BCAS to specify the challenges/shortcomings as far as use of Civil

 (Para 57.1) 
Reply of the Ministry 
41.1 At Civil enclaves, AAI has to face the challenge of limited slot availability sometimes 
due to limited watch hours provided by Defense authorities, restriction imposed by Defense 
authorities on civil flight operations for certain period of time during day for military 
operations and also restriction on permissible Runway movements per hour for civil flight 
operations eventually resulting in limited flight movements and connectivity by airline 
operators.

inter alia, defines certain rights to passengers in case of flight delays, flight cancellations,

CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
 
DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (2021-22) OF THE MINISTRY 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee understands that many of the programmes / schemes relating to Port 
modernization, Port infrastructure development, ship building, ship repairing and inland 
waterways transport are lagging behind because of the drastic cuts effected and would 
ultimately lead to both time and cost overruns. The Committee is of the view that if the 
Ministry wants adequate/ substantial budgetary support to complete its projects, the pace of 
implementation of the projects will have to be spruced up and the allocate d funds be 
optimally utilized. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should initiate 
and implement measures for better financial discipline and ensure that the scarce resources do 
not remain locked up and surrendered later on.  
                   (Para 6) 
Reply of Ministry 
1.1 Noted for necessary compliance. In this connection, necessary instructions in 
compliance of above recommendations/directions of the Hon’ble Committee have been 
issued by IWAI vide O.M. dated 23.08.2021 to all concerned. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee would like the Ministry to ensure effective coordination among the 
Central Line Ministries, State Governments/ State Maritime Boards and SPVs for 
implementation of projects earmarked under the Sagarmala Programme and constitute a 
Committee to encourage convergence at Central and State level and also to sort out various 
inter-Ministerial issues at the Central level as well as the issues with the States and other 
stakeholders. Since there is a huge difference between the projected demand and all ocated 
funds, the Committee would advise the Ministry to implement effective measures to 

3 
  
optimally utilize the allocated resources instead of keeping a vast chunk of its resources 
locked up and surrender them towards the end of financial year.  
                  (Para 11) 
Reply of Ministry 
2.1 The recommendation of the Committee has been noted. 
2.2 It is mentioned that as per Cabinet mandate a National Sagarmala Apex Committee 
(NSAC) has been constituted for overall policy guidance and high level coordinati on, and to 
review various aspects of planning and implementation of the plan and projects. 
2.3 A Sagarmala Coordination and Steering Committee (SCSC) was constituted under the 
chairmanship of the Cabinet Secretary with Port, Shipping & Waterways (formally Ministry 
of Shipping), Road Transport and Highways, Tourism, Defence, Home Affairs, Environment, 
Forest & Climate Change, Department of Revenue, Expenditure, Industrial Policy and 
Promotion, Chairman, Railway Board and CEO, NITI Aayog as members. 
2.4 Three meetings conducted under the chairmanship of the Cabinet Secretary dated 1 st 
October 2015, 4 th April 2016 and 25 th November 2016. As recommended in 3 rd meeting of 
SCSC, major responsibilities related to projects identified in NPP and Master Planning of 
Major Ports were allocated to MoPSW. 
2.5 It is also informed that Maritime States Development Committee (MSDC) is an apex 
advisory body for the development of the Maritime sector and aims to ensure integrated 
development of Major and non -Major Ports. The MSD C was constituted in May, 1997 to 
assess in consultation with State Governments, the future development of existing and new 
minor ports by the respective maritime States either directly or through captive users and 
private participation. Further, MSDC also  monitor the development of minor ports, captive 
ports and private ports in the Maritime States with a view to ensure their integrated 
development with Major Ports and to assess the requirements of other infrastructure 
requirements like roads/rail/IWT and make suitable recommendations to the concerned 
Ministers. 
2.6 The MSDC is a platform which gives an opportunity for deliberating upon steps and 
measures for creating a synergy between the Major Ports & Minor Ports. Besides, the Major 
Ports, the Non-Major Ports have an essential role to play in the Maritime trade. 

4 
  
ANALYSIS OF ANNUAL PLAN 2020-21 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee after taking note of the variations between Budget Estimates, Revised 
Estimates and Actual Expenditure had, in its 279 th Report on Demands for Grants (2020 -21) 
of Ministry of Shipping, desired the Ministry to be realistic in its projection of fund 
requirements and exercise due diligence in its Budget formulation after proper assessment 
and planning. The Committee, is theref ore, constrained to note the failure of the Ministry to 
fully utilize the budgeted funds under various heads during 2020 -21. For instance, Rs 211.00 
crores were allocated at the stage of BE 2020 -21 under the head “Sagarmala Schemes and 
Projects” which got reduced to Rs 96.69 crores at the RE stage whereas the actual 
expenditure incurred till 05.02.2021 is only Rs 74.92 crores. Similarly, ship building which is 
an essential arm of the Shipping sector witnessed reduction in allocation under the head 
“Assistance to Ship Building, Research and 71 Development” from BE of Rs 151.00 crores 
to Rs.129.30 crores at RE 2020 -21 stage and the actual expenditure till 5th February, 2021 
under the head is only Rs 103.62 crores which accounts for only 75% of allocated sum an d 
roughly 25% has remained unspent. Under the head “Grants to Inland Water Transport 
Authority of India”, a sum of Rs 301.80 crores was proposed in BE 2020 -21, which got 
reduced to Rs 203.20 crores at the RE stage. However, the Ministry was able to spend o nly 
Rs 146.45 crores till 05.02.2021. All this clearly reflects the poor financial management on 
the part of the Ministry. The Committee apprehends the same trend this year also , which will 
hamper the progress of some of the ongoing projects of ship buildi ng sector. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry should regularly track and monitor the progress of 
all the projects under various heads and address the bottlenecks arising during the 
implementation stage to ensure optimum utilization of t he allocated funds. The Committee 
also recommends that the Ministry should put in place a rigorous monitoring mechanism for 
the ongoing projects and ensure that the available resources for 2021 -22 are utilized more 
efficiently and execution of the projects  is done within the approved costs and designated 
timelines. The Committee also implores upon the Ministry to undertake a thorough analysis 
of the persistent underutilization of the funds vis -à-vis the allocated funds and delineate the 
steps taken so far a nd to be taken in future to plug the gaps so as to minimize the variations 
between BE, RE and AE.       
                  (Para 15) 

5 
  
Reply of Ministry 
3.1 The recommendation of the Committee has been noted.                  
3.2 Budgetary Figures are projected to the Ministry of Finance based on the status of the 
projects furnished by the State Government /Major Ports, on the basis of projects where in -
principle approval has been conveyed by the Ministry and keeping in view the expected 
development of projects which are under consideration in the Ministry. 
3.3 For projects under Sagarmala Programme, MoPSW has also developed a new 
Management Information System  (MIS) tool that provides a platform for the proper 
monitoring and implementation of the Sagarma la projects. Phase I & II of MIS tool has gone 
LIVE. The Tool provides the access to nodal officials to create users for their specific 
organizations, provides specific permissions and assign the projects to them.  
3.4 Most of the stakeholders have been given login credentials to the MIS tool and they 
shall be required to update their respective projects directly on the MIS on a monthly basis 
and/or provide “No Update” declaration for projects where there has been no pro gress. An 
escalation matrix has  also been developed in order to maintain veracity of the information 
provided in the system and to ensure timely updation of the projects. 
3.5 Further, to efficiently monitor and track updations, bottlenecks and delays, 
SMS/Email integration has been unde rtaken which sends alerts & notifications seeking 
project proponents and MoPSW users for required information and updation. 
3.6 In addition to above, regular VCs, meeting s are being held with Implementing 
Agencies to track the development. 
3.7 In respect o f Sagarmala funded projects, around 10 projects are facing problems due 
to EC, CRZ, ASI, Forest Clearances etc. On the request of State Government/State Maritime 
Board, UT Administration, the matter is taken up with Central Line Ministries to resolve the 
issue and ensure smooth execution of project.                                                                              
i) Analysis of the under utilization of the funds vis-à-vis the allocated funds: 
The reduction in estimate at RE stage was due to dela ys in vessels construction and 
delivery due to COVID 19. The allocated amount, based on the RE provided in the 
financial year 2020-2021, was utilized to the maximum as detailed here. Para 15 notes 
that Rs. 103.62 crore is actual expenditure till 05 th February 2021. It is submitted that, 

6 
  
in addition to this, during the period between 6.02.21 and 31.03.21, the Directorate 
spent further around Rs. 25.66 Crore under the head “Assistance to Ship Building, 
Research and Development”. Therefore, out of Rs.129. 30 crores allocated under RE 
2020-21, the actual expenditure till 31.03.2021 under the said head comes to around 
Rs.129.28 crores, which accounts for more than 99.98% of the allocated sum in RE 
2020-21 and only about Rs. 2 lakhs had remained unspent. 
It may be noted that the Directorate has spent Rs. 49.98 Crore out of the allotted Rs. 
50 Crore for use by the Directorate towards the new SBFA scheme and the balance 
amount was spent at the Ministry level.  
ii) Steps to be taken in future to plug the gaps so a s to minimize the variations 
between BE, RE and AE: 
A quarterly and half yearly status will be obtained from shipyards towards the 
disbursement and will be provided to the Ministry. The status shall be based on the 
actual status of vessel's construction and the latest schedule for delivery of vessels. 
 
CARGO HANDLING CAPACITY  
Recommendation/Observation 
4.  The Committee is constrained to note that despite introduction of schemes/ 
programmes for the development and modernization of Major Ports, the figures of Cargo 
handling capacity has remained almost stagnant. The Committee apprehends that failure to 
adopt latest technologies from the best Ports of the world could be the reason behind poor 
cargo capacity. The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the M inistry should chalk out 
new plans/ policies based on the best practices adopted and applied by the American and 
European Ports in terms of handling cargo with latest technologies.   
(Para 24) 
Reply of Ministry 
4.1 The recommendation is noted. MoPSW has been working closely with all the Major 
Ports and taken numerous measures for development and modernization of Major Ports. All 
new terminals being developed on PPP basis are based on latest technologies. Multiple 
initiatives including infrastructural up-gradations, digitization and automation measures have 

7 
  
been at the core of transformation of India’s maritime trade ecosystem, through interventions 
focused on creating the right facilities to promote schemes like Direct Port Entry and Direct 
Port Delive ry, introduction of RFID container tracking system, Port Community System 
(PCS) aimed at seamlessly integrating all maritime trade related stakeholders on a single 
platform, deployment of additional scanners, and other reductions in time and cost and 
procedural simplifications. 
4.2 In a significant development, the Major Port Authorities Bill 2020 was passed in 
Rajya Sabha which will empower Major Ports to function with full autonomy and enable 
them to perform with much greater efficiency. It will also facilitate the modernization of the 
institutional framework of ports. 
4.3 In a notable move to drive India to the forefront of the Global Maritime Sector,

A.  The number of oil spill incidents that took place in the last five years: 03 (Three). 
B.    The details of the steps taken for prevention of the same: 
 Following are the steps in regards to prevention oil spills from ships: 
a. Annex 1 of MARPOL convention, to which India is party to, deals with Prevention 
of Pollution by Oil. The aforesaid convention, besides mandating the construction and 
operational requirement for ships to prevent pollution by oil, also specifies the 
requirements for emergency response in case of oil spill. Indian ships are surveyed at 
periodic intervals to ensure compliance with the requirement of the MARPOL 
Convention. 
b. In addition, to discourage operati on of sub -standard vessels in Indian water, Flag 
State Inspections (FSI) and Port State Control (PSC) Inspections of ships in Indian 
ports are carried out to ensure compliance of ships with applicable regulation, for 
prevention of pollution by oil. 
c. Nati onal response mechanism to deal with oil spill incidents has been prepared 
(NOS-DCP). 

23 
  
d. Merchant Shipping (Regulations of Entry of Ships into Ports, Anchorages and 
Offshore facilities) Rules, 2012 has provisions that require older vessels to conform to 
the standards of members of the Association of International Classification Societies 
and also all vessels calling at Indian  Ports are required to carry insurance against oil 
spills under Civil Liability    Convention and Limitation of Liability Convention et c, 
so that possibility of oil-spill from such vessel is minimized. 
e. Coast Guard has been designated as the nodal authority to combat oil spills in 
Indian waters. All major ports have also been equipped to handle minor oil spills in 
their waters. 
f. In ad dition, India is a member of International Oil Pollution Convention Funds 
(IOPC Funds) which provides compensation in the event of oil pollution if the amount 
of compensation exceeds the CLC/LLMC limits to deal with compensation matters in 
case of an oil-spill from certain types of oil.  
g. Further, 'Traffic separation scheme' have been promulgated in West coast of India, 
off Cochin and Lakshadweep islands, to avoid collisions of the vessels, which might 
lead to severe oil pollution cases.

PERFORMANCE OF PORTS 
Recommendation/Observation   
5. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry regarding the values of parameters of 
Average Turn-around time and Average Output Per Ship Berthday at Major Ports across the 
country. The Committee is not aware about its competitiveness when compared with oth er 
Ports of the world. The Committee is of the view that the performance of a Port is not solely 
dependent on these parameters but also on other factors such as manpower supply and regular 
supply chain. The Committee would urge the Ministry to develop an e fficient system which 
can address these inadequacies and also support seamless movement of cargo across all 
modes. The Ministry should emphasize all the Major and Minor Ports to enhance the 

32 
  
productivity and infrastructure to the level of best Ports in the world which will enable them 
to compete globally.           
(Para 36) 
Reply of Ministry 
5.1 Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways have been focussing on interventions 
which would streamline the EXIM process and help in reducing dwell time and transacti on 
costs at the Major Ports. Initiatives such as Direct Port Entry and Direct Port Delivery, and 
the Radio Frequency Identification system and Port Community System (PCS), were all 
aimed at reducing the time and cost of clearance of goods. 
 
5.2 One of the key measures towards EXIM procedure is Direct Port Entry (DPE) and 
Direct Port Delivery (DPD). The percentage of DPD has increased from 5.42% in April -2016 
to 61.19% in March, 2021. The facility of DPE is well received by trade and the percentage 
of containers cleared under DPE is 46.44% in financial year 2020-21. 
 
5.3 As far as the creation of paperless trading environment is concerned, major strides 
have been taken at the Major Ports towards the digitization of key EXIM processes. The PCS 
1x has digitized  processes such as Electronic Invoice (e -Invoice), Electronic Payment (e -
Payment) and Electronic Delivery Order (e -DO) for physical release of cargo by custodians. 
Further, the process of generation of electronic Bill of Lading (e -BL) and enabling the Lett er 
of Credit (LC) process to be conducted digitally have already been implemented in the PCS 
1x. Uploading of documents by the importers and exporters is done on e -SANCHIT (e -
Storage and Computerized Handling of Indirect Tax Documents) launched by CBIC. 
Electronic communication of Out of Charge (OOC), Bill of Entry and gate -pass to 
importers/customs brokers has been enabled in the Indian Customs EDI Gateway 
(ICEGATE). Further, the Radio Frequency Identification Device (RFID) solution has been 
implemented at  all Major Ports to enable seamless movement of traffic across port gates, 
including substantial reductions in documentation checks. All Major Ports have already 
implemented Radio Frequency Identification Device (RFID). Upgradation and integration 
with recent technologies- IoT, Blockchain to ease transaction and real time basis tracking has 
been envisaged in Maritime India Vision 2030. 
5.4 Moreover, to streamline the process of scanning and reduce the time for scanning and 
checking of containers, 8 Mobile X -ray Container Scanners (in addition to existing 4 X -ray 

33 
  
container scanners previously installed by customs) have been installed recently at various 
Major Ports. 
5.5 The aforementioned measures have had considerable positive impact in the trade 
ecosystem. Key operational metrics have displayed overall improvement in 2020 -21 as 
compared to 2019 -20. The overall average pre -berthing time (under port account) has 
reduced from 7.23 hours in April -March 2020 to 5.57 hours in April -March 2021. Further , 
overall average turnaround time (under port account) improved from 49.38 hours in April -
March 2020 to 46.69 hours in April-March 2021.

Recommendation/Observation 

36 
  
9. Dredging is used to remove the deposits percolated underwater for the purpose of 
clearing the water pathway for ships to pass, to create adequate space to construct important 
bridges, dykes and dams and to weed out silt, intoxicants and pollutants f rom the bottom of 
the water. Dredging being an integral part of shipping operations needs to be done on regular 
basis with effective end -results. The Committee appreciates the projects undertaken by the 
Ministry in this direction. Though the DCI is able to  meet around 80% of dredging activities 
of the Ports, i.e. 60 million cubic meters per annum, still there is a shortage of 20% to be met

Committee, therefore, urges the Min istry to take necessary steps to procure dredgers of 
higher hopper capacity at the earliest. 
         (Para 58) 
Reply of Ministry 
9.1 The Dredging Corporation of India (DCI) after studying the capacity of dredgers 
available and assessing the requirement of  additional dredger of higher hopper capacity, had 
decided to go for procurement of 12000m 3 TSHD dredgers to be constructed at Cochin 
Shipyard Limited., a PSU under the Ministry under the Atma Nirbhar Program. In the first 
phase, one dredger TSHD of 12000 cubic meters hooper capacity is planned to be built by 
2022-23, second by 2024 -25 and the procurement of third dredger would be taken up on the

9.2 The Ministry has also approved the proposal of the DCI for p rocurement of 12000 m3 
TSHD dredger under the Atma Nirbhar program to be constructed at Cochin Shipyard 
Limited (CSL) 
 
DREDGING ACTIVITIES  
Recommendation/Observation  
10. The Committee is of the view that Port development requires safe tidal windows for 
navigation, sufficient berthing space and depth and acceptable conditions for operations on 
the berth. The Committee suggests that the Ministry should adopt advanced dredging 
strategies such as maintaining local and regional sediment levels, recharging salt  marsh areas 
with fine grained dredging, beach recharge with sand and fine gravel dredging and habitat 
restoration/creation or ecological enhancement of Port structures. The Committee also wishes 

37 
  
to point out that the cost of maintenance of dredging varies  at each Port while the average 
cost is at around Rs. 10 crores, It is at the highest level at SMP Kolkata, Deendayal and 
JNPT. Suitable measures may be taken to reduce the same at these Ports.    
          (Para 62) 
Reply of Ministry  
10.1 Dredging work is undertaken by the Port based on the littoral drift and sedimentation 
pattern either during pre -monsoon or post -monsoon except SMP Kolkata, Cochin and 
Deendayal Port wherein due to the estuary/riverine port requires continuous dredging is 
required throughout the year. 
10.2 Dredging cost is dependent on the dredging volume and quantities vis-à-vis the 
haulage distance to dumping ground, therefore the dredging project cost varies between ports. 
10.3 The Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata is a riverine  port subjected to heavy 
siltation. The Deendayal Port located in creek is also subjected to heavy siltation by natural 
phenomena. The JNPT is subjected to heavy siltation in the channel due to littoral drift. 
Hence, the maintenance dredging with high volu me is necessary. However, the Ports are 
taking steps to bring down the cost of dredging. 
10.4 Dredging activities are governed by Environment clearance and all the dredging 
projects adhere to preservation of eco-system and ecology. 
10.5 The SMP Kolkata, De endayal Port and Jawaharlal Nehru Port have been adopting 
steps for reducing the dredging cost which are as follows :- 
i. Timely hydrographic survey of the channel, turning circle, basin etc., for 
identifying optimal dredging requirements; 
ii. Undertaking studies on the behavior of the channel for siltation erosion and other 
natural phenomenon; 
iii. Deployment of suitable dredgers with adequate hopper capacity for reducing the 
cost and time for the project; 
iv. To reuse the dredge material for various activities including beach nourishment, 
construction activities etc., where feasible, thus reducing the cost of dredging 
 
 SHIPBUILDING INDUSTRY  

38 
  
Recommendation/Observation  
11. The Committee welcomes the steps taken by the Ministry to promote shipbuilding 
industry. Rising glo bal trade and strong replacement demand boosted the prospects of the 
Indian shipbuilding industry in the recent past. It is a matter of satisfaction that from an 
industry dependent on government orders till late 90s, the Indian shipbuilding industry has 
turned export oriented focusing on the niche offshore segment. India is emerging as a major 
destination for the construction of offshore and oil industry ships, such as offshore supply 
vessels and anchor handling tugs. Though our country is able to build shi ps upto the capacity 
of 1 lakh 20 thousand tons, when compared with the global level, where the capacity is in the 
range of two and a half to three lakh tons, our capacity is far behind. This being the case, the 
Committee now feels that the Ministry should  focus on building large ships and chalk out 
policies for it, for, we have a natural advantage in terms of availability of low cost labour and 
skilled people. Moreover, India also enjoys a long coastline of around 8,000 km long with 
several deep water Port s serving as good locations for setting up shipyards. The Committee 
notes that one of the major challenges faced by the Indian Ship Owners/shipyards as 
intimated by the Ministry, is the availability of long -term finance at competitive rates. The 
Committee feels that this hampers the growth of Shipbuilding Industry which, of late, has 
been getting good export orders. The Committee, therefore, desires that this issue may be 
taken up with the Ministry of Finance on an urgent basis which will help in boosting o ur 
‘Atmanirbhar Bharat Programme’. 
                      (Para 70) 
Reply of Ministry 
11.1 Government of India vide Gazette Notification No. 112 dated April 13, 2016 has 
provided infrastructure status to shipyards. Infrastructure status would enable Indian 
shipyards to avail cheaper long -term source of capital and would enable the shipyards to 
reduce their cost disadvantage and invest in capacity expansion, thereby giving a boost to the 
Indian shipbuilding industry. Further, a proposal is under consideration wherein Sagarmala 
Development Company Limited would provide long -term finance at competitive rates to 
shipyards.

Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee observes that allocation made to the Ministry for FY 2021 -22 is 45 
percent less than the projected demand and the shortfall between the projected demand of Rs. 
3101.34 crore and the Budget Estimates of Rs. 1702.5 for the Ministry of Shipping is to the 
tune of Rs. 1398.95 crore, which is massive by any standards and is certain to have an 
adverse bearing on the implementation of various modernization projects of the Ministry. 
Major reduction has been effected under Sagarmala Schemes and Projects  and other schemes 
under Sagarmala in the Revenue section. The same is the case with Grants to Inland Water 
Transport Authority of India, D.G. Shipping and Kolkata Port Trust. This being the case, the 
Committee is convinced that it would be an insurmountab le task for the Ministry to 
efficiently run a flagship scheme like Sagarmala and other schemes under Sagarmala with 
this limited allocation and achieve goals envisaged under Sagarmala Scheme. The Committee 
further notes a steep cut in allocation to IWAI an d D.G. Shipping, the two important offices 
of the Ministry. The Committee apprehends that the working of these two offices may get 
hampered due to less allocation. The Committee further notes that on the capital expenditure 
of DG Shipping, against a sum of  Rs. 108.4 crore sought, only Rs. 25 crore has been 
allocated. The Ministry submitted that due to this inadequate allocation, the priority project of 
e-Governance will suffer. In this era of digital technology, where the Government has been 
emphasizing for moving towards digitization, less allocation to e -Governance project is not 
acceptable. The Committee observes that India has been emerging as a modern economy and 

42 
  
successive Governments have targeted to increase the economic growth at a high rate in a 
sustained manner. However, the COVID -19 pandemic has had a disruptive impact on the 
Indian economy and almost all the sectors have been adversely affected. The Committee is of 
the view that post -COVID, the economic growth of the country will come through Ind ia’s 
Port and shipping sector because Maritime Transport is a critical infrastructure for the 
economic growth as 95% of the country’s trade by volume and 68% by value is moved 
through Maritime Transport and the ports and shipping sector is, thus, a key dri ver of trade 
for India. Keeping all the above facts  in view, the Committee is of the considered opinion 
that the outlay of Rs. 1702.35 crore would not be sufficient to meet the fund requirements of 
the Ministry during 2021 -22. The Committee, therefore, re commends that the Ministry 
should once again assess its financial requirements realistically and thereafter, move the 
Ministry of Finance for augmentation of financial resources for it for 2021 -22 at RE stage. 
The Committee also recommends that the Ministr y of Finance should have a re -look at the 
allocation made for the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways and revise it upwa rdly at 
the RE 2021-22 stage.

DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (2021-22) OF THE MINISTRY 
Realizing the fact that our ports and shipping sector is a key driver of trade for our 
country and that the Sagarmala Programme has been instituted to improve India’s 
maritime transport infrastructure and boost its export competitiveness and 
simultaneously appreciating the fiscal constraints f aced by the Government due to 
deceleration in economic growth in the wake of Covid -19 pandemic induced lockdowns, 
the Committee while making its recommendation in Para 5 of its 290 th Report had 
expected the Ministry to exercise more prudence in its budget formulation and move the 
Ministry of Finance for enhancement of funds at the R.E. 2021 -22 stage for maritime 
transport infrastructure and e -governance projects by drawing a roadmap with 
detailed explanation. Therefore, merely informing that the Committee’s  
recommendation has been “noted for necessary compliance” is not sufficient. The 
Committee feels that the notable reduction in allocation made at B.E. 2021 -22 stage, in 
comparison to that at the B.E. 2020 -21 stage, coupled with the drastic cut in the 
budgetary allocation of the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways at the R.E. 
2020-21 stage, must have had a significant adverse impact on the various schemes/plans 
made by the Ministry for the FY 2021 -22. The Committee would, therefore, like to 
know the al location made to the Ministry at the R.E. 2021 -22 stage. In case no 
significant budgetary enhancement has been made, the Committee may be apprised of 
the reasons, if any, given for the same by the Ministry of Finance. The Committee 

67 
  
would also like to know the steps taken by the Ministry to exercise due diligence in its 
budget formulation taking into account objectively its needs as well as its capabilities to 
utilize the budgeted funds.  
(Para 1.2) 
 
PORT CAPACITY  
The Committee while making its recommendati on in Para 17 of its 290 th Report had 
inter alia intended that the Ministry should pay more attention to improvement of port 
productivity and port operations through modernization of port infrastructure and 
adoption of sophisticated technology. Instead of dwelling upon the measures taken in 
this regard, the Ministry seems to have washed its hands off the matter by stating that 
Non-Major Ports are under the control of State Maritime Boards or State 
Governments. The Committee observes that India has not been able to reap the full 
potential of its port and shipping sector which is evident from the fact that the 
contribution of this sector to our GDP is just 1%. The Committee, therefore, desires to 
be apprised of the policy measures initiated to overcome structural and organizational 
impediments to increase port production and productivity. Considering the fact that the 
number of Minor Ports in the country is more than 200 and therefore, their role in the 
overall Shipping sector is indispensible, the Committee is of the view that the Ministry 
of Ports, Shipping and Waterways should encourage the Major Ports across the country 
to lend technical assistance and expertise to the regional Minor Ports in order to help 
them expand at a faster pace.  
(Para 2.3) 
 

68 
  
 
The Committee notes with great concern that a lot of rai l and road port connectivity 
projects face huge delays in completion, thus causing significant adverse impact on the 
Average TRT. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should 
strongly pursue the matter with the concerned Ministries/Departm ents and hold 
regular meetings with them in this regard to ensure that these connectivity projects are 
completed within a reasonable timeframe. The Committee also desires to know whether 
Ministry of Railways, in coordination with Ministry of Ports, Shippin g and Waterways, 
has undertaken any PPP policy measures in Railway infrastructure in order to attract 
private sector participation in rail connectivity projects. 
(Para 3.3) 
DEVELOPMENT AND MODERNIZATION OF PORTS  
The Committee feels that having essential equipments available at the Major Ports, 
along with trained personnel to operate them, is a precursor to improve the overall 
efficacy of the service delivery at the respective Ports and effectively, the output of t he 
Shipping sector in our country. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that 
the Ministry may take concrete action to ensure that essential equipments such as X -
Ray Container Scanners, are made available at all Major Ports without any further 
delay.  
(Para 4.4) 
 
 
CONNECTIVITY TO PORTS  

69 
  
The Committee takes note of the various steps taken by the Ministry to work in close 
coordination with Ministry of Road Transport and Highways to improve road 
connectivity at Ports across the country. The Committee h owever notes that the 
Ministry has not furnished any information regarding the inclusion of the requirement 
of linkage roads for upcoming ports, in the master plan for communicating the same to 
NHAI. The Committee desires to be apprised of the action taken  by the Ministry in this 
regard.  
(Para 5.4) 
 
SAGARMALA 
The Committee is dismayed to note that the Ministry could release only Rs. 10 crores 
out of the Rs. 90 crores earmarked for the project Development of National Maritime 
Heritage Complex due to delay in finalization of the complex structure, which, the 
Committee apprehends, may result in cost escalation and time overrun in the project. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should take corrective action 
to expedite execution of National Maritime Heritage Complex within the approved cost. 
The Committee further recommends that the Ministry should implore upon the various 
State Maritime Boards to strive to make full utilization of the assistance being granted 
to them by the Ministry and tak e steps to remove impediments like delays in tendering, 
and forest/ environment/ wildlife clearances, because in a resource -constrained country 
like ours, the Ministry should utilize the available scarce financial resources in most 
optimal manner.  
(Para 6.6) 
 

70 
  
 
The Committee notes that presently, 802 projects worth Rs. 5.53 lakh crores have been 
proposed for implementation under the Sagarmala Programme by 2035. The 
Committee observes that though the Ministry, in its reply, has submitted that all 
projects un der implementation will be monitored for their completion, no specific 
timeframe has been provided for each project. The Committee, therefore, desires to be 
kept apprised of the timeframe set for execution for each project within the approved 
cost.  
(Para 7.5) 
The Sagarmala Programme being a flagship initiative of the Ministry, the prime 
objective of which is to promote port -led direct and indirect development along India’s 
7500 km long coastline, leading to industrialization and job creation. The projects 
under the Sagarmala Programme need lakhs of crores of funding. Given the fact that 
the Covid -19 pandemic’s economic fallout has impacted India’s macroeconomic 
landscape, the Committee desires to know whether the implementation of projects 
under Sagarmala are facing challenges in terms of mobilization of the investments in a 
timely manner and if so, the corrective measures taken to meet the requirement of 
funds for the projects under implementation.  
(Para 7.6) 
The Committee also recommends that the Ministry may put a strong coordination 
mechanism in place at the State level to iron out any bottlenecks being faced in the 
implementation of these projects and facilitate Sagarmala -related projects under the 
established principles of cooperative federalism. The Ministry should also formulate 

71 
  
detailed plans to ensure that the amount of investments required for these projects are 
made available, so as to avoid delays on account of lack of funding support.  
(Para 7.7) 
 
SHIPBUILDING INDUSTRY 
The Committee appreciates the technical collaborations and MoUs signed under 
International Cooperation, such as India Russia Inter -Governmental Agreement. The 
Committee, however, feels that the Ministry must make concerted efforts to s ign more 
such agreements and also effectively utilize local resources and expertise as well, by 
introduction of schemes/ programmes for training, research and development and 
introduction of modern technologies in the Shipbuilding sector in order to furthe r boost 
the growth of this sector in our country.  
(Para 8.3) 
 
DIRECTORATE GENERAL OF LIGHTHOUSES AND LIGHT SHIPS  
The Committee is happy to note that DGLL has established National Automatic Identification 
System Network in which 87 Lighthouses provide rad io linkage to vessels equipped with AIS. 
The Committee recommends that DGLL may strive to install this technology at the remaining 
and upcoming Lighthouses in the country in order to further boost the coastal security of the 
country and further to aid search and rescue operations in the regions nearby such lighthouses.  
(Para 9.3) 
 
INLAND WATERWAYS AUTHORITY OF INDIA  

72 
  
The Committee agrees with the observations of the Ministry regarding IWT being more 
economical, less polluting and environment -friendly mode of transport, as compared to 
other modes of transport and therefore, for overall development of IWT Sector in the 
country, it is necessary that Governments at the Central and State levels simultaneously 
undertake development works. The Committee feels that  IWT’s present share is 2% of 
total transport scenario, which leaves a huge scope for promotion and growth of IWT as 
an alternate mode of transport in the country. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Ministry may develop a long-term vision to boost IWT in the country and come 
up with suitable policies and schemes to work towards this goal. The Committee also 
recommends that the connectivity of ports through IWT should be conceptualized by 
the concerned port and necessary investments made therein t o exploit the full potential 
of IWT.  
(Para 10.3) 
 
INDIAN MARITIME UNIVERSITY  
The Committee desires to be kept apprised of the updated status regarding the SFC -II 
Proposal for the Indian Maritime University.  
(Para 11.2) 
The Committee desires to be apprised about the specific action taken by the Ministry 
with regard to designing of training policies/ programmes for marine cadets/ trainees in 
consultation with industry experts.  
(Para 12.2) 
 
 

73 
  
MARITIME TRAINING  
The Committee feels that the existence of shortage of manpower at some of the Ports, 
while more than required manpower at certain other Ports, is a matter of grave concern 
and this issue needs to be urgently addressed. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that keeping  in view the dynamic changes in the port scenario and introduction of 
sophisticated port equipments, specific programmes may be designed for retraining and 
multi-skilling to facilitate redeployment of the surplus workforce, wherever it is needed.  
(Para 13.2) 
 
Mormugao Port Trust  
The Committee desires to know the reason behind the delay in acceptance of NHAI 
Technical Committee’s recommendation to accept all items of change of scope, by the 
SPV of Mormugao Port Road Co. Ltd. The Committee recommends that the Ministry 
may thrash out  the remaining long pending and unresolved issues in the Port 
Connectivity Project at Mormugao Port Trust, in close coordination with the involved 
organizations so as to ensure that the construction of Four -lane highway from 
Varunapuri Junction to Sada Jun ction and Flyover, which was originally scheduled for 
completion by 13 th October, 2018, does not face any further delays.  The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry and Mormugao Port Trust may request the State 
Government of Goa to finalize the Coastal Zon e Management Plan, so as to allow for 
capital dredging to be done when the requirement for the same is felt at the Mormugao 
Port.

CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
Airport Infrastructure  
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee notes that the aviation industry in India has witnessed tremendous 
amount of growth over the last decade as is eviden t from the fact that India’s domestic 
passenger throughput has reached around 137 million in FY 2019 -20 from 61 million in FY 
2013-14 and international passenger traffic has reached 67 million in FY 2019 -20 from 47 
million in FY 2013 -14. Prior to the outbr eak of COVID -19 pandemic, the Indian civil 
aviation sector was growing at a CAGR of 14% and was among the fastest growing civil 
aviation sector in the world. Despite India being the world’s fastest growing aviation market, 
its airports are grappling with s erious capacity constraints because such a pace of growth 
has resulted in a strain on the aviation infrastructure, resulting in traffic congestions and 
delays at majority of the airports. If a high growth in civil aviation sector is to be sustained, 
it is imperative to augment and modernize India’s aviation infrastructure. The Committee 
notes with satisfaction that the AAI and private airport operators have envisaged a 
modernization and development plan with an estimated cost of ₹89,000 crore by 2024. The 
Committee urges the Ministry to make privacy a focus of the regulatory framework for the 
Ecosystem of Drones. 
(Para 7.5) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 Ministry of Civil Aviation has notified liberalized Drone Rules 2021 on 25 August 
2021. The Rules are based on  trust, self -certification and non -intrusive monitoring. The 
essential features include: 
a) Every drone, except for those meant for research, development and testing 
purposes, is required to be registered and should have a Unique Identification Number 
(UIN). 
b) An airspace map of the country segregating the entire airspace into red, yellow 
and green zones is available on the digital sky platform. Operation of drones in red and 
yellow zones is subject to the approval of Central Government and Airports Au thority 
of India (AAI) respectively. No approval is required for operation of drones in green 
zones. 
c) The State Government, the Union Territory Administration and Law 
enforcement agencies have been empowered under the Rules to declare a temporary red 
zone for a specified period. 

3 
 
d) Drones are required to have the necessary type certification issued by 
Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA). No type certification is however 
required in case of nano drones (up to 250 gram all -up weight) and model drones made 
for research and recreation purpose. 
e) The owner and operators of drones are required to furnish the necessary 
personal details including their Indian passport number etc. for issuance of any 
registration or licence. 
f) Rule 17 of the Drone Rules, 2021, lays down the provision of transfer of drone 
to another person by way of sale, lease, gift or any other mode, after providing requisite 
details of the transferor, transferee and unique identification number of the drone on the 
digital sky platform along with the applicable fees. 
g) Drone operations that violate the provisions of the Drone Rules, 2021 are 
punishable under Rule 49 of the Drone Rules, 2021 as well as provisions of any other 
law, for the time being in force. 
Recommendation/Observation  
2. The Committee urges upon the Ministry to develop a comprehensive, strategic and 
futuristic Master Plan for implementation of projects to provide world class airport 
infrastructure, by bringing in cutting edge technology and the global best practices o f the 
aviation industry, so as to encourage growth in passenger and cargo traffic and catapult 
India into the league of top aviation markets within a period of 5 years. The Committee 
would like the Ministry to address not only the existing capacity constra ints in various 
airports, but also address infrastructural requirements in the context of growth scenario 
forecast for the coming years. It should be strictly ensured that the development/ upgradation 
of airport projects are completed as per the prescribed timelines. 
(Para 7.6) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 All Airports are being comprehensively planned and developed considering long term 
forecast.  Accordingly, land is earmarked / additional land is requested from State 
Government based on long -term futuristic development of single runway or parallel runway 
configurations and the type of aircraft expected to operate in future considering the potential 
of traffic it will be handling.  Due to the dynamic nature of development, the Master Plans are 
reviewed regularly based on the revised growth forecast. The expansion of development of 
infrastructure facilities at the airports is a continuous process and is undertaken on the 
operational requirements for safety of aircraft operation and demand from airlines, dependi ng 
upon availability of land and viability, as well as other facilities with reference to intended 
aircraft operations. To create additional capacity, work is in progress at Goa, Port Blair, 
Agartala, Guwahati, Chennai, Lucknow, Dehradun, Leh, Trichy, Pune , Patna, Darbhanga 
(CE), Kolhapur, Bareilly (CE), Jabalpur, Surat, Adampur (CE), Kanpur (CE), Bhubaneshwar, 
Vijayawada etc.  Work is in planning stage at Jaipur, Srinagar, Agra, Indore, Ahmedabad, 

4 
 
Bihta (CE), Bhubaneshwar, Varanasi etc. AAI is not just building new Greenfield airports but 
is also upgrading its airside infrastructure with works like runway extension, strengthening 
and resurfacing of runways, construction of parallel taxiways, rapid exit taxiways, ATC 
Tower cum Technical block, setting up adequate ground installations like Instrument Landing 
System (ILS), DVOR, ASR/MSSR etc.418 additional parking bays are planned at various 
airports in next five years for night parking of new aircrafts being purchased by airline 
operators.  The list of additio nal parking bays (proposed / under construction) is enclosed as 
Annexure A. Route optimization, CDO (Continuous Descent Operation), Upper Airspace 
harmonization, ATM Automation, Flexible Use of Airspace, R&D, Telecommunication 
Infrastructure upgradation, A utomation system backup, Remote Tower and alternate towers, 
Procurement of aircraft for FIU, Replacement of CNS facilities, etc. are other initiates which 
are taken up at airports for making these upto date. 
Recommendation/Observation  
3. The Committee als o urges the Ministry to ensure that adequate parking space and 
slots are available at the airports. The Committee notes that potential growth in the 
passenger and cargo traffic would require enormous investments in terms of construction of 
new airports and  expansion and modernization of existing airports. Given the risks, lenders 
are cautious about issuing long -term debt to airport operators. The Committee, therefore, 
would like the Ministry to formulate necessary policies, schemes and guidelines, to attrac t 
much needed investment for airport projects so that the way for raising resources towards 
funding the development, modernization and upgradation plans of airports could be paved 
and multiple funding option including external commercial borrowing, capital  markets long-
term borrowing etc. could be explored. 
(Para 7.7) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 All Airports are being comprehensively planned and developed considering 30 years 
forecast. Accordingly, land is earmarked/ additional land is requested from State 
Governments based on long-term futuristic development of single runway or parallel runway 
configurations and the type of aircraft expected to operate in future considering the potential 
of traffic it will be handling. Due to the dynamic nature of development , the Master Plans are 
reviewed regularly based on the revised growth forecast. Based on the futuristic traffic 
projections adequate Aircraft parking bays and slots are created and planned at the airports, 
such that it would be able to meet all the future traffic demand. Around Rs.90,000 crores of 
investments are expected to be pumped into Civil Aviation Sector. To meet the demand, AAI 
has embarked upon a capital expenditure (CAPEX) plan of Rs. 25000 crores in next five 
years for development / modernization / up gradation of airport infrastructure projects of AAI 
airports in the country. 418 additional parking bays are planned at various AAI airports in 
next five years for night parking of new aircraft being purchased by airline operators. The 
remaining approximately Rs. 65,000 is being spent by the private sector. Big ticket projects 
like expansion of existing Delhi, Hyderabad and Bangaluru airports are being executed by 
private airport operators. Further, mega Greenfield airports such as Navi Mumbai, Mopa, 
Jewar, Dholera, Rajkot etc. are also under implementation. 

5 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
4. The Committee has been given to understand that large numbers of institutional 
clearances are required for airport projects, which lead to delays and cost escalation.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should set up a single-window clearance 
mechanism to facilitate institutional clearances for airport projects and ensure timely 
completion of such projects. 
(Para 8.1) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 For an y airport to be developed, activities relating to Air Traffic Services (ATS), 
security, customs and immigration are reserved for Central Government agencies. Provision 
of these services are governed by the policy to be laid down by the Central Government f rom 
time to time. These activities include Defence clearance, Air Traffic Services (ATS) 
Functions by AAI, issued by the Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) from time to time, 
Customs clearance from the Department of Revenue for provision of Custom services,  MHA 
Clearance for Immigration in case of an international airport, BCAS Clearance for security 
and IMD clearances for Airport Meteorological Services. MoCA has been signing MoUs 
with all the airport operators given under lease to private parties where the re is a provision to 
provide single window clearance for necessary clearances. Further, under the Greenfield 
Airports Policy of MoCA, clearances for new airport projects are granted by MoCA as a 
single window. Therefore, single-window clearance mechanism for airport projects is already 
in place. 
 
Regional Connectivity Scheme  
Recommendation/Observation  
5. The Committee urges upon the Ministry to closely and meticulously, monitor the 
implementation and impact of the UDAN Scheme and formulate plans and guidelines to 
ensure that the benefits of the Scheme actually reach the passengers, as per the spirit of the 
Scheme. 
(Para 9.7) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1. Noted. There is a well -structured monitoring system. A number of Committees have 
been set up at appropriate level to oversee the implementation and monitoring of the Scheme. 
Further, Ministry of Civil Aviation has been reviewing the Scheme in consultation with the 
stakeholders and appropriate course corrections are being taken. Robust institutional 
mechanism has been incorporated in the Scheme. A Steering Committee at the level of 
Secretary, Civil Aviation has been constituted for effective monitoring and c ourse correction. 
Airports Authority of India (AAI) has been designated as Implementing Agency. The 

6 
 
Implementing Agency has awarded 948 valid routes across the country. Out of these 948 
awarded routes, 403 routes have been operationalized involving 65 airp orts including 8 
heliports and 2 water aerodromes. 1,55,776 UDAN flights have taken off and 80.12 Lakh 
passengers till 14.11.2021 have flown under UDAN. Thus, the Scheme is successful in 
meeting its purpose.   
 
Air Cargo  
Recommendation/Observation  
6. The Committee notes that besides geographical location, India’s cargo industry has 
the advantage of a growing economy along with a population of 1.3 billion plus India’s 
impressive growth in international and domestic trade in the last decade. However, despit e 
tremendous potential, India’s total annual freight volumes stood at 3.33 MMT in fiscal 2019 -
20 and has not reached close to any one of the top three world -class airports, viz., Hong 
Kong, Memphis and Shanghai. The Committee is constrained to note that th e total air cargo 
throughput handled by all Indian airports put together is less than that handled by individual 
airports like Hong Kong, Memphis and Shanghai. It is, therefore, evidently clear that despite 
having all the ingredients to be one of the world’s air cargo hubs, India has not fully realized 
its potential in terms of air cargo. The Committee is of the view that inadequate 
infrastructure is a major bottleneck in developing the country’s air cargo sector. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should take effective steps to address the 
crippling infrastructure constraints by way of establishing dedicated cargo airports in the 
country and developing new airports with a focus on making them cargo hubs so that the 
Ministry’s ambitious cargo throughput target of 10 MMT by 2027 could be realized. 
(Para 12.6) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 The observations of Hon’ble Committee have been noted. In this regard, the following 
submissions are relevant: 
● Traffic restrictions in the Indian major cities  for movement of heavy vehicles to/fro 
Air Cargo Terminals also play a vital role in deciding the dwell time of import and 
export cargo processed through Air Cargo Terminals. 
● In Indian Customs scenario, majority of the consignments for import and export ar e 
subjected to Customs examination/inspection, whereas in the foreign Airports under 
reference, very few consignments are subjected for examination/inspection. 
● So far as the setting up of dedicated cargo airports is concerned, it may be noted that 
this option would be feasible if there is critical minimum level of cargo is available 
for air transportation. Presently, establishment of dedicated cargo airports in India is 
not feasible on account of following: 
⮚ Current tonnage handling capacity in India is alre ady around double the cargo 
presently handled at various terminals in India. 

7 
 
⮚ Bulk of air cargo handled in India as Belly cargo in passenger aircrafts 
whereas in other countries most of the cargo is transported in dedicated 
freighter aircraft. 
⮚ India has too few dedicated freighter aircraft as compared to other countries. 
⮚ There is less trans -shipment cargo handled in India as compared to other 
countries. 
● Hong Kong, Memphis and Shanghai model are different from India’s model as they 
are primarily Trans-shipment based Air Cargo Terminals.   
 
Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) prices and aviation taxes 
Recommendation/Observation  
7. The Committee takes serious note of the high ATF prices prevailing in the country 
which is further aggravated by high taxes such as customs  duty, excise duty, sale/State tax, 
Value Added Tax (VAT) levied thereon. The Committee has been given to understand that the 
cost of ATF nearly forms 40% of the total operating cost of airlines and impacts the financial 
viability of their operations and h urts their competitiveness because Indian carriers are 
unable to compete against their global counterparts on account of the exorbitantly higher 
prices of ATF. The Committee is constrained to note that ATF prices in the country are 
distorted because it is subjected to multiple taxes by different Government entities. The 
airline industry is capital -intensive and works on very thin profit margins. This is why most 
Indian carriers are reeling under losses despite tremendous growth in air traffic. Therefore, 
relief on ATF is crucial for the viability of airline industry and would be a major incentive for 
airlines to augment their operations. 
(Para 16.5) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1. The observations of the Hon’ble Committee are absolutely valid. It is, however, 
submitted that the taxation issues come within the purview of Ministry of Finance (MoF). 
Ministry of Civil Aviation has on its part requested MoF, on multiple occasions to bring ATF 
under the ambit of GST. Most recently, vide Hon’ble Minister of Civil Aviatio n’s (HMCA) 
D.O. letter dated 12/10/2021, also our request has been reiterated to MoF. Meanwhile, we are 
also advocating with MoF and State Governments to reduce Central Excise Duty and VAT 
respectively which will provide much needed relief for the sector. 
Recommendation/Observation  
8. The Committee is of the opinion that ATF is a small component of overall petroleum 
products and hence, deserves to be treated separately. The Committee notes that despite ATF

Force to cull out those activities related to navigation and landing facilities which are,

Airport Infrastructure  
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee has been given to understand that there is a need to look at the entire 
structure of airports and the way the airport concessions are given. At present, the rights to 
operate airports are given to individuals or entities who bid the highest with the Airports 
Authority of India. When those services are given to the highest bidder, the highest bidder 
charges the highest amount of money from the airlines, which has little or no bearing on the 
actual cost of the service. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should 
look into these issues and take urgent steps to ensure that such anomalies and structural 
problems are rectified in the interest of the aviation sector. 
(Para 8) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 Airports Economic Regulatory Authority of India (AERA),an autonomous tariff 
regulator formed under an Act of the Parliament, determines the aeronautical tariffs of major 
airport in accordance to AERA Act and AERA Guidelines issued  from time to time. The 
tariffs are not determined to recover the investments made but to maintain and operate the 
airport along with a reasonable return on investment. Therefore, a fair and transparent 
mechanism is in place to determine tariffs at major a irports. As such, the tariffs are not 
decided by the airport operator but by AERA.

change in the operations of Indian carriers. Further, Indian carriers are being a ctively

Recommendation/Observation  
11. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should take proactive steps to 
encourage Indian fi nancial institutions to enter into the aircraft leasing and financing 
business. The Committee urges upon the Ministry to examine the regulations existing in the 
country in this field, identify the bottlenecks and modify the regulations, as per the present

11.1 Coupled with strong demand fundamentals and high liquidity in aircraft financing, 
airlines in India are expanding their fleet.The buoyant demand for aircraft by Indian carriers

and regulatory changes have been provided through Union Budget 2020 -21 to create an 
enabling ecosystem for such activities in IFSC and to bring the IFSC in India at par with

from corporate tax for leasing units in IFSC. Further, a new tax regime introduced w.e.f. 1 
April 2020 makes Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) inapplicable to domestic companies. 
Similarly, MAT provisions would not apply to units in the IFSC. Also, exemption has been 
provided from corporate tax for a block -period of 10 years within the first 15 years for 
leasing units. In a significant development, licenses to conduct operations fr om GIFT -City 
Gujarat have been issued to 6 aircraft leasing entities with 3 applications under process.
