Recommendation/Observation  
13. Land acquisition is a major problem due to land scarcity and huge capital 
requirement. The Committee feels that there are many regional airports which can be 
developed by States on their own or in collaboration with the Airports Authority of India 
(AAI) and that the State Governments should explore the setting up of “no-frill airports”. 
(Para 20.3) 
Reply of the Ministry 
13.1 Government of India (GoI) has formulated a Greenfield Airports (G FA) Policy, 2008 
which provides guidelines, procedure and conditions for establishment of new Greenfield 
Airports in the country. As per Policy, an airport developer, including the State Government, 
willing to establish an airport is required to send a pro posal to the Ministry of Civil Aviation 
(MoCA). There is a 2-stage process for approval of the proposal i.e., 'Site Clearance' and 'In -
Principle' approval stage. In accordance with this policy, MoCA receives proposals from the 
State Governments or Airport Developers from time to time for establishment of airports. 
After due examination, the approval for development of a new Greenfield Airport is granted. 
The responsibility of implementation of airport project including funding of the project rests 
with the concerned airport developer. Generally, land for airport projects is provided by 
concerned State Government/ Union Territory (UT) Administration to AAI free of cost and 
free from all encumbrances. As per the AAI Act, in case a State Government wishes to 
facilitate setting up of the airport, it could provide the following incentives to an Airport 
Company: 
(a) land, concessional or otherwise; 

24 
 
(b) real estate development rights in and around the airports; 
(c) airport connectivity; rail, road; 
(d) fiscal incentives by way of exemptions from State taxes; and 
(e) any other assistance that the State Government deem fit. State Governments may 
evolve their respective policies for providing any or all of the aforesaid incentives to an 
Airport Company. If the sel ection of a private entity or JVC partner is to be made by the 
State Government or its entity it shall be done through open competitive bidding. While 
granting land and other benefits, the State Government may, if it deems fit, stipulate the 
rights and obl igations of the Airport Company as conditions of such grant. State 
Governments can also provide land to AAI for development of greenfield airports through 
concessions to be granted to private entities in accordance with the provisions of the AAI 
Act. State s may also provide any of the above concessions to AAI for facilitating the 
development of airports in their respective States. 
Recommendation/Observation  
14. The Committee understands that major airports find it difficult to allocate slots to 
regional airlines, which mostly fly turboprop aircraft that take longer to land and take off. 
This forces some of the regional airlines to depend on larger aircraft, which do not have 
adequate demand. The Committee is of the view that if the States tie up with the to urism 
boards and other tourism stakeholders and formulate packages in order to market potential 
tourist destinations under the RCS scheme, it would attract more passengers, thereby, 
enhancing the demand for air travel. 
(Para 20.4) 
Reply of the Ministry 
14.1 RCS-UDAN is market driven scheme. Interested airlines depending upon their 
assessment of demand on a particular route submit proposal at the time of bidding under 
UDAN. MoCA has been working in association with the Ministry of Tourism  (MoT) and 
offered t ourist destinations suggested by MoT under UDAN for bidding. To facilitate the 
allied sector of tourism, RCS -UDAN introduced the concept of Tourism RCS routes in 
collaboration with Ministry of Tourism. These were routes connecting airports in line with 
the aspirations of MoT to boost tourism and connect iconic tourist destinations. So far, 48 
Tourism RCS routes awarded to SAOs and out of these 48 tourism routes, 31 routes have 
been operationalized. Prominent tourist destinations viz. Dimapur, Agra, Bhopal, Bengaluru, 
Mysuru, Amritsar, Jaipur, Kolkata, Patna, Bhubaneswar, Varanasi, Rajamundri, 
Vishakhapatnam, Calicut, Delhi etc. have been connected under RCS.  MoCA has also been 
interacting with the MoT, tour operators and other stakeholders to promote tourism  
destinations and offering under bid.

Recommendation/Observation

security standards are adopted in the country. The Committee recommends that BCAS should 
take periodic steps  to ensure that the international best practices with respect to air safety

25.1 Director General, Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS) is designated by 
Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) as Appropriate Authority for development, 
implementation and maintenance of National Civil Aviation Security Programme of India in 
line with Annex 17 of Chicago Convention on International Civil Aviation. BCAS lays down 
AVSEC norms in accordance with ICAO (International Civil Aviation Organization) Annex -
17 for Airport Oper ators, Aircraft operators, Regulated Agents, Caterers, Ground Handling 
Agents, Central Industrial Security Force (CISF)/Aviation Security Group (ASG) and Airport

included the review of regulatory provisions, aviation security policies and 
programme and national level quality control documentation and records.

correspondence dated 17.09.2018 that “Your CAP has been carefully reviewed by the

1.4. Implementation of security rules and regulations is monitored by BCAS through

surveys and security tests to check professional efficiency and alertness of secu rity 
staff and mock exercises to test efficacy of contingency plan and operational 
preparedness.  

34

matters. 
25.2 Digi Yatra uses a central platform for identity management which is a  Mobile wallet-

Post-COVID scenario 
Recommendation/Observation  
27. The Committee is aware of the grim fact that the aviation sector has been hit hard by 
global economic slowdown and the COVID -19 pandemic. The Committee understands that 
the adverse effect of the COVID-19 pandemic, on the airlines operating in the country, which 
were already reeling under heavy losses, was unprecedented. The Committee takes note of 
the steps taken by the Ministry to tackle the pandemic. While acknowledging the resilience 
shown by the civil aviation sector in t he country during such trying times, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should envisage immediate and long term measures, to 
strengthen the civil aviation sector in the country and to enable its resurgence. 
 (Para 45.7) 
Reply of the Ministry 
27.1 a) The aviation sector in India has been affected due to severe disruption caused 
by the COVID -19 pandemic. The estimated losses incurred by airlines in India is around 
Rs.19,564/- crore and airports in India is around Rs. 5,116 crores in the financial year  2020-
21. 
b) Due to the outbreak of COVID 19, scheduled domestic operations were suspended 
w.e.f. 25.03.2020. These were subsequently resumed in a calibrated manner w.e.f. 25.05.2020 
with 33 percent of the capacity and fare capping (lower and upper limit o n different sector) to 
ensure that airlines do not charge excessive fare. Evaluating the emerging scenario of the 
Covid-19 pandemic, the capacity restrictions have been relaxed  w.e.f. 18.10.2021, and the 
domestic operations have been restored without any restrictions on the capacity deployed. 
c) The Government has taken several steps to strengthen the aviation industry keeping in 
view the safety and health of the passengers. Steps taken include: 
i. Adoption of Covid protocols, use of protective gear, contac t-less passenger handling 
processes like 100% online check -in, submission of self -declaration forms and self -baggage 
drop etc. 
ii. Benefits under Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) 3.0 extended to 
civil aviation sector. 
iii. Exclusive air-links or 'Air Bubbles' have been established with 31 countries. 
iv. AAI has taken up development of new airports and upgradation of existing airports at 
around Rs. 25,000 crores in the next 4 -5 years which includes expansion and modification of 

36 
 
existing termina ls, new terminals, expansion or strengthening of existing runways, aprons, 
Airport Navigation Services (ANS), control towers and technical blocks etc. 
v. Three Public Private Partnership (PPP) airports at Delhi, Hyderabad and Bengaluru 
have undertaken a ma jor expansion plan to approximately Rs. 30,000 Crores by 2025. 
Additionally, Rs. 36,000 Crores have been planned for investment in the development of new 
greenfield airports across the country under PPP mode. 
vi. Government of India (GoI) has accorded 'in -principle' approval for setting up of 21 
greenfield airports across the country. So far, eight greenfield airports namely, Sindhudurg 
and Shirdi in Maharashtra, Durgapur in West Bengal, Pakyong in Sikkim, Kannur in Kerala, 
Orvakal in Andhra Pradesh, Kalabu ragi in Karnataka and Kushinagar in Uttar Pradesh have 
been operationalized. 
vii. Under Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS), also known as the Ude Desh ka Aam 
Nagrik (UDAN) Scheme, as on 14 Dec 2021, 403 routes have commenced connecting 65 
unserved and underserved airports, including two water aerodromes and six heliports. 
viii. Goods and Services Tax (GST) rate has been reduced to 5% from 18% for domestic 
Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) services. 
ix. A conducive aircraft leasing and financing environment has been enabled.

28 in 2021. As a result, share of Indian carriers in international freighter movements 
increased from 2% to 19% over the last two years.

activities, which would be the result of increased air connectivity to the region.  The

needed relief and help, to the airline sector.

Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO)  
Recommendation/Observation  
8. The Committee observes that India has the potential to be an MRO hub due to 
locational advantage, growing aircraft fleet, low labour costs and the  natural talent to drive 
innovation. However, the country has not yet been able to fully exploit the opportunities 
available in this sector and a major deterrent for growth of the MRO industry is high 
taxation of MRO components. Aircraft MRO services are c ritical in aviation value chain and 
it would be of a huge loss for the country, if we do not tap the vast technical and skill base 
available in the country. The Committee takes note of the various steps taken by the Ministry 
to rationalize the tax regime f or MROs and promote MRO activities in the country. The 
Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry should give requisite focus on the issues 
presently faced in the MRO sector and remove the remaining policy distortions and address 
regulatory limitations to ensure that India evolves into a key international player in offering 
MRO facilities. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should take necessary steps to 
ensure that MRO workshops are set up in all the metro cities in the country, in order to 
attract international business. The Committee also emphasizes the need for enhanced 
collaboration between defence and civil MROs. 
 (Para 17.6) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 Investment decisions in any industry including MROs are dependent on various 
factors whic h include market forces and regulatory environment. Government has taken 
several measures for a more congenial regulatory environment. In September 2021, Ministry 
of Civil Aviation (MoCA) announced a new MRO policy, which includes leasing of land 
through open tenders and abolishing royalty charged by the Airport Authority of India (AAI) 
for the Maintenance Repair and Overhaul (MRO) business for ease of doing business and to 
provide further incentive to the sector. Other key measures undertaken for supportin g the 
growth of the Indian MRO sector include the following:  
(i) GST on MRO has been reduced from 18% to 5% with full Input Tax Credit from 1 
April 2020. 

47

(iv) Relaxed restriction on utilization of duty-free parts from one year to three years. 
(v) The Airports Authority of India (AAI) has come up with a business -friendly 
proposal for MRO with zero airport royalty charges and significantly rationalized 
land rentals for eight AAI airports (Begumpet, Bhopal, Chandigarh, Chennai, Delhi, 
Juhu, Kolkata and Tirupati). 
(vi) Stay of foreign aircraft for MRO in India permitted till co mpletion of MRO work or 
six months, whichever is earlier. 
(vii) Rules simplified for export of leased aircraft in complete or knocked -down 
conditions, opening up new opportunities in redelivery checks and aircraft 
component recycling.

11.1 Presently, out of the total Commercial Pilot License (CPL) issued by Directorate

pilots: 
a) Airports Authority of India (AAI) has, on 25 September 2020, come up with a 
liberalized Flying Training Organisations (FTO) policy wherein the concept of airport royalty 
(revenue share payment by FTOs to AAI) has been abolished and land rentals have been 
significantly rationalized. 
b) AAI has issued award letters on 31 May 2021 and 29 October 2021 for nine FTOs to 
be established at five airports at Belagavi (Karnataka), Jalgaon (Maharashtra), Kalaburagi 

51 
 
(Karnataka), Khajuraho (Madhya Pradesh) and Lilabari (Assam). Soft launch of two FTOs at 
Kalabuargi was done on 15 August 2021 under the liberalised policy. 
c) Directorate General of Civil Aviation  (DGCA) has introduced new Online On 
Demand Examination (OLODE) for the AME and flight crew (FC) candidates with effect 
from November 2021. These license examinations provide an opportunity to the candidates to 
choose date and time to appear in the examina tion as per his/her choice on the available slots 
of the examinations. 
d) DGCA has modified its regulations to empower Flying Instructors with the right to 
authorise flight operations at FTOs. This will help increase the flying hours and aircraft 
utilization at each FTO and lead to faster completion of the CPL requirements. 
e) India's largest flying academy - Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Uran Akademi (IGRUA) at 
Amethi (Uttar Pradesh) - has been permitted to carry out pilot training in Gondia 
(Maharashtra) and Kalaburagi (Karnataka) to enhance its flying hours and aircraft utilization, 
which get severely affected during winter months due to visibility issues. 
f) IGRUA has started operating on all weekends and holidays in order to enhance its 
flying hours. Other private FTOs are also encouraged to do so.

Cancellation charges 
Recommendation/Observation  
15. The Committee expresses its deep con cern that there is no uniformity in the 
cancellation charges levied by the airlines. The Committee emphasizes the need for 
rationalizing the cancellation charges and prescribing an upper limit of cancellation charges 
that can be collected from the passenge rs. The Committee reiterates its recommendation in 

55 
 
this regard, made in its 276th and 291st Reports, requiring the airlines to restrict not more 
than 50% of the base fare as cancellation charges. The tax and fuel surcharge collected 
should be refunded to the passengers on cancellation of tickets. The Committee hopes that the 
Ministry would be able to persuade the airlines for such rationalization in the interest of the 
passengers. 
(Para 39.2) 
Reply of the Ministry 
15.1 It is submitted that cancellation char ges are not regulated by the Government. With 
regard to cancellation charges are not more than 50% of base fire. However DGCA has issues 
Civil Aviation Requirements (CAR) SECTION 3 SERIES M Part 11 titled “Refund of 
Airlines Tickets to passengers of Public  transport undertakings” wherein the following 
provisions in respect of cancellation charge has been laid down as follows: 
● “Cancellation charges must be indicated at the time of booking.”  
● The airline shall refund all statutory taxes and user development fee (UDF)/ Passenger 
Service Fee (PSF) to the passengers in case of cancellation /non –utilisation of tickets 
/ no show this provision shall also be applicable for all type of fares offered including  
promos/ special fares and where the basic fare is non-refundable. 
● Under no circumferences, the airline or its agent shall levy cancellation charge more 
than the basic fare plus fuel surcharge. This will execute any charges levied by the 
travel agent, which have been fully disclosed at the time of booking, It s hall be the 
responsibility of the airline to ensure this through their contacts with travel 
agents/portals. 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
15.2  The Committee notes with concern the reply of the Ministry that cancellation 
charges are not regulated by Government, which has resulted in no uniformity in 
cancellation charges levied by different airlines. The Committee feels that it defies logic 
that flights of different airlines on a particular sector having the same starting and 
destination points, and wh ere the duration of the flight is also the same, should have 
different cancellation charges. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that 
there should be uniform cancellation charges across all airlines.

CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
 
DEVELOPMENT AND CONSERVATION OF MUSEUMS: CHALLENGES AND 
OPPORTUNITIES 
Recommendation/Observation 
 1. The Committee takes note of the steps taken by the Ministry for the upgradation of the 
security infrastructure, Reception Halls, Auditorium etc., with the latest technology. and 
desires that the betterment of the Galleries may be completed at all the Museu ms within a 
fixed timeframe. The Committee strongly recommends that the Museums in India should be 
adequately equipped with conservation labs, storage facilities, written and graphic records, 
documentation facilities, modern photography techniques etc. 
(Para 4.6)  
Reply of Ministry  
 
1.1 National Museum:  National Museum has recently upgraded reception area, CCTV 
infrastructure and auditorium with latest technology. NM has also upgraded 6 halls with latest 
technology. Remaining galleries and storage spaces are being upgraded in phased manner. 
NM has also recently upgraded its Conservation Laboratory. NM has also created digital 
infrastructure for safekeeping on digital record.   
1.2 Indian Museum: - Indian Museum, Kolkata has made the following progress 
pertaining to the upgradation of security infrastructure –  
 CISF personnel have been deployed at the Indian Museum. 
 The Security Surveillance system is operational and is being upgraded further in phases 
within the limitations of fund availability. 
 Door Frame Metal Detectors and Hand Held Metal Detectors are being utilised for 
frisking of visitors. 
 For the convenience of visitors, online ticketing facility has been introduced. 
In addition, approval has been accorded by the Board of Trustees for construction of a new 
building to house modern storage facility of artefacts in the reserve collection of the Museum 
and for setting up of a state -of-the-art conservation and preservation laboratory.  This work 
has been initiated through CPWD.  
1.4 NCSM: - NCSM has 25 centres functioning in different parts of the country. Annual 
action plans are made for the upgradation/ modernization and addition of new galleries using 
latest digital display technolog ies. However, funds are required to take up such works in a 
phased manner. The Central Research & Training Laboratory in Kolkata , which provides 
catalytic support to several institutions in terms of display technologies , requires funds in a 
phase manner to enhance the R&D capability. 

3 
 
1.5 Allahabad Museum: - The security infrastructure of Allahabad Museum has been 
upgraded with round the clock CCTV monitoring. The Conservation Lab of Museum is 
functional and very efficient in functioning. All the record of Museum are being digitalised. 
1.6 Salar Jung Museum: - Salar Jung Museum is already equipped with Security 
Infrastructure, Auditorium and Lecture Halls with latest Audio/video technologies. Salar Jung 
Museum is also equipped with full fledged Conservation Lab and Photography Department, a 
Modern Library and Ma nuscript Library and Digitization equipment and adequate Storage 
facility for Reserve Collections. 
1.7 NGMA: - The National Gallery of Modern Art, New Delhi is already equipped with 
Security Infrastructure, Auditorium and Lecture Halls with latest Audio/vi deo technologies. 
NGMA, New Delhi is also equipped with full -fledged Conservation Lab.  An Art Reference 
Modern Library and Manuscript Library and Digitization equipment and adequate Storage  
facility for Reserve Collections. 
1.8 ASI:- ASI has its own Science branch which is well equipped with latest equipment/ 
technology. As and when required, antiquities from the museums under ASI are sent for 
preservation/ conservation. All museums under ASI have documented the antiquities in site 
museum documentation registers. These have also been digitized by the museum in -charges. 
Besides, most of the museums under ASI are well equipped with security instruments such as 
CCTV, burglar alarms, fire-fighting system, etc., along with manual frisking staff.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee notes the general view of the experts/stakeholders that the present 
state of museums under the Ministry leaves much to be desired. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may prepare action p lans in consultation with the best experts 
in this field, for each museum for the short -term as well as the long -term, and monitor the 
progress made to follow these plans. 
 
(Para 4.10)  
 Reply of Ministry  
 
2.1 Salar Jung Museum: - Action plans have been prepared by SJM for the Short term 
and Long term perspectives upto 2024. However, due to the Pandemic conditions, the action 
plans could not be moved. 
2.2 NGMA:- Action plans have been prepared by NGMA for the Short term and Long 
term perspectives upto 2024.   However, due to the Pandemic conditions, the action plans 
could not be moved. 
2.3 ASI:- Museums under ASI plan their annual works program considering various  
reforms mentioned in 14 points museum reforms such as security/ safety of antiquities, daily 
maintenance, better display techniques, change of textual panels, etc. The action plan 
prepared by the MOC in this regard will be strictly followed in ASI site museums. 

4 
 
 
Challenges:- 
Innovation and Design 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should come up with a robust 
monitoring mechanism to ensure that a comprehensive Museum Policy is in place and is put 
to implementation at each of the museum under it. 
(Para 4.11.4)  
Reply of Ministry  
3.1 A Programme Monitoring Cell has been constituted under the Chairmanship of 
Additional Secretary/Joint Secretary for effective implementation of the Schemes being 
administered by various Divisions of the Ministry. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee feels that once internal resources are raised, it would be easy for the 
Ministry to approach the Finance Ministry to supplement its efforts to complete any 
undertaken projects. 
(Para 4.11.5)  
Reply of Ministry  
4.1 Each museum under the Ministry of Culture is striving to raise the Internal Revenues 
wherever possible. 
 
Audience Engagement 
Recommendation/Observation 
5. The Ministry, in its written submission apprised the Committee about the installation 
of QR code based mechanism to allow interactivity in two of its Museums - National Museum, 
Delhi; Victoria Memorial, Kolkata. The Committee notes that QR codes provide link to a web 
page which will display an online map of the Museum so that visitors do not have trouble 
reaching any particular section of the Museum, showcasing the detailed history of the 
artefacts and interesting facts about the Museum. The Committee recommends the Ministry to 
introduce QR codes in all its Museums for an interactive experience which would especially 
appeal to young visitors. Making wifi available in every Museum would be crucial for 
ensuring an enriching experience for the visitors. 

5 
 
(Para 4.11.23)  
Reply of Ministry 
5.1 National Museum has already installed QR code based Audio Guides for more than 
200 objects. These QR codes are also available in NM Website for universal access. 
5.2 NGMA: Museum will implement and provide QR codes to visitors at entry point of 
Galleries.  
Museum will also make efforts for availability of Wi -fi. Mobile app/ Audio Guide based on 
QR Codes. 
5.3 NCSM: - QR codes for downloading information about the exhibition/  galleries/ 
facilities have been introduced in some of the centres under NCSM. Wi -Fi system to be 
provided subject to availability of funds.  
5.4 Other museums such as Indian Museum, Allahabad Museum & Salar Jung Museum 
are in process of implementing this.  
5.4 ASI:- Arrangements are being made to provide information on museums under ASI 
through the ‘Indian Heritage’ app. Museums under ASI are in secluded locations or in the 
monuments/ near monuments where provision of Wi -Fi is limited. Except for museums 
involving security reasons, Wi-Fi facilities are being provided in site museum/ monuments. 
 
Funding 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee further recommends that efforts may be made to encourage voluntary 
donations for the purpose of development and conservation of the Museum and its artefacts. 
This can be done by making the tickets pay -as-you-wish, setting a minimum price that  needs 
to be paid for an entry ticket and suggesting a higher amount to help the Museums generate 
funds for its operations. An option may also be provided to interested people to contribute 
towards the maintenance of any given artefact for a certain time p eriod. The possibility of 
providing special tours of Museums before and after public hours, by charging higher ticket 
prices may also be explored. The Committee suggests that Museums across India should look 
into the issue of charging higher fees to foreig n nationals and analyzing the possible impact 
of lowering the same on the footfall received and revenue generated by the Museums, 
targeting the maximization of both the footfall and the revenue.  
(Para 4.11.29)  
 Reply of Ministry 
6.1 Salar Jung Museum : Efforts will be made for voluntary donations and providing 
special tours for a group before and after Public hours by charging higher on entry tickets. 

6 
 
The foreign visitors to the Museum are very minimal. Hence, there may not be much 
variation in the revenue from Foreigners by reducing the price. 
6.2 Indian Museum : Indian Museum shall place this matter before the Finance 
Committee and Board of Trustees for further deliberations and recommendations of the 
Trustees. However it may be appropriate to place on  record that Indian Museum has already 
implemented higher entry fee for foreigners. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee is of the view that Museums may be encouraged to enter into 
partnerships with the private sector to sponsor their exhibitions, and also through 
contribution under Corporate Social Responsibility. The Committee understands that the 
condition of Indian Museums can be improved to a large extent if sufficient funds are made 
available. The Committee would also like the Ministry to look  into the administration, 
functioning and revenue models of successful international Museums in developing countries 
and emulate the best practices with modifications suiting to the Indian context. 
(Para 4.11.31) 
Reply of Ministry 
7.1 Indian Museum : Indian Museum shall place this matter before the Finance 
Committee and Board of Trustees for further deliberations and recommendations of the 
Trustees. 
7.2 NCSM: NCSM has collaborated with agencies including Science Museum Group 
London to fully support travellin g exhibition on “Superbugs: The End of Antibiotics?” and 
“Hunt for the Vaccine”. Private agencies are being approached for sponsorship and 
contributions under CSR. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
8. The Committee observes that out of the abovementioned grant of Rs. 72.51 crores 
under the Museum Grant Scheme from FY 2015 -16 to FY 2019 -20, Rs. 35 crores i.e. 48% of 
the total amount, has been allocated to just 2 States – Nagaland and Andhra Pradesh. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry should take steps to ensure equitable allocation of 
the financial aid to State Governments under the Museum Grants scheme. The Committee 
desires the Ministry to ask all States to submit their proposal for this scheme and ensure that 
at least one Museum gets this grant in each State. The Committee further recommends that 
the Ministry may allocate some funds to National Museums with the specific purpose to lend 
technical and conservational assistance to State controlled Museums, when needed.  
(Para 4.11.35) 

7 
 
Reply of Ministry 
8.1 The comments of the Committee have been noted. 
Safety and security of Museum artefacts 
Recommendation/Observation 
9. The Committee takes note of several media reports pointing out theft of antiquities 
and artefacts, involving the participation of organized international mafia, This, according to 
the Committee is a major cause of concern in safeguarding the artefacts in o ur country. The 
Committee underlined the need of security of artefacts deployed at the different National 
Museums across the country to ensure the safety of our valuable antiquities and artefacts. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may come up with a set of rules to 
ensure certain level of safety and security across all the National Museums. Needless to 
mention, installation of CCTV systems, armed personnel, burglar alarm systems, etc. in the 
museums are must and therefore the budgetary requirements, alongwith provisions thereof 
within strict timeline be made for compliance of security requirements. The Committee 
recommends the Ministry to explore the usage of blockchain technology for digital 
cataloguing of Museum artefacts, so as to mai ntain permanent, unalterable records of the 
artefacts. The Committee hopes that this would also deter the possible connivance of the 
Museum staff with organized art smuggling groups.  
(Para 4.11.37)  
 Reply of Ministry. 
9.1 National Museum:  NM has fully operational CCTV system and CISF security

31.1 As per Section 20E(1) of the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and 
Remains (Amendment and Validation) Act, 2010, the Regional Directors of Archaeological 
Survey of India (ASI) notified as the competent authority for preparation of Heritage bye -
laws, in consultation with Indian National Trust for Arts and Cultural Heritage (INTACH), or 
such other expert Heritage bodies as may be notified by the Central Government, shall 
prepare Heritage bye -laws in respect of each protected monument and protected ar ea. The 
roadblocks or constraining factors in the preparation of Heritage bye -laws of all the Centrally 
Protected Monuments and areas were discussed in detail during a meeting chaired by the 
Hon’ble Culture Minister (HCM) on 2 nd November, 2021. The decisio ns taken for 
overcoming these roadblocks or constraining factors given the volume of work involved, are 
detailed below:- 

20 
 
(i) Regional Directors are to be empowered with sufficient Manpower for preparing 
Heritage bye-laws: The Ministry is examining a proposal to provide additional Conservation 
Architects, Surveyors and Data Entry Operators (DEOs) to the Regional Directors, to be

(ii) Additional number of appropria te agencies/ institutions may be empanelled for 
preparation and consultations of Heritage bye -laws: The Ministry is examining a proposal 
for notifying all the Indian Institutes Technology (IITs), National Institutes of Technology 
(NITs) and Central Universities having Departments of Architecture or Archaeology or

Architectures (SPAs) , for notification as expert Heritage Bodies within the meaning of

Ministry is examining a proposal for fixing a standard rate payable to a notified expert 
Heritage body for preparation of Heritage bye -laws to cover the expenses of the institutions

(iv) Creation of posts of in -house Hindi Translators in National Monum ents Authority: A

the State Government or from the public for inclusion of a monument as Centrally 

67 
 
Protected Monument, ASI examines and approves the proposal, if it is found suitable. 
The Committee feels that the approach of State Governments towards protection and 
preservation of historical monuments is often lethargic  and therefore, ASI must also 
proactively consider taking up important historical monuments presently in neglected 
state of conservation, for inclusion in the list of Centrally Protected Monuments. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
24. The Committee recommends that ASI may take necessary steps to ensure well-planned 
illumination of historical monuments, wherever feasible, since the same would act as a major 
attraction for night -time tourism. The Committee further recommends that urgent steps may 
be taken to ensure that the ASI monuments are easily accessible by differently-abled visitors.  
(Para 5.8.35) 
Reply of Ministry 
24.1 The proposals of illumination of CPMs by ASI, received from State tourism 
departments/agencies are examined at ASI HQs level and based on feasibility, the proposals 
are approved. ASI also provided illumination in certain monuments. With regard to 
accessibility various measures such as tactile Pathways, ramps, wheelc hairs, Braille, films in 
sign language, toilets for differently abled are put in place.  
Further Recommendation/Observation 
24.2 The Committee recommends that ASI may analyze the  positive impact of 
illumination of monuments on the footfall received by such monuments and on the basis 
of the same, ASI may take a proactive approach towards illumination of more Centrally 
Protected Monuments across the country.

MONUMENTS 
Partnering with the private sector for development and conservation of Museums and 
archaeological sites 
Recommendation/Observation 
25. The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry has come up with the idea of 
identifying some start -ups, who will then incubate the idea and then put it out for main -
streaming of investment, in respect of iconic heritage structures identified in the cou ntry, by 
the Ministry. The Committee appreciates the proposal mooted by the Ministry to create a 
Section 8 company which will actually monitor and execute all these projects and it will be 
self-sustaining. No money will be provided by the Government. The company, for the purpose 

68 
 
of viability gap funding, will take some money from the Central Government which the 
Ministry already has for schematic assistance to the Museums.  
(Para 6.1.3) 
Reply of Ministry 
25.1 Earlier Development of Museum and Cultural Spaces (DMCS) was supposed to have 
been created as a Section 8 Company. However, the post of CEO, DMCS stands abolished

Further Recommendation/Observation 
25.2 The Committee desire s to be apprised of the reasons behind abolishing the post 
of CEO, DMCS and the fate of the proposals that were being worked upon by DMCS 
for development of Museums and Cultural Spaces. 
 
Re-examination and updation of Acts and Laws pertaining to Museums and 
Archaeological Sites 
Recommendation/Observation 
26. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may undertake an exhaustive review of 
the Indian Museum Act, 1910 and the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and 
Remains Act, 1958 and come up with s uitable amendments, in consultation with the Ministry 
of Law & Justice. The Committee further recommends that the blanket ban on construction 
works within the prohibited area of 100 meters around the monument, should be reviewed in 
consultation with expert s and stakeholders, and suitable amendments may be proposed to 
ensure a balance between developmental works and heritage conservation. It should be 
ensured that prohibitions are still in place against.  
(Para 6.3.9) 
Reply of Ministry 
26.1 Amendment in AMASR Act, 1958 is under process. Several workshops have been 
organized to consult the stake holders.  
Further Recommendation/Observation 
26.2 The Committee recommends that the Ministry may undertake review of the 
Indian Museum Act, 1910 in order to ensure that the legislation in place suffices the 
present day requirements for development of museums across the country. The 
Committee further reite rates its recommendation that the blanket ban on construction 
works within the prohibited area of 100 meters around all Centrally Protected 
Monuments, should be reviewed in consultation with experts and stakeholders.

69

the Ministry of Culture, the Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry may request 
that the re venue so generated should be allocated to the Ministry itself for the purpose of 
development and conservation of Museums and archaeological sites/monuments. This would

 the observations of the CAG Report,

INTEGRATED TOURISM DEVELOPMENT 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
 
4. The Committee observes that the tourism sector not only provides employment to wide 
spectrum of job seekers from the unskilled to the specialized but also makes significant 
contribution to the national e conomy by stimulating other economic factors through its 
backward and forward linkages. Since tourism is multi -sectoral activity and the related 
sector includes airlines, surface transport, hotels, basic infrastructure, etc, the growth of the 
sector cannot  be attained unless issues related to all these sectors are addressed 
simultaneously. The Committee notes from the information furnished by the Ministry that 
with a view to make India a 5 trillion dollar economy by 2024 -25, the SGoS Tourism Sector 
Plan aims at implementation of 21 tourism development projects over the next five years. The 
Committee is of the considered view that if the goal of becoming a 5 trillion dollar economy 
is to be achieved, the Government needs to fastrack the development of these 2 1 tourism 

6 
 
infrastructure projects in collaboration with all the Ministries/ entities concerned. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that convergence and synergy be created across 
programmes of Ministries/ Departments so that the implementation of these 21  tourism 
development projects could be expedited and an integrated development of enabling 
infrastructure through partnerships with all the stakeholders could be accomplished. The 
Committee desires to be kept apprised of the strategies adopted in this regard. 
(Para 31) 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
 
4.1 Ministry of Tourism works in close collaboration with Central Ministries/State 
Governments/various Stakeholders for the development of tourism in the country. Different 
mechanisms and strategies to seek synergy and  convergence with stakeholders for integrated 
development of enabling tourism infrastructure are: 
 
i. National & Regional Conference of State Tourism Ministers are held to discuss 
various issues related to the development of tourism sector in the country. 
ii. National Tourism Advisory Council serves as a ‘Think Tank’ of experts in the field 
of tourism and advises the Ministry on various tourism related issues. It includes 
representatives of various Union Ministries, Trade and Industry Associations and 
Individual Experts in the field of travel and tourism management.  
iii. The Inter -Ministerial Coordination Committee on Tourism Sector (IMCCTS) 
facilitates resolution of Inter -Ministerial issues involved in the development of 
tourism in the country.  
iv. A Task Force has been constituted under the Chairmanship of Secretary (Tourism), 
Govt. of India to address various issues related to tourism as per the 
recommendations of the Sectoral Groups of Secretaries (SGoS) for Tourism 
Sectoral Plan. The Task Force comprises representativ es from the Ministries of 
Civil Aviation, External Affairs, Home Affairs, Railways, Road T ransport & 
Highways, Culture, DoNER, Environment & Forests and IRCTC, ASI. 
 
4.2 Meetings/Consultations are held from time to time with various stakeholders to 
take suggestions/inputs for the development and promotion of tourism sector in the country.

Recommendation/ Observation 
 
17. Tourism is a multi -sectoral activity by multiple services and therefore, the tourism 
industry is one of the largest generators of employment across the world and has the 
potential to emerge as a key economic driver. Servicing the sector with skilled manpow er is 
therefore of utmost importance. The Committee takes note of the fact that the scheme of 
"Capacity Building for Service Providers" aims to train and upgrade manpower at every 
stratum of service. The Committee also notes that under the “Hunar se Rozgar  Tak” 
programme, 11,624 persons have been trained against the target of 19,250 during 2018 -19

23. The Committee observes that the tourism, travel and hospitality sector which has 
direct as well as multiplier effect on a host of sectors and contributes significantly to the  
national economy, has suffered unemployment and bankruptcies due to the COVID -19 
pandemic. Though the Government of India has undertaken various fiscal and relief 
measures under the Atmanirbhar Bharat to restore the growth momentum of the economy, 
these m easures have not been supplemented with sector specific credit measures for the 
tourism sector. The Committee notes that as per  the "Report of the Working Group on

Tourism" of the 12th Five Year Plan in India, the travel and tourism sector is estimated to 
create 78 jobs per million rupees of investment compared to 45 jobs in the manufacturing 
sector for similar investment. This critical sector is one of India's large st contributors to 
GDP. The sector which has huge potential to stimulate overall economic growth and can act 
as a catalyst for the recovery of the currently battered economy needs direct Government 
support by way of relief measures like a stimulus package,  rationalization of GST, liquidity 
support, etc.  
 
23.1 The Committee has been informed that governments across the world are undertaking 
measures to mitigate the impact of COVID -19 pandemic on this critical sector. For example, 
the United Kingdom has prov ided a 12 -month business tax rates holiday for all retail,

the consequent lockdowns have a crippling blow to the Indian tourism, travel and hospitality

targeted support to the sector. The Committee accordingly recommends that the Government 
should inject tourism sector -specific financial/monetary stimulus in the system and  offer 
immediate liquidity support and rationalization of the GST structure for the sector. The 
Committee observes, even at the cost of sounding repetitive, that such a critical sector 
contributing so much to the GDP and generating employment opportunities  should not be

Recommendation/ Observation 
 
3. The Committee takes note of the of the Ministry that the Public Private Partnership 
(PPP) model bas been explored for certain components of projects under the Swadesh 
Darshan Scheme and PRASHASD Schemes also have a provision to explore for PPP partner 
for operation, maintenance and sustenance of the facilities created. The Co mmittee observes 
that creation of quality infrastructure for developing tourist products and for providing better 
services to both domestic and international tourists is a pre -requisite not only to generate 
employment and achieve broad based and inclusive growth of the economy on a sustained 
basis, but also to have a favorable impact on the preservation of art, culture and heritage. 
However, projects like the SDS and PRASHAD have high social but an unacceptable 
commercial rate of return and are generally ch aracterised by long gestation periods, 
substantial investments, fixed returns due to which they require financial support from the 
Government through appropriate financial investments and incentives. Since the development 
of tourism infrastructure requires  very large investments and cannot be undertaken out of 
public financing alone, the engagement of the private sector in provisioning of tourism 
infrastructure under the SDS and PRASHAD is warranted. The Committee is of the firm view 
that the involvement of  the private sector will not only bring in the efficiencies of the private 
sector and commercial enterprise but will also go a long way in supplementing the scarce 
public sector resources vis -a-vis the requirements of bridging the infrastructure deficit. T he 
Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to meet the funding gap, make SDS and 
PRASHAD commercially viable and facilitate private sector efficiencies in the development 
of tourism infrastructure under the SDS and PRASHAD, the Ministry should formu late a 
transparent policy framework for participation of private operators in developing products 
such as hotels, resorts, convention centers, tourist trains, etc., with the Government acting as 
a facilitator and catalyst and also set up a Viability Gap Fu nding window for tourism 
infrastructure development under the SDS and PRASHAD.

Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee notes that Highway Safety has been given 35% weightage in NHAI’s 
parameters for assessment and ranking of National Highways. Number of accidents and 
deaths happening on the particular National Highway must be taken into account while 
calculating such scores. 
(Para 21) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1. As per the highway rating criteria for evaluation of Highway Safety scores, 4 marks 
have been allocated to Accidents per km per annum and 4 marks have been allocated to 
Accident Severity Index (fatalities per 100 accidents). 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
2. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may take steps to assign scores to all 
the National Highways projects, including the ones executed by State Government PWDs, 
after assessing their quality of construction. A central database may store the scores obtained 
by the different road projects of each concessionaire/contractor, which may be analyzed to 
ascertain the quality of work executed by all the concessionaires. Th e Committee 
recommends that the quality of previous works carried out by the concessionaires should also 
be a factor, besides the bid amount, during the awarding process of a road project tender. 
This would ensure that concessionaires that produce quality roads are not left out of having 
the opportunity to work on a project because of minor differences in bidding amounts. 
(Para 22) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1. Ministry has issued a letter no. RW/NH-33044/15/2021-S&R (P&P) dated 16.04.2021 
regarding Highways Rating Criteria and SOP for undivided carriageway upto 2 -Lane with 
paved shoulders on National Highways. Similarly, NHAI has prepared Highways Rating 
Criteria and SOP for undivided carriageways (four lanes and above) vide its letter 
NHAI/HO/Highways rating/2020 dated 07.07.2020. The rating shall be used to prioritize the 

3 
 
allocation of funds for improving/widening/strengthening different sections of NH on 
different elements of efficiency, safety and user services. The r ating shall also help in 
performance appraisal of deployed contractor/concessionaire/maintaining agency. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
3. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may consider breaking down big road 
projects into smaller chunks so as to attract the interest of the small contractors themselves. 
The Committee feels that provisions should be in place to ensure that there is a well -defined 
lower limit, below which bids for a road project would not be accepted. The Committee 
agrees with the ap prehension raised by the Member of the Committee regarding a likely hit 
on the quality of work that can be carried out by a contractor who bids substantially lower 
than the approved project cost. The Committee believes that such bids are made with the sole  
intent of winning the bid and more often than not, it would not be possible for such bidders to 
do quality work with such low bids. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry 
may lay even greater focus on arriving at accurate estimates for the  project cost for a given 
road project and specify an upper and lower limits within which bids can be placed. 
(Para 25) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1. The Ministry has been able to reduce the overall cost of development of highways 
through increasing competition by right -sizing of construction packages to ensure optimum 
competition during the bidding stage and refinement of eligibility criteria to promot e 
competition. For example, flagship corridors like Delhi Mumbai Expressway and Delhi 
Amritsar Katra Expressway have been segmented into packages of INR ~ 1,000 Cr which has 
made it accessible for upcoming firms. Combined with improvements to the model 
concession agreements the competitiveness of the overall sector has been improved 
significantly.  
3.2. The reduction in average project package sizes (~55 km before FY 17 to ~ 30 km 
currently) led to higher competition - average no. of bids from 5 – 7 in FY 2 0 to 15+ in Q4 
FY 21. This has led to higher discounts competition and increased average discount on EPC 
projects from 7% in FY 20 to 10% in FY 21. 
3.3. The Ministry adheres to the procurement guidelines set by the Ministry of Finance for 
procurement, bidd ing and awarding contracts. The authority is cognizant about such 
aggressive bidding practices by some contractors and has installed checks and balances to 
ensure that project completion is not hindered due to lack of financial resources required for 
the project. One such step is the mandating of the contractors and concessionaires to provide 
additional performance security in cases where significant discounted prices are quoted. 
Recommendation/Observation

their land is that the land is often their only source of livelihood. A mechanism may be 
worked out where an upfront payment is made to the land -owner and they are guaranteed a 
payment in the form of annuity f or the long-term, financing the same through the land value

13.1 Compensation is paid to the Land owners whose land is being acquired for

Resettlement ( RFCTLARR) Act, 2013. The land compensation includes Solatium @100% 
plus multiplication factor, additional market values and the compensation for trees and other 
assets. The compensation paid is substantially enhanced after implementation of RFCTLARR 
Act, 2013.

16. The Committee takes note of the discrepancies pointed out by the Punjab PWD in the 
value of land determined at present based on registered sale deed/ collector rates and the 
actual market rate of the land. The Comm ittee feels that such discrepancy, if present, would 
invariably cause dissatisfaction among the land owners and the ensuing delays on account of 
arbitration and legal procedures cost the public exchequer a lot of money due to project cost 
overruns. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may review the accuracy 
of the provisions existing at present in determining the amount of compensation to be paid to 
land-owners, as compared to the actual market value of the land. If substantial difference s 
are noticed in the compensation value and the market value in many instances, the Ministry 
may come up with a suitable mechanism for determination of a more fair value for the land to 
be acquired. 
(Para 94) 
Reply of the Ministry 
16.1 The compensation for the Land acquired for NH is determined in accordance with the 
First scheduled of the RFCTLARR ACT, 2013 with effect from 01.01.2015. As per Section 
26 of the RFCTLARR ACT, 2013, the market value of the land is determined as (a) the 
market value, if any specified in the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 for the registration of sale deed 
or agreement to sale, as the case may be, in the area where the land is situated; or (b) the 
average sale price for similar type of land situated in the nearest vil lage or nearest vicinity 
area. The average sale price refer to in clause (b) is determined by taken into account the sale 
deeds of the agreement to sale registered for similar type of area in the near village or near 
vicinity during the year immediately pr eceding the issue of notification under Section 3A of 
the NH Act, 1956. The higher rate arrived from (a) and (b) above is adopted for 
determination for compensation of land acquisition in NH Projects  
16.2 Hence, the value of land which is more beneficial to the land owner is paid to him/her. 
It is a matter of fact that the Circle rate of land is notified by concerned State Governments 
and this Ministry has no role in this regard. 
Recommendation/Observation

1. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may review the Model Concessionaire

challenges faced by the concessionaire/contractors in the current MCAs and reform relating 
to latest policies announced by the Government of India from time to time to fulfil the larger 
objective of creating a quality infrastructure in the country while taking into account the 
interests of all stakeholders. 
1.2. The necessary amendments are done in the MCA after discussion in the Inter -
Ministerial Committee comprising MoRTH, Department of Financial Services, Department

explained framework, Ministry has recently done amendments in MCAs of Bot (Toll), TOT,

2. The Committee takes note of the various stages involved in the execution of a National 
Highways Project. The Committee f eels that the Ministry must undertake a holistic review of 
the DPR preparation stage of road projects. Preparation of DPR should be aided by the 
latest technology available for the purpose and the inputs of the stakeholders and public 
representatives, incl uding the local M.P., and the demands and concerns of the local 
populace should be taken into account during the process of preparation of the DPR. The 
Committee desires that the Ministry may come up with Rules/ necessary statutory provisions 
to fix the ac countability of the officials/ organization responsible for drafting the DPR till a 
stipulated period of time after the completion of the project, for any negligence on their part, 
that results in construction of poor quality roads. Forethought may be give n at this stage to 
ensure ample provisions for road safety; mandatory service lanes; avoidance of traffic 
bottlenecks; and minimization of adverse environmental and heritage impact caused by the 
project. The Committee further recommends that traffic projections for the long-term must be 

25 
 
taken into account while preparing DPR for any road project and where feasible, additional 
land may be acquired adjacent to the alignment planned at present, so as to enable widening 
of the highways, when the widening of road is needed at a future date. 
(Para 15) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 The Ministry adopts technologies like LiDAR, Satellite imaging, automated traffic 
counting system while preparing the detailed project report of a project. These technologies 
enable the Ministry to optimize road alignment and minimize the environmental impact of the 
project. The Ministry is committed to using state of the art technologies for the preparation of 
DPRs. 
2.2 The Ministry is considering a check and balance mechanism to hold th e concerned 
parties accountable for any negligence on their part across any stage in the execution of the 
project.  
2.3 Road safety and passenger comfort are of paramount importance to the Ministry. 
Wayside amenities and service lanes are planned on key ro ad stretches while ensuring road 
safety measures across all its projects. In addition, advanced traffic management system is 
being mandated across National Highways to ensure superior safety standards and real time 
incident response.  
2.4 The Ministry take s into account the projected vehicular traffic during the 
conceptualization of any new project and for flagship greenfield corridors, acquisition of 
ROWs are planned keeping into account any future road widening/expansion. 
2.5 Starting from the conceptuali zation of a project, the Ministry ensures that the 
alignment is reviewed at the highest level to analyse the overall impact of the project – 
including the impact of land acquisition in displacement of population, the economic growth 
plans of the regions th at the alignment of the projects. Once the alignment is finalized by the 
Ministry, state level consultation is held with the respective state governments to ensure 
synergizing of highway network and other infrastructure network projects planned in the 
region. 
2.6 After the discussions are finalized with the state governments, an initial Land 
Acquisition Committee review of the alignment is conducted internally by the Ministry and 
approval is provided for initiating on -ground land acquisition process. Post t his, review of 
alignment and progress development is conducted across different levels during the internal 
project appraisal by Member of NHAI and senior officials of the Ministry. During the final 
approval of the project with the competent authority, inpu ts from external stakeholders like 
NITI Ayog are also sought to finalize the alignment and project features.  
2.7 In addition, the Project Directors and Regional Officers in NHAI have been 
empowered to suggest changes to alignment at the grass root level w ith inputs from local 
representatives and public. Beyond this, discussions with public are also held directly while 
obtaining environmental clearance wherein the details of the project are explained to the 

26 
 
public, representation from different sections of the society are solicited in the presence of the 
state and district administration officers.  
2.8 Hence, reviews are conducted at multiple levels to ensure that public representation 
and inputs are incorporated in the finalization of the project alignment,  well before the 
initiation of land acquisition process with continuous inputs received through the project 
implementation units and regional offices across the country

1. The Committee notes that the concessionaire is responsible for the Operation and 
Maintenance (O&M) of the road projects for the entire Concession Period (BOT (Toll) and 
BOT (Annuity) projects) or 15 years (HAM projects) in PPP projects, but in case of Public 
funded projects, the contractor is responsible for rectification of defects/ maintenance only 
during the defects/maintenance-cum-defects liability period which varies between one to four 
years. Since a large number of road projects are Public funded projects, especially the ones 
that are deemed not to be financially viable for private sector participation, the o nus of their 
maintenance falls on the Ministry/NHAI/State PWDs. In this regard, the Committee feels that 
the amount of funds allocated for the maintenance of National Highways every year is 
minuscule given the vast lengths of the National Highways across t he country. The 
Committee strongly recommends that the maintenance of the existing network of National

(Para 12)   
 Reply of Ministry 
1.1  Maintenance and Repair (M&R) of National Highways (NHs) is carried out for the 
stretches not covered under any programme or completed stretches where there are no 
liabilities of contractors to maintain such stretches. For the NH stretches developed on  EPC 
mode (Engineering, Procurement, Construction), the contractor is responsible for rectification 
of the defects and concurrent maintenance of project highway during the defect liability 
period after completion of the work. For the NH stretches developed  on BOT mode/ HAM, 
the Concessionaire is responsible for the maintenance of the project highway during the 
concession period. For some of the developed NH stretches through public funding, 
maintenance contracts have been taken up for a definite time period  (4 to 9 years) on 
Operation, Maintenance and Transfer (OMT) basis. Maintenance of the project highway 
under OMT contracts is the responsibility of the Concessionaire. 
1.2 For the remaining NH length, not covered under any programme, the Ministry 
allocates funds under for their M&R. Since inception of Bharatmala Pariyojana, Ministry is 
taking up more and more stretches under development and after development of these 
stretches, maintenance & operation is being done through contract, e.g. OMT, TOT etc. InvIT 
is also being initiated. Further, to overcome the shortfall in allocation under M&R head, the 
scheme of Periodical Repair/IRQP from Revenue Section (M&R) has been shifted to Capital 
Section (NH -O) w.e.f. 2021 -22. Hence, more fund is available for keeping the National

 (Para 16)

economic viability and environment sustainability.  
2.2    This is to inform that the existing National Highway Right of Way (ROW) varies 
from 12 -60 m and depending upon the availability of space in ROW, permissions to lay 
utilities in a width of 2 m on extreme edges of ROW are bei ng given. As the different 
agencies approach this Ministry for such permissions at different timelines, the utility space is 
utilized mostly in an unorganized manner. While developing the National Highways of 
standards to serve projected future traffic, th e additional ROW is being acquired to make a 
consistent ROW of 30 -60 m. For a 4 -lane divided carriageway development, 45 -60 m ROW 

59 
 
is maintained through acquisition while for a 2 -lane paved shoulder development ROW upto 
30 m is maintained. Further the Natio nal Highways passes through rural and urban areas and 
in some cases, ROWs are compromised in urban areas.  
2.3    The need of utility corridors may also be divided into two parts i.e.   long distance 
utilities viz. OFC, gas/oil pipelines etc. passing through rural areas and short distance utilities 
viz. power lines, drainage/ sewerage, water pipelines etc. needing urban space. There are also 
security/safety & operational issues related to par allel and close running of power & OFC 
lines, power & gas/oil pipelines etc. 
Another area of concerns is: - 
i. The economical viability - whether such ducts are compulsorily to be built 
along highways without actual assessment of need in the area, or to be bu ilt 
on the basis of need after getting requirements from various agencies and 
ii. Cost of such ducts - cost sharing of construction of ducts and required land to 
be acquired specifically for such utility corridor, investments & tariff, 
operation & maintenance cost etc. 
2.4    In order to get all the above issues examined and to have a draft Policy Note/SOP, it has 
been decided by Ministry to take consultancy services of Andhra Pradesh Urban 
Infrastructure Asset Management Limited (APUIAML). Necessary instructio ns have been 
given to NHAI on 25th September 2020 to engage APUIAML. The draft policy so prepared 
shall be shared with all stake holders before its finalization. Based on the finalized policy, the 
decision on creation of a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) for  the purpose of monetization of 
the utility corridors may be taken. 
2.5  In this connection, APUIAML has recently submitted an interim feasibility report for 
laying of integrated utility corridors along greenfield NHs.   
 Further Recommendation/Observation:

provisions for utility corridors and the decision regarding creation of a Special Purpose 
Vehicle for the purpose of monetization of the utility corridors, based on the finalized 
policy.

17) with central financial assistance of Rs.17.00 crore and land requirement of 10 acre. A

projects under SARDP -NE but given the huge delays that are currently faced in the 
programme, the Committee recommends that the Ministry may undertake a holistic 
review of the reasons for which the remedial efforts of the Ministry are not effective in 
resolving the delays being faced in SARDP-NE.  
(Para 22.2) 
  
 

101 
 
 The C ommittee feels that awarding road projects, especially in the North -East 
region, to the lowest bidder might be leading to below -par quality of roads being 
constructed, besides incapable concessionaires causing delays in road projects because 
of their financial and technical incapacities. T he Committee, therefore, reiterates its 
recommendation made in Para 26 of its 296 th Report, which is reproduced below 
verbatim: 
“The Committee further recommends the Ministry to carefully analyze the 
shortcomings of the existing mechanism for awarding road  projects to the lowest 
bidder, since doing so includes little thought for ensuring quality of the work. The 
Committee believes that there should be consideration for other importance factors 
besides the bidding amount, while awarding a project to a conces sionaire. A 
qualitative approach must be formulated for awarding road projects. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may take up with the Central Vigilance 
Commission (CVC), the shortcomings of the existing system of awarding a project 
to the lowest bidder, presenting its arguments for modification of the CVC 
guidelines for awarding of tender in a suitable way to permit an element of 
qualitative approach in the tender awarding process for road projects. The 
Committee feels that a criterion may be deve loped where certain weightage is given 
to objective parameters such as the awards presently being executed by the 
contractor, their financial record, and most importantly, the past performance of a 
contractor, in terms of quality of work and timely executi on. The database 
recommended by the Committee in para 22 of this Report may be useful for such 
purposes.” 
(Para 23.2) 
 
 The Committee recommends that the Ministry may lay special focus on timely 
completion of road projects in LWE affected areas in close co ordination with local law 
enforcement and other concerned departments.  
(Para 24.2) 
 
 The Committee may be apprised of the details of the various research activities 
that are being carried out by the SRD& Q Division of NHAI. The Committee further 
recommends that the Ministry may consider increasing the budget for research 
purposes in the upcoming years so as to allow research for improving construction 
quality in hilly and flood -prone regions, improving roa d safety across the country and 
developing a mechanism to effectively monitor the pliability of National Highways 
across the country so as to proactively prevent accidents from happening because of 
shoddy quality of roads.  
(Para 25.2) 
 
 The Committee notes the various steps being taken by the Ministry and the 
policy guidelines brought out by NHAI to improve road safety across the country but 
feels that given the ever-increasing number of deaths occurring due to road accidents in 
the country, a lot more  needs to be done urgently in order to minimize the same. The 

102 
 
Committee recommends that the Ministry/NHAI may review the safety audit process 
itself and ensure that the same is carried out in a transparent and honest manner. The 
Committee further recommend s that the identified black spots may be rectified at the 
earliest and the definition for identification of black spots may be tightened so as to 
identify and rectify more accident-prone spots across the NH network in the country.  
(Para 26.3) 
 
 The Committee recommends that the Ministry may speed up the process of 
rectification of black spots that have already been identified since these spots are very 
likely to cause more accidents if left unrectified. The status of all black spots may be 
kept regularly updated on the NHAI website and any delay in the rectification of black 
spots may be looked into urgently.  
(Para 27.3) 
 
 The Committee recommends that the tender for Computer Aided Dispatch 
System may be finalized at the earliest since providing timely emergency care during 
the golden hour can help save countless lives involved in road accidents across the 
country. The Committee desires to be kept apprised in this regard.   
(Para 28.2) 
 
 The Committee recommends that dedicated efforts may be made to promote the 
tollfree helpline number 1033 amongst highway users. The Committee may be apprised 
of the action taken by the Ministry to promote the usage of the number 1033 through 
social media and other means.  
(Para 29.2) 
 
 The Committee appreciates the  efforts of the Ministry to rope in the private 
sector by vesting Driving Training Centres with functions such as testing of aspirants 
for issuance of driving licence, which will hopefully make such centres a successful 
business proposition. Having well -trained drivers on the Indian roads would go a long 
way in improving road safety and aiming to have Driving Training Centres in all 
districts of the country would be the first step towards that. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry may cons ider providing some aid to the interested 
parties in terms of lending for setting up such Driving Training Centres, in 
collaboration with financial institutions.  
(Para 30.6) 
 
 The Committee recommends that latest safety standards adopted for vehicles 
globally, may be suitably incorporated in the Indian vehicle safety standards from time 
to time, so as to minimize the number of deaths occurring on Indian roads due to road 
accidents.  

103 
 
(Para 31.4) 
 
 The Committee hopes that the Ministry would be able to complete the remaining 
projects under the Char dham Pariyojana within the targeted date of completion of 
December, 2024. The Committee recommends that all possible measures may be taken 
from the planning stage itself to ensure that the road projects of the M inistry cause 
minimal impact on the environment, especially in eco -sensitive hilly regions. This would 
help lower the delays faced on account of Court litigations and petitions in the NGT.  
(Para 32.2) 
 
 The Committee reiterates its recommendation made in para 32.2 of  Chapter III 
of this Report.  
(Para 33.3) 
 
 The Committee notes the reply. The Committee further recommends that in 
future, such Rapid Environmental Impact Assessment may be proactively carried out 
by the Ministry for all of its major National Highways projects in ecologically sensitive 
regions.  
(Para 34.2) 
 
 The Committee may be apprised about the action taken by the Ministry in this 
regard.  
(Para 35.2) 
 
 The Committee notes the advisories put in place at present by the Ministry with 
regard to PUC centres. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may  consider 
incorporation of stricter guidelines in its advisory  in order to curb malpractices that 
allow polluting vehicles to pass the pollution test, by way of video recording when 
pollution tests are conducted.  
(Para 36.8) 
 
 The Committee recommends that NHAI may include the option to report 
requirement of maintenance of roadside plantations on National Highways, so that 
highway users can bring such requirement to the notice of NHAI for timely  action. 
Besides, NHAI may ensure that such maintenance activities are carried out periodically 
without fail, since overgrown trees and bushes can lead to visibility issues, which in turn 
can lead to lethal accidents.  
(Para 37.5) 
 

104 
 
 The Committee recommend s that guidelines similar to those that have been 
issued regarding construction of bridge structures passing over declared National 
Waterways, may be issued for construction of such bridge structures over other inland 
waterways as well. The guidelines in t his regard may be framed in close coordination 
with the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways and other concerned departments. 
The Committee feels that doing it is necessary to ensure the development of road 
infrastructure may not cause hindrance in us age of inland waterways as a means of 
transportation.  
(Para 38.2)
