REPORT  
 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Civil 
Aviation on the recommendations/observations as contained in its Two Hundred Ninety 
Seventh Report on the subject ‘Functioning of Airports Authority of India’ which was 
presented to both the Houses of Parliament on 2nd August, 2021.  
 
2.  The Action Taken Replies were received from the Ministry on 16th December, 2021 
in respect of all the observations/ recommendations contained in the Report. The repl ies have 
been categorized as follows:-  
 
Chapter-I: 
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Ministry: 
Paragraph Nos.:  9.8, 10.8, 10.9, 10.10, 10.12, 11.10, 11.11, 12.3, 12.7, 13.9, 18.5, 
18.6, 22.3, 30.12, 31.1 and 33.  
Total: 16 
 
Chapter-II:  
Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in 
view of the replies of the Ministry: 
Paragraph Nos.: 9.3, 9.7, 10.7, 10.11, 12.5.1, 12.6, 13.8, 13.10, 14.3, 15.1, 16.10, 
19.1, 21.4, 21.5, 21.6, 23.3, 24.4, 25.1, 26.2, 27.A.1 and 29.1. 
Total: 21 
 
Chapter-III: 
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Ministry have not 
been accepted by the Committee: 
Paragraph Nos.: 9.5, 9.6, 10.6, 11.12, 12.2, 12.4, 13.7, 14.2, 17.1, 21.3, 26.3, 27.5, 
28.1, 28.A.1 and 32.    
Total: 15 
 
Chapter-IV:  
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the final replies of the Ministry 
are still awaited: 
Paragraph Nos.: Nil  
Total: Nil 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

2 
 
 
CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
Air Traffic Services 
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee recommends that a High Powered Committee should be constituted 
both for flexi air space management and issues related to Civil Enclaves to address these 
issues comprehensively. 
(Para 9.8) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 NHLAPB (National High Level Airspace Policy Body) has been constituted in 2013 
for the flexible use of Airspace  (FUA) in accordance with the FUA Manual approved by 
Government of India in 2011  
1.2 Based on the directives of Government of India under the AtmaNirbhar Bharat 
Abhiyan (ANB), AAI had taken up issue of e fficient use of airspace usi ng Flexible Use of 
Airspace concept with IAF, Indian Navy and HAL for optimum use of airspace in May 2020. 
The airspace released on daily basis is being utilized by all stakeholders. 
1.3 Actions Taken:- 
(i) 116 Conditional Routes (CDRs) implemented. 
 
(ii) National Airspace Management Cells (NAMC) at Delhi Air Traffic Flow 
Management (ATFM) centre and Regional Airspace Management Cells (RAMC) 
at Delhi (IGIA) & Chennai Airport have been established. 
(iii) Upper Airspace of 46 Restricted Areas of IAF has been converted as Temporary 
Reserved Airspace (TRA). 
(iv) 24 Danger Areas of Army de-notified. Upper limit of Two Danger Areas lowered 
to 10000 ft Above Mean Sea Level (AMSL). 
(v) Five new CDR proposals sent to IAF for concurrence in September 2021. 
 
Development, Upgradation and Modernization of Airports 
Recommendation/Observation  
2. The Committee underlines the need for a well chalked out Master Plan with regard to 
aviation infrastructure, in order to ensure that the requirements of the growth in the civil 

3 
 
aviation sector are properly catered to. The Committee urges the Ministry to ensure that 
adequate parking space and landing slots are available at the airports. 
(Para 10.8) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 All Airports are being comprehensively planned and develo ped considering 30 years 
forecast. Accordingly, land is earmarked/ additional land is requested from State 
Governments based on long-term futuristic development of single runway or parallel runway 
configurations and the type of aircraft expected to operate  in future considering the potential 
of traffic it will be handling. Due to the dynamic nature of development, the Master Plans are 
reviewed regularly based on the revised growth forecast. 
2.2 Based on the futuristic traffic projections adequate Aircraft parking bays and slot 
management are created and planned at the airports, such that it would be able to meet all the 
future traffic demand. 
2.3 Around Rs.  90,000 crores of investments are expected to be pumped into Civil 
Aviation Sector in the next 5 years  out of which AAI alone will invest Rs.25000 crores for 
infrastructure creation. The remaining approx. Rs. 65,000 is being spent by the private sector. 
2.4 To meet the demand, AAI has embarked upon a capital expenditure (CAPEX) plan of 
Rs. 25000 crores in next five years for development / modernization / up gradation of airport 
infrastructure projects of AAI airports in the country.   418 additional parking bays are 
planned at various AAI airports in next five years for night parking of new aircrafts being 
purchased by airline operators. In addition, big ticket projects like expansion of existing 
Delhi, Hyderabad and Be ngaluru airports are being executed by private airport operators. 
Further, new mega Greenfield airports such as Navi Mumbai, Mopa, Jewar, Dhol era, Rajkot, 
Hollongi etc. are also under implementation.  
Recommendation/Observation  
3. The Committee notes that potential growth in the passenger and cargo traffic would 
require enormous investments in terms of construction of new airports and expansion  & 
modernization of existing airports. The Committee understands that lenders are cautious 
about issuing long -term debt to airport operators. The Committee, therefore, would like the 
Ministry to formulate necessary policies, schemes and guidelines, to attr act the requisite 
investment for airport projects. 
(Para 10.9) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 Government of India has put the Greenfield Airports Policy, 2008 in place. The policy 
outlines the guidelines for setting up of Greenfield Airports across the country by Government 
or private entities. A Greenfield airport can be developed and operated eit her by AAI / State 
Government or by an Airport Company that has been given a license by DGCA as per its 

4 
 
licensing conditions. As per the policy provisions, the airport developer is solely responsible 
for execution of the airport including funding arrangement.  
3.2 Government has granted “In -Principle” approval for construction of 21 green -field 
airports, out of which 8 airports Durgapur, Kurnool, Shirdi, Kannur, Pakyong  & Kalaburagi 
,Kushinagar and Sindhdurghave been commissioned and the other airports like  Dholera, 
Hirasar, Navi Mumbai, Jewar, Mopa (Goa), Hollongi are under development. 
 
Vande Bharat Mission (VBM)  
 Recommendation/Observation  
4. The Committee desires that the Ministry should ensure that amenities which match up 
to international standards a re available at all the airports and that periodic maintenance is 
carried out efficiently. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should ensure sufficient 
space for commercial shops, while granting approval for new airports. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should consider mandatorily earmarking minimum 100 acres 
of land, while making plans for future airports. Further, 5 Star/3 Star hotels and multiplexes 
should be constructed near the new airports. The Committee also desires that extra land,  if 
any, that has been allocated for the airports should not be sold and should be kept for future 
aviation developmental activities. 
(Para 10.10) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 The prevailing best practices followed in the world have already been adopted by the 
Airports Authority of India (AAI) while developing Airport infrastructure. Terminal 
Buildings are being designed to accommodate state of Art technologies with world class 
facilities. Terminals are being incorporated with technologies to have touch less movement of 
passengers which includes scanners and monitors at various check points such as entry gates, 
immigration etc. Further Body scanners are being procured for touchless Security checks at 
the Indian Airports. 
4.2 To have a smooth Passenger experience, AAI is in process of implementing Biometric 
Access Control System at 43 airports. AAI also has plans to initiate DIGIYATRA, Bio -
Metric e-boarding system with a facial recognition facilitating seamless passenger movement 
across multiple touch points at  Airport Terminal Buildings, being implemented at 4 AAI 
airports. Kolkata, Pune, Varanasi and Vizag. 
4.3 AAI is also emphasizing the barrier free environment at the Airport by providing 
ramps, toilets for differently abled persons, Braille symbols in lift and auditory signals in lift 
as well as escalators and aerobridges. Efforts are being made to provide ambulifts wherever 
the aerobridges could not be provided. The disabled friendly passenger coaches on airside are 
also being procured.  

5 
 
4.4 Further, Airports Authority of India earns revenues from Aeronautical and Non -
Aeronautical resources. Non -Aeronautical resources include earmarking 10 -15% area of a 
Terminal building for Offices, Retail and F&B. Also city side land is leased for non -
Aeronautical activities as identified in the AAI Act which include hotels, restaurants, 
warehouses etc. 
Recommendation/Observation  
5. The Committee has been given to understand that large num ber of institutional 
clearances are required for airport projects, w hich leads to delays and cost escalation. 
Therefore, the Committee recommends in this regard that the Ministry should set up a single -
window clearance mechanism in order to facilitate timely grant of institutional clearances for 
airport projects and ensure completion of such projects within the stipulated time period. 
(Para 10.12) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1. For any airport to be developed, activities relating to Air Traffic Services (ATS),

Air Traffic Services 
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee is of the considered opinion that keeping in view the exponential air 
traffic growth witnessed in the country in the past few years, it is essential that best 
international practices as regards the Air Navigatio n Services are adopted and implemented

Committee emphasizes the need to ensure strict adherence to the international standards of

(Para 9.3) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 Airports Authority of India (AAI) is continuously upgrading its Air Navigation 
Services (ANS) Infrastructure to meet the air traffic growth. AAI has undertaken Upper 
Airspace Harmonization (UAH) Programme for better capacity and efficiency facilitating 
safe and seamless movement of air traffic within Indian airspace. Harmonization of Chennai 
and Kolkata airspace has been completed. 
1.2 The entire terrestrial airspace of India is under surveillance  coverage through a 
network of Primary & Secondary Radar and Automatic Dependent Surveiilance -Broadcast 
(ADS-B) surveillance system. From January 2020, the entire oceanic airspace controlled by 
AAI has been brought under surveillance coverage by hiring Satellite based ADS-B services. 
1.3 The communication facilities have been upgraded to Internet Protocol (IP) based 
technology for seamless coverage. AAI has established Futuristic Telecomm Infrastructure 
(FTI). It is a Service Level Agreement (SLA) based sys tem ensuring 99.99% to 99.999% 
availability, using latest technology and communication infrastructure at each AAI location. 
This will help improve airspace safety, capacity, and efficiency. ATM Automation equipment 
completing its lifecycle are continuously  upgraded. AAI planned to upgrade/ replace ATC 
automation System at 38 airports to modernize the ATC System. 
1.4 For optimum use of airport resources and airspace and thus reducing airspace/airport 
congestion AAI has implemented Central Air Traffic Flow Ma nagement (C -ATFM) from 
2017. This will also reduce environmental impact due to less emission and helping fuel 
saving by airlines. 

13 
 
1.5 To continue this modernization effort to meet the future demand, Airports Authority 
of India (AAI) entered into an agreeme nt with United States Trade and Development Agency 
(USTDA) to develop a Communications, Navigation and Surveillance/Air Traffic 
Management (CNS/ATM) roadmap to improve airspace utilization and implement 
CNS/ATM air and ground infrastructure in the short, m edium and long term (upto 10 years)  
for modernization on 16th November, 2018. 
1.6 The study has been carried out by M/s Boeing, USA in consultation with all 
stakeholders such as Airlines, Airport Operators, DGCA and AAI to assist AAI in preparing a 
futuristic comprehensive Masterplan for CNS and ATM facilities and services along with 
guidance on implementation process and regulatory requirements.    
1.7 The report has been submitted by M/s Boeing in October 2021.Based on this 
document, AAI will prepare its roadmap by December 2022 for next 10 years .The Roadmap 
will be dovetailed with th e National Air Navigation Plan to be developed by MoCA , which 
is an ICAO requirement. 
1.8 AAI is upgrading its ANS training facilities with state -of-the-art Training simulators 
(such as Aerodrome Tower Visual Simulator, Flight Simulator Training Device, A TC 
Procedural Simulator, ATC Radar Simulator) as part of training improvement plan.

Aviation Research Organization (CARO) at Hyderabad. The establishment will provide an 
integrated platform for all Indian stakeholders.

air connectivity in the country is largely confined to routes connecting State capitals and 
large towns; and many parts of the country still remain unconnected by air services. 
Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation should take urgent 
effective steps to ensure adequate air connectivity in different parts of the country under RCS.

covid-19 pandemic situation. For sustainability of awarded routes and scheme in general 
extension of 1 year benefits has been granted under the scheme in respect of the r outes which 
have completed or going to complete its tenure by 31.12.2021.

Recommendation/Observation  
7. The Committee recognizes the fact that India’s strategic geographical location, 
swelling economy and the growth registered in international & domestic trade in the last 
decade are congenial to the growth in the air cargo sector. The Committee is disappoint ed to 
note that despite these advantages, India has not fully realized its potential in terms of air 

37 
 
cargo. The Committee realizes the sad fact that inadequate infrastructure is a major 
bottleneck in developing the country’s air cargo sector. The Committee , therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry should take effective steps to establish dedicated cargo 
airports in the country and to provide requisite facilities for the enhancement of air cargo 
facilities, while setting up new airports. 
(Para 13.7) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 Currently, in the Air Cargo Sector, the Passenger flights are carrying 80 to 90% of 
Cargo in its belly. Exclusive cargo freighters are handling only 10 to 20% Air Cargo. 
7.2 To establish dedicated cargo Airports the following facilities are the basic needs: 
i) Airport with adequate Runway length to operate scheduled & Non -Scheduled 
Freighters. 
ii) Immigration facility for Crew. 
iii) Customs presence for Crew & Cargo clearances. 
iv) Ground Handling Agencies with fully equipped equipment for handling of 
Aircrafts, pallets & containers. 
v) Accommodation of Airlines Offices. 
vi) Customs Brokers presence for Import Cargo Clearance & Export Cargo process. 
vii) Break Bulk/Consolidation Agents presence as 80 to 90% of cargo are handled in 
“Consolidation” basis. 
viii) Customs app ointed Custodians presence with appropriate warehouse facility 
including for Trans-shipment facilities. 
ix) BCAS/DGCA Clearance/Presence. 
x) Appropriate Security Deployment. 
7.3 Considering the above aspects, the recommendations of the committee can be 
considered by MoCA for strategic planning based on viability. 
7.4 AAI while constructing new Airport or extension activities in the existing Airports, 
consider the development of Air Cargo Terminal as an integral part, which AAICLAS is now 
taking-up. 
7.5 Further, the green field airports established on PPP mode like Bengaluru, Hyderabad 
Airports have already taken care this by providing exclusive Air Cargo handling facilities. 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
7.6 The Committee notes that the requirement of basic facilities which are needed to 
develop dedicated cargo airports and reiterates its recommendation for establishment of 
such cargo airports , keeping in view the expected economic growth of the country and 
the consequent increase in domestic and intern ational trade. The Committee strongly 
recommends that effective plan s should be formulated for  the basic facilities for cargo 
airports and cargo facilities should be expanded at existing airports and new facilities 
may be created in a time bound manner.

observes that in the reply submitted by the Ministry, Aero Club of India has been 
erroneously stated as a Flying Training Club, whereas it is a nodal agency which 
promotes and facilitates aviation and airsports.  Moreover, it is an autonomous entity 
working under the MoCA. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  

48 
 
 
CHAPTER-IV 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE FINAL 
REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY ARE STILL AWAITED 
 
 
 
-N i l - 
 
**** 
 
 
 
  

49 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/ OBSERVATIONS AT A GLANCE 
 
CHAPTER-III 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF 
THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
 
Air Traffic Services 
The Committee is constrained to note that the Instrument Landing System (ILS) CAT III 
system has been implemented at only six airports whereas ILS CAT II and CAT I have 
been implemented at one and sixty -four airports, respectively. The Committee reiterates  
its recommendation for the immediate installation of the advanced ILS CAT II and CAT 
III systems at all the airports in the country where it is technically feasible in order to 
mitigate the problems of flight delays or cancellation of flights due to weath er conditions. 
The Committee would like to stress upon the installation of advanced ILS facilities, 
especially in those airfields across the country, where the pilots face difficulty throughout 
the year in landing and take offs due to adverse weather and g eological conditions, such 
as table -top runways in Westerns Ghats, North -Eastern Region, J&K and other hilly 
areas.  
(Para 1.7) 
The Committee notes that AAI has got exemption for Global Tender Enquiry (GTE) for 
procurement of ILS under Make -in India Policy for Public Procurement (MII -PPP) from 
Government of India in July 2021. The Committee is of the firm opinion that manufacturing  of 
the ILS systems should be promoted in India under ‘Make-in India’ policy and partnerships with 
top global ILS manufacturing firms for transfer of technology should be explored. The 
Committee believes that the ILS system have a huge domestic and global market, in  view of the 
expected exponential growth in Civil Aviation Sector. The Ministry in coordination with the 
Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of 
Commerce and Industry, shoul d urgently make a futuristic Master Plan in this regard 
which will help in boosting the manufacturing sector as well as aid the economic 
development of India. 
(Para 2.7) 
Development, Upgradation and Modernization of Airports 
The Committee is of the opinion that water aerodromes which is a new concept, holds a 
great amount of potential for the country, as our country has many big rivers and lakes. 
The Committee hence recommends that the plans for creation of 14 water aerodromes 
should be expeditiously  implemented across the country and plans should be made for 
connectivity of water aerodromes as well. 
(Para 3.7) 

50 
 
Privatization of Airports 
The Committee desires to know whether the provision of employment of existing staff as 
contained in the Concession A greement(s), on implementation of PPP at six airports viz. 
Lucknow, Ahmedabad, Guwahati, Mangaluru, Jaipur and Thiruvananthpuram, has 
been followed in letter and spirit. The Committee recommends that the staff who put in 
years of service, should not be lef t in the lurch and proper benefits should be extended to 
them on implementation of PPP scheme. 
(Para 4.2) 
UDAN Scheme 
The Committee notes with concern that among 403 routes that have commenced 
operations so far, nearly 300 routes have been affected due to poor demand on account of 
Covid-19 pandemic situation. The Committee recommends that the ministry should 
formulate plans and expeditiously revive all the 300 UDAN routes, as and when Covid -19 
pandemic situation improves across the country. 
(Para 5.5) 
The Committee notes that out of the 106 TRCS routes floated by Ministry of Tourism, 
only 31 TRCS routes have commenced operation so far. The Committee strongly  
recommends that the ministry should make an exhaustive plan for coordination with 
Ministry of Touris m to start UDAN flights in the rest of the routes in a time bound 
manner as there is an urgent need to revive the tourism sector which is one of the worst 
affected sectors, after Covid-19 pandemic.  
(Para 6.5) 
Development of Cargo Sector 
The Committee notes that the requirement of basic facilities which are needed to develop 
dedicated cargo airports and reiterates its recommendation for establishment of such 
cargo airports, keeping in view the expected economic growth of the country and the 
consequent incre ase in domestic and international trade. The Committee strongly 
recommends that effective plans should be formulated for  the basic facilities for cargo 
airports and cargo facilities should be expanded at existing airports and new facilities 
may be created in a time bound manner. 
(Para 7.6) 
Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) infrastructure 
The Committee strongly recommends that the ministry should give renewed focus on the 
adequate requirements and growth of aircraft MRO service in the country, keeping in 
view the rapid growth of civil aviation sector. This would also help in generating job 

51 
 
opportunities for ample technical manpower available in the country, besides saving 
valuable foreign exchange. 
(Para 8.3) 
COVID-19 Pandemic 
The Committee desires that the technical feasibility of use of HEPA filters at airports 
may be examined, keeping in view the possibility of transmission of Covid -19 cases at 
airports, such filters may be installed at all major airports in the country in a time bound  
manner. 
(Para 9.2) 
Vacancies in AAI 
The Committee again expresses its serious concern at the huge number  of vacancies, 
which is bound to have a serious impact on the work efficiency of ATCOs. The 
Committee while noting the steps taken by the Ministry, recommends that a time 
schedule for completion of the procedural requirements should be adhered to, in view of 
the urgent need to fill up the vacancies of ATCOs. 
(Para 10.2) 
Optimal Utilization of Airspace 
The Committee notes that a saving of only Rs. 131 crore could be made by various 
airlines as compared to the target of Rs. 1000 crore, through the implementat ion of 
rationalization in the flexi air space policy. The Committee expresses its concern and the 
desires to know the reasons for such a huge difference in the targeted and the actual 
saving achieved and the steps that the ministry proposes to take to achieve this target. 
(Para 11.3) 
Seaplane Operations 
The Committee appreciates the initiative of the ministry in introduction of a new mode of 
transportation in seaplane operations from water aerodromes under UDAN scheme. The 
Committee however expresses its co ncern that at some places, namely Sabarmati River 
Front and Sardar Sarovar Dam (Gujarat), the operations have been closed down due to 
operational reasons. The Committee recommends that all the operational issues at the 
aforesaid site may be sorted out expe ditiously. In future, detailed planning maybe made 
before initiating seaplane operations, so that there is no stoppage of such flights due to 
technical, operational or any other reason.   
(Para 12.13) 
 
 
 

52 
 
Adequate connectivity of airports with roads and railways 
The Committee appreciates the proactive action taken by the Ministry, to ensure 
connectivity, and notes that a letter has been sent by Chairman, AAI to Chief Secretary 
of various State Governments to align and relate the city master plan with the air port 
master plan. The Committee desires to know the progress made on the proposal of 
Chairman, AAI and whether any progress has been made in aligning the city and Airport 
Master Plans. The Committee also desires to know the opinion of the various States 
across the country to this idea.  
(Para 13.3) 
Cancellation or delaying of flights 
The Committee strongly reiterates its recommendation made in view of the Covid -19 
pandemic guidelines, which prohibits gathering of huge crowds at public places including 
airports, to decrease the possibility of transmission of the disease. The Committee 
recommends that additional counters may be opened and more staff should be deployed 
to manage the passengers.  
(Para 14.3) 
Aero Club of India 
The Committee is aware that at a given point of time, a proposal to renew the license was 
considered and intimated to the Ministry by the AAI in its 157 th board meeting. The 
Committee would like to know in what situation the same was rescinded to by AAI 
subsequently in its 167 th board meeting where the property was not a lease but a license 
and had a right in perpetuity. The Committee was further given to understand that the 
land was allotted to ACI by the Government on 27.12.1984 for a period of 30 years as a 
license to be used for specific purpose which included construction of buildin g as 
approved by the authority at that time and the license agreement, which was done for a 
nominal fee of Re.1/- for 30 years, is irrevocable. The Committee further observes that in 
the reply submitted by the Ministry, Aero Club of India has been erroneou sly stated as a 
Flying Training Club, whereas it is a nodal agency which promotes and facilitates 
aviation and airsports. Moreover, it is an autonomous entity working under the MoCA. 
(Para 15.9)

on the recommendations/observations as contained in its Three Hundredth  Report on 
“Promotion of Infrastructure in India‟s Maritime Sector” of the Ministry of Ports, Shipping & 
Waterways which was presented to both the Houses of Parliament on 4th August, 2021. 
 
2.  The Action Taken Replies were received from the Ministry on 29 th December, 2021 
in respect of all the observations/recommendations contained in the R eport. The replies have 
been categorized as follows:-  
 
Chapter-I:  
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Ministry: 
 
Paragraph Nos.:  16, 24, 28, 29, 37, 38, 59, 61, 66, 72, 79, 86, 90, 96, 108.

2 
 
CHAPTER I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
Recommendations/ Observations:- 
1 The Committee would like the Ministry to elaborate upon how the establishment of 
various Coastal Employment Units (CEUs) creation of Port -linked industrial clusters have 
resulted in reduced logistics cost for EXIM and domestic trade. The Committee would also 
like the Ministry to formulate policies for generation of employment opportuni ties with 
involvement of personnel in various activities of construction, operations and maintenance of 
projects in regard to creation of Coastal Economic Zones (CEZs), Coastal Economic Units 
(CEUs), Port-Linked Industrial & Maritime Clusters and Smart Industrial Port Cities. 
   
(Para: 16) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 The Government of India, under Sagarmala Programme, intends to develop Coastal 
Employment Unit in proximity to Major Ports. These industrial developments are envisaged 
to be large scale integrated multi -product industrial zone catering to both domestic and 
export-oriented manufacturing.  
1.2 The Coastal Economic Zone (CEZ) has been envisaged to facilitate p ort led 
industrialization and/or Export Import (EXIM)/coastal trade of goods & commodities. CEZ is 
a spatial economic region comprising a large area in a single district or in a group of coastal  
districts or in district(s) with strong linkage to ports in that region/vicinity with an intent to 
reduce the logistics costs from demand/supply center to port and vice versa. 
1.3 It has a dual focus – direct contribution of port traffic coupled with empl oyment 
generation and reduction of logistics costs. Such a zone is envisaged to comprise industrial 
areas / estates, housing & urban infrastructure, and logistics/ transport infrastructure within 
itself to be a self-contained region with a direct or a strong port linkage. 
1.4 The aim is to achieve the following objectives:  
a. Creating large scale employment opportunities in the coastal regions across identified 
sectors to promote development in coastal regions.  
b. Increasing competitiveness of India's EXIM trade  by reducing logistics costs through 
proximity and connectivity to ports.  

3 
 
c. Increasing freight traffic through the ports in proximity to the industries, on account 
of trade generated by these manufacturing capacities  
d. Provide an impetus to coastal shipping by creating supply and demand centers close 
to the coastline for domestic movement of goods and passengers  
1.5 As per the Minutes of Meeting of EFC held on 9 July 2019, it was recommended that 
MoPSW should explore possibility of Industrialization at land available with Ports. So far, 
more than 8000 Acres of land have been used for Industrialization by Major Ports which has 
generated more than 2 Lakh direct and indirect employment. The details of industrialization 
initiatives at major ports are attached in Annexure A. 
Recommendations/ Observations: 
2 The Committee would also like to recommend to the Ministry that a dedicated 
mechanism should be put in place for effective coordination and monitoring of PPP projects 
undertaken for development of Private Ports in the country. Further, ways should be chalked 
out to link Private Ports with the Major and Minor Ports of the country in order to cater to 
the growing requirement for import/ export of manufactured goods/ raw materials, 
immediately after the phase of Covid-19 pandemic is over.      
(Para: 24) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 There is a dedicated PPP Cell in place in the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and 
Waterways to effectively deal with all proposals related to Public Private Partnership 
projects.  The Cell processes all proposals received from major ports under the administrat ive 
control of the Ministry and accords approval to the ports for implementation of these projects.  
The Cell monitors the progress of these projects implemented by the ports which is also 
monitored by the NITI Aayog and Cabinet Secretariat from time to time.  
Recommendations/ Observations: 
3 The Committee notes from the reply of the Ministry that a large extent of land 
belonging to Major Ports is under lease with Departments of Government of India and the 
State Governments on which interest and penal inter est have been levied in cases of unpaid 
lease rentals. The Committee also takes note of the fact that “One Time Settlement Scheme” 
on 13th August, 2019 and desires to be apprised of the outcome of this Scheme.         
   (Para: 28) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 Major Ports Wise information on „One Time Settlement Scheme‟ is at the Annexure-
B.         

4 
 
Recommendations/ Observations: 
4. The Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways in coordination with the Ministry of 
Renewable Energy should also work towards es tablishment of solar power plants and wind 
power generation units on the unutilized land rather than on sea, wherever possible near the 
harbors to reduce the burden on non -renewable resources of energy and to increase the 
employment opportunities. 
(Para: 29) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 Ministry of Ports Shipping and Waterways is under process of formulating a “Green 
Port Policy” document that would bring out a framework and guidelines for incorporation of 
green initiatives in the port sector. It would be app licable to all major ports and non -major 
ports of India. 
4.2 Major Ports currently have approx. -118 MW generation capacity through solar PV 
and 20.71 MW of wind power capacity has been installed using port premises and studies are 
to explore possibility of  utilizing suitable port spaces for installation of solar and wind 
energy. 
4.3 Recommendations/ Observations is noted. 
Recommendations/ Observations: 
5 The Committee would urge the Ministry to develop an efficient system which can 
support seamless movement of cargo across all modes. The Ministry should emphasize all the 
Major and Minor Ports to enhance the productivity and infrastructure to the level of best 
Ports in the world which will enable them to compete globally. In this regard, the Committee 
would l ike the Ministry to appoint consultants to suggest solutions to the logistical and 
infrastructural bottlenecks. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to take both 
statutory as well as administrative measures, to ensure that the consultants of p roven track 
record are appointed who should be mandated to furnish their Report within a defined 
timeframe by assessing all the infrastructure/ performance parameters related to the Major 
and Minor Ports of the country. 
(Para: 37) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1 Recommendations/ Observations is noted please. 
 
 

5 
 
Recommendations/ Observations: 
6. The Committee notes from the reply of the Ministry that in order to develop Ports of 
global standard in India, the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways has identified 
Maritime India Vision (MIV) 2030. The Ministry should apprise the Committee of the 
implementation strategy that has been envisaged for the same. The Committee should also be 
apprised whether the Ministry has issued guidelines for its implementation to various Port 
Authorities/ Major Ports or has given autonomy to them for formulation of t he strategy 
regarding the (MIV) 2030.           
(Para: 38) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (MoPS &W) is closely monitoring the 
implementation of initiatives identified under MIV 2030 across all organizations. MoPSW 
has formed two committees viz. Apex Committee for Monitoring (ACM) under the 
Chairmanship of Secretary (PS&W) and Maritime Vision Implement ation Committees 
(MVIC) under Chairmanship of the Head of the Organizations at each organization under the 
MoPSW. MVICs have been made responsible for implementing MIV 2030 initiatives in their 
respective organizations, while ACM will monitor and review th e progress of Maritime 
Vision Implementation Committee (MVIC) on quarterly basis.  
 
PUBLIC PRIVATE PARTNERSHIP PROJECTS  
Recommendations/ Observations: 
7. The Committee note so that Shipping industry in India is subjected to multiple taxes 
as compared to leading maritime nations due to which shipping companies are not attracted 
to invest in India. The Committee observes that it is critical for the growth of Shipping in 
India that a level playing field is created as compared to other maritime nations in res pect of 
taxes. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the Ministry should take effective steps 
to modify relevant policies with a view to formulate a new tax regime in line with other tax 
regimes of leading maritime nations.         
   (Para: 59)

MODEL CONCESSION AGREEMENT  
Recommendations/ Observations:- 
13 The Committee observes that the resources required to build the necessary Port 
infrastructure are huge and therefore, supplementation of public investment by private sector 
investment through PPP mode is inevitable. It is in this context that successful working of 
PPP model assumes added significance in realizing the targeted Port capacity augmentation. 
The Committee, therefore, welcomes th e changes ushered in by the MCA, 2018. While 
endorsing the revised MCA, 2018, the Committee desires to know as to what extent the Model 
Concession Agreement, 2018 (amended) has succeeded in obviating the problems faced in 
execution of PPP projects and make  the investment in Port sector attractive. Further, the 
Ministry should apprise the Committee of the provisions in MCA, 2018 which are proving to 
be impediments in the implementation and maintenance of PPP projects. 
 (Para: 90) 

11 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
13.1 The Model Concession Agreement (MCA) governing the PPP Projects in the Ports 
Sector was first introduced in the year 2008 and was subsequently revised in 2018 based  on 
the stakeholders‟ feedback.  Recently, Government of India has enacted Major Port 
Authorities Act, 2021 that aims to reorient the governance model in Major ports to landlord 
port model in line with the successful global practice. Further, the Act empowers the Major 
Ports to perform with greater efficiency on account of increased autonomy in de cision 
making and it also aims to make the sector more responsive to dynamic market needs.  The 
existing MCA needs to be aligned with these developments to encourage participation of the 
private players and address the requirements of stakeholders (Private  terminal operators, Port 
Authorities, and lenders) to ensure that risks of each of the stakeholder are well balanced. 
Accordingly, The Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways (MoPSW), has revised the MCA, 
2018 for PPP Projects at Major Ports  and issued new MCA, 2021 on 12 November 2021.  
The new MCA will be applicable to all  the future PPP projects at Major Ports as well as 
projects which are already approved by the Government and are still under bidding stage. 
13.2 Some of the key changes ma de in the  new MCA, 2021 are as follows : - First, 
provision of Change in Cargo due to Change in Law or Unforeseen Events has been 
introduced. There have been cases in the past wherein due to external and unforeseen factors, 
traffic for a particular commodit y has dropped during the concession period thereby 
impacting the overall viability of the terminal. The concessionaire did not have flexibility to 
handle a different cargo and the asset constructed was not being utilized optimally. This 
provision gives the flexibility to undertake change in cargo in such situation and reduces risk 
for the concessionaire. Second, flexibility provided to the concessionaires to fix tariff based 
on market conditions which will allow level playing field for the private terminals  at Major 
Ports to compete with private ports for cargo. Further, to reduce risk to the lenders and make 
the project more bankable, provision of compensation for Concessionaire‟s event of default 
before Commercial Operations Date (COD) has been added. Anot her provision which lays 
out process for extension of concession period on the basis of performance and mutual 
agreement has been introduced. Overall, more clarity has been provided in terms of 
responsibilities of both public as well as private party while balancing the risks. 
13.3 With many other changes drawn from best practices from across the sectors and 
extensive stakeholder consultation, the MCA, 2021, will bring more confidence of 
developers, investors and lenders and other stakeholders in the Ports sector and catalyze the 
investment in the sector.

Reply of the Ministry 
16.1 The MPA Act 2021 has been brought into effect from 03.11.2021. Ta riff Policy for 
Major Port Authorities 2021 for fixation of SoR for assets and services , along with Working 
Guidelines to operationalize the Tariff Policy, have been issued on 23.11.2021.  
The Major Port Authorities Act 2021 has come into force and the Tariff Authority for Major 
Ports (TAMP) is no longer empowered to fix tariff or assets and services of the major ports.  
The powers of tariff fixation has been given to the concessionaire in c ase of PPP projects  of 

25 
 
the Major Ports based on prevailing market conditions.  The Ministry has  already issued 
tariff guidelines in this regard on 21.12.2021.  
 (i).   Under the MPA Act, 2021 the tariff setting functions of Major Ports and PPP 
Concessionaires operating in Major Ports mandated on TAMP has been withdrawn. 
(ii).  The MPA Act, 2021 empowers the Board of Major Port Authority to frame their own 
Scale of Rates for services performed by Major Ports and for access to and usage of port 
assets. 
(iii).   The Tariff Policy 2021 issued by the Ministry recently  grants full flexibility to Major 
Ports to fix their tariff within the ceiling Annual Revenue Requirement (ARR) so as to react 
to the market forces and to fix tariff based on commercial judgment. T he Tariff Policy states 
that the port  may draw a comparison of the major tariff items for their ports and ascertain 
itself that the tariff is comparable and competitive with neighboring and competing ports. The 
Tariff Policy also requires ports to periodic ally review the SOR to respond effectively to 
dynamic market forces or to optimise asset utilization. The tariff of Major ports shall be 
notified in the State Gazette to bring in transparency. 
 (iv).   Further, the MPA Act 2021 prescribes that the tariff f ixation by Major Ports shall not 
be inconsistent with the provisions of the Competition Act, 2002.   Thus, apprehension of 
cartelization by port / operators will be taken care by this provision. 
 (v).  With the commencement of the MPA Act, 2021,  the Major P orts and PPP 
concessionaires now  shall have full flexibility to fix the tariff based on market conditions. 
This will bring in level playing field and healthy competition in the port sector.

PROMOTION OF COASTAL SHIPPING  
Recommendations/ Observations 
7 The Committee is of the considered view that coastal shipping is a fuel efficient and 
an environment friendly mode that can ease traffic congestion. Despite having an extensive 
network of inland waterways in the form of rivers, canals, backwaters and creeks, freight 
transportation by waterways is highly under-utilized. Waterways currently contribute around 
6% to India's transportation modal mix, which is significantly less than that in deve loped 
economies and some of the developing economies as well. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that availability of dedicated infrastructure will go a long way in promoting 
coastal shipping as a mode of freight transportation. Hence infrastructure at P orts and 
supporting infrastructure using rail/road and waterways to facilitate coastal movement 
should be created which includes development of dedicated coastal berths, bunkering and 
storage at Ports and creation of supporting hinterland transport infrast ructure with last mile 
connectivity.            
(Para: 65)

in promoting coastal shipping as a mode of freight transportation. Hence infrastructure  at 
ports and supporting infrastructure using rail/road and waterways to facilitate coastal

bunkering and storage at ports and creation of supporting hinterland transport in frastructure 
with last mile connectivity. 
 7.2 To boost trade with up -gradation of port facilities to global standards and for making 
coastal shipping viable at many instances, there are 17 projects worth Rs. 1815 Crore which

Comments: (A) Background of Policy Guidelines for Land Management (PGLM) 2015: 
 
(1)          Mumbai Port Trust has about 275 Ha. of land falling under township areas and 
consisting of 524 Nos. of expired leases, 1977 Nos. of Monthly Tenancies & Fifteen Mon thly 
Leases and 250 Nos. of running leases. In the past when Mumbai Port Trust revised its rentals 
with effect from 1982 based on the valuation done by the Valuers in 1980, it led to a spate of 
litigations and the revision was struck down by the Hon‟ble Bo mbay High Court.   At the 
suggestions of the Hon‟ble Bombay High Court, the rates had to be substantially moderated 
under the “Compromise proposals” formulated by the Port, which was further adjudicated 
and the rates further moderated by the Hon‟ble Supreme  Court. These litigations continued 
for almost 24 (twenty-four) years with multiple litigations. Ultimately, the issue of revision of 
rent and Board‟s compromise policy was settled by the judgment given by the Hon‟ble 
Supreme Court in the Civil Appeal No.5 559 of 2001 dated 13th January, 2004 and 9th 
January 2006. The prolonged litigation affected the revenue from let out land of MbPT.  
  
(2)          Policy Guidelines for Land Management (PGLM), 2015 for all Major Ports of India 
and Clarification No.1 of 20 18 and Clarification No.2 of 2019 thereon were issued by 
Ministry.  Vide these clarifications, the PGLM 2015 guidelines were extended to township 
areas of the Port land which were earlier excluded from the PGLM 2015.   Many of the 
expired leases, which coul d not be renewed in the absence of policy guidelines for township 
areas from the Ministry for leases/ renewal of leases.   By clarification No.1 of 2018 and 2 of 
2019 and para 13 of PGLM 2015, Ministry laid down procedure for renewal of expired leases 
and allotment of vacant lands by computation of Schedule of Rates (SoR) based on highest of 
5 factors on the basis of approved land values.   In case of Township of MbPT, the revised 
SoR was due from 1.10.2012 onwards, since earlier rentals were fixed in accorda nce with the 
Compromise policy modified by the Hon‟ble Supreme Court Judgment dated 13.1.2004 and 
were valid upto 30.9.2012.  
 
Bottlenecks in implementation of the PGLM 2015: 
  
(1)          Most of the leases in township areas have expired and there is lar ge number of sub-
tenants/Third parties in occupation of the existing structures constructed by the lessees. In 
most of the cases, lessees/licensees have transferred possession of lands/tenements to third 
party occupants without the approval of the Board. T hus MbPT has to engage into protracted 
52

 
litigations with these sitting occupants to get these lands/tenements vacated. In some cases, 
these litigations take up to 20 years to be finally adjudicated by the courts. 
 
(2)          (i) As per Para 11 of PGLM 201 5, fresh allotment or renewal of expired leases 
without renewal clause should be allotted through e -Tender cum auction by public notice on 
the Reserve Price as per Para 13 of PGLM 2015. 
     
         (ii) The reserve price based on the upfront premium as p er the SoR is worked out in 
accordance with para 13 of PGLM 2015 as per highest of the five factors for determination of 
land values.  The revision of SoR rate are only 36 times more than the existing rentals billed 
by MbPT as per the Hon‟ble Supreme Court  Judgement rates.   The revised SoR are not 
acceptable to any of the Lessees / Tenants / Occupants. 
 
        (iii) The existing lessee is to be given RoFR and opportunity to match the highest tender 
offer, provided they clear all past dues as per the applic able SoR from the date of expiry of 
the lease and also payment of required charges of regularisation of breaches, if any in the 
matter.  The exorbitant increase in the revised SoR and considering high reserve price and 
recovery of differential arrears for retrospective period from 1.10.2012 onwards are not 
acceptable to many lessees and is a major deterrent in renewal of expired leases. 
 
(3)          There are large scale objections to the MbPT‟s proposal for revision of SoR 
w.e.f.1.10.2012, which was submi tted to the TAMP. Many lessees/tenants/ occupants have 
contended that proposed new rents are very high in comparison with present rentals fixed 
under Hon‟ble Supreme Court (Wadia) Judgement 2004 which are almost 36 times higher on 
an average, which is not acceptable to many of the lessee/tenants. Such disputes with 
lessees/tenants could lead to protracted litigation by disputing parties and could stall the 
process of recovery of the revised rates. Even the government bodies, public sector 
undertakings, oil companies, etc., have expressed their inability to make the payment of past 
rentals which is from retrospective period, i.e. from 1.10.2012 onwards and also the high 
upfront premium payable for further period of 30 years for grant of fresh lease. 
  
(4)          PGLM 2015 do not provide any provision to the existing tenants / sub -tenants / 
lessees /actual occupants to transfer the land under expired leases in the name of actual 
occupant/sub-tenant who are in occupation of these premises for more than 30/50 y ears or 
even more.  Some of the occupants are even protected under Rent Control Act. Eviction of 
such large number of sub -tenants/Third parties and lessees by due process of law is a tedious 
and long time consuming process which takes several decades by wa y of multiple litigations 
and appeals.   
  
53

 
(5)          Existing land use and the layout plans and infrastructure in many parts of the 
township area are unutilised potential of land and are outdated with the present urban 
planning norms. There is no provision in PGLM 2015 Policy for rehabilitation and relocation 
of existing occupants/lessees/tenants at other locations by reconstitution of plots for 
redevelopment with change of use. Lack of provision in PGLM 2015 has restricted the 
untapped and under-utilized the development potential of the prime land of Mumbai City. 
  
(6)          The maximum period of lease that can be granted by Ports under PGLM 2015 is 
only 30 years and beyond 30 years, proposal needs to be recommended to Empowered 
Committee constituted by Ministry of Shipping, Government of India. Limiting period of 30 
years is also proving to be deterrent for getting good response from the market for land 
monetization of Port Trust lands falling in township areas and may be changed to 60 years. 
Two of the vacant plots were put for tender cum auction for industrial purpose but have not 
received any single bid due to high reserve price, limited lease period and due to restriction 
on subletting and transfer of the lease premises. 
  
(7)          By Clarification No.1 of 2018, Port Trust vacant plots / lands cannot be put for real 
estate development / residential development.  As most of the vacant plots of MbPT township 
land are falling under residential zones / commercial / industrial zones as per the 
Development Plan of Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai and not suitable for port 
related activities.  Such restrictions on proposed use are the bottlenecks in asset monetization 
of Port land.  
  
These are some of the bottlenecks / deterrent factors, w hich needs to be examined by the 
Ministry as these provisions are leading to large scale disputes and increase in litigation with 
lessee/tenants/occupants, affected revenue from let out land in Township area. The relevant 
provisions of PGLM 11, 12 & 13 may  be suitably examined to remove these bottlenecks so 
that Port Trust can generate revenue and fair rental returns by its landed assets in township 
areas.

Annexure – F 
A write up on Tonnage Tax Scheme 
1. Tonnage tax is a presumptive method of taxation which gives a shipping company an 
option to have its profits derived from the operating of ships to be taxed on the net tonnage of 
the ships as against the actual variable business profits / losses. A shippin g company which 
has opted for tonnage tax has to fulfill the following statutory compliances as per provisions 
of Chapter XII -G (Special provisions relating to income of shipping companies) of the 
Income Tax Act, 1961.  
 
2. Two main requirements of Tonnage  Tax Scheme under  Income Tax Rules are i) to 
acquire new ships by utilizing minimum 20% of book profit for acquiring new ships and ii) to 
fulfill Minimum On Board Training Requirement.  
 
3. Minimum Training Requirement (MTR) for tonnage Tax Company: 
Section 115V of the Income Tax Act, 1961 deals with Minimum Training 
Requirement (MTR) to be fulfilled by a Tonnage Tax Shipping Company which highlights as 
under:  
i. A tonnage tax company shall comply with the minimum training requirement in 
respect of trainee officers in accordance with the guidelines framed by the Director -
General of Shipping and notified in the Official Gazette by the Central Government. 
ii. As per present rulings 15% of Compliment as per Safe Manning Document of a 
qualifying ship shall be provid ed on Board Training on qualifying ships by a 
qualifying co. every year. 
iii. Qualifying ships are: 
a) Sea going ships or vessel with 15 net tonnage or more 
b) Ships registered under Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 or a ship registered 
outside India for which license has  been issued by the Director General of 
Shipping 
c) Following ships are not included in qualifying ships –  
Fishing vessels, factory ships, pleasure crafts, and harbor and river ferries, 
offshore installations 
62

 
iv. Qualifying Company requirements: 
 An Indian Company 
 The place of effective Management is in India 
 main objet of co. is to carry on the business of operating  ships 
 Company which own at least one qualifying ship

I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do 
hereby present this Three Hundred Tenth Report on ‘Functioning of Central Libraries in the 
country’.  
2. The Committee heard the views of the Secretary, Ministry of Culture on the subject 
on 1st November, 2021. The Committee heard the views of Additional Sec retary, Ministry of 
Culture; Prof. Alok Tripathi, Additional Director General; Archaeological Survey of India; 
Shri T. J. Alone, Joint Director  General; Archaeological Survey of India; Adv. A.D.N. Rao, 
Senior Advocate on the panel of Supreme Court of India; and Adv. Jayant Tripathi, President 
Legal Advisor to ASI, on the subject on 9 th December, 2021. The Committee heard the views 
of the Secretary, Ministry of Culture on the subject on 6th January, 2022.  
3.  The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the officers of Ministry of Culture and 
Domain Experts for placing before the Committee , the material and information desired in 
connection with the subject and for clarifying the points raised by the Members. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the  31st 
January, 2022.

1 
 
REPORT 
 
Libraries exist in our country from ancient times. The world famous universities like 
Nalanda and Taxasila had magnificent libraries with a massive collection of manuscripts 
covering the universe of knowledge. However,  the modern concept of public library has its 
origin in the provincial and British colonial period when many public libraries got established 
across the country. In the post -independence era, the main  focus was on building knowledge 
society. Public libraries were considered to be very helpful in achieving this goal. Public 
library is a catalyst  to the society. 
2. A public library acts as a social institution  which caters to the information needs of 
the society without any discrimination. In a developing country like ours, special emphasis is 
laid on literacy, adult education, formal and informal education. The UNESCO defines Public 
Library as "the local gateway to knowled ge, provides a basic condition for lifelong learning, 
independent decision making and cultural development of the individual and social groups".  
3. Given the crucial role played by the Central Libraries across the country in 
dissemination of knowledge amo ng students, research scholars as well as the general public, 
the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and 
Culture decided to take up the subject ‘Functioning of Central Libraries in the country’ for 
detailed examinatio n and report. The Committee had its deliberation with the Secretary, 
Ministry of Culture on this subject on 1 st November, 2021 and 6 th January, 2022. The 
Committee also heard various representatives of the Ministry and domain experts on the 
subject in its meeting held on 9th December, 2021. 
4. In India, t he public library scenario has improved considerably during the post -
independence period. The Delhi public library was founded in 1951 as the first UNESCO 
Public Library Pilot Project under the joint auspic es of UNESCO and Government of India. 
The purpose of t his library was to adapt “modern techniques to Indian conditions” and to 
serve as a model public library for Asia. 
5. As per the Seventh Schedule under Article 246 of Constitution of India, Libraries is  
enlisted in the State List. Ministry of Culture, however, because of historical and legal 
reasons, has been the  custodian of select major public libraries of national importance in the 
country. 
6. The following are the 7 Libraries/Organisations financed by Ministry of Culture. 
Budget is allocated to these organisations/offices every financial year for their administration 
and to ensure organisational goal: 

2 
 
1) National Library, Kolkata (Subordinate Office) 
2) Central Reference Library, Kolkata (Subordinate Office) 
3) Central Secretariat Library, Delhi 
4) Delhi Public Library, Delhi (Autonomous org.) 
5) Rampur Raza Library, Rampur, Uttar Pradesh (Autonomous Org.) 
6) Khuda Bakhsh Oriental Public Library, Patna, Bihar (Autonomous Org.) 
7) Raja Rammohun Roy Library Foundation, Kolkata (Autonomous Org.) 
 
National Library, Kolkata 
7. The National Library, Kolkata is an “Institution of National Importa nce” under 
Article 62 in the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India. 
8. The library is designated to collect, disseminate and p reserve printed material 
produced within India. All forms of published materials in India are to be deposited at the 
National Library under the Delivery of Books and Newspapers (Public Libraries) Act, 1954 , 
subsequently amended in 1956 (Newspapers an d periodicals). It is also a legal depository 
library of the country and a largest repository body of Government Of India. It is a storehouse 
of 26,41,615  printed books, more than 125000 e -books, 7000 e-journals, about 88162 maps, 
5744 manuscripts, 147331  bound printed periodicals titles, 598 foreign print journal, 905 
newspaper titles comprising of more that 11000 newspapers bound volumes, 104388 
microfilms roles, 97000 mircrofiches and over 21425 digitized books covering over 72 lakh 
pages. 
9. The Nation al Library , Kolkata is one of the four designated libraries entitled to 
receive a copy of every publication published anywhere in the country, under the Delivery of 
Books and Newspapers (Public Libraries) Act, 1954. The National Library is a permanent 
depository of all reading and printed materials produced in India, or written by any foreigner, 
wherever published and in whatever language both in printed and digital format. 
10. One of the domain experts who appeared before the Committee on the subject , 
commented about this library as under:- 
 Federation of Indian Publishers have estimated tha t more than one lac printed book s, 
journals, monographs, etc., are published in India every year. But the National 
Library is estimated to receive only about one -third of the publications under DOB 
Act. 

3 
 
 There is no provision in the National Library yet to receive and create database of 
digital publication published in the country. 
 This means the nation has almost lost its intellectual property of about   65% in 
printed form and 100% in digital form for more than 50 years. 
11. The Committee finds that there is no proper preservation of books/manuscripts 
in the National library in printed and digital format. The library is also not receiving 
copies of printed as well as digital publications published in the country. The 
Committee finds it extremely important that the Ministry of Culture and National 
Library, Kolkata come up with a mechanism for collection , preservation of material 
and digital publications and making  them accessible not only to general public but also 
to posterity since the objective of the National Library being a permanent depository of 
all reading material produced in India cannot be achieved. It is understood that a 
project has been submitted to develop Repository of Indian publications ensuring 
almost 100% of delivery under D elivery of books Act,1954 amended subsequently in 
1956 and 2005. The project has been approved by M inistry of Culture.  The Committee 
would like to know how the Ministry is ensuring this.  
12. The well trained and adequate number of staff can play a dominant role in providing 
effective and efficient services to the users of the public library. At present, there is 
inadequacy of trained and competent staff to render effective p ublic library services, forcing 
most services to be operated by semi and non -professional staff, which damages information 
organization and services. The problem of educated and competent professionals preferring to 
work in special and academic libraries r ather than public libraries, also needs to be resolved. 
Some of the libraries don't even have administrative staff. The National Library doesn't have 
a Director General for the last few years. 130 posts in national Library have been abolished. 
13. The Committee fails to comprehend how the National Library could be expected 
to function to its maximum potential when the top -level post of Director -General of the 
Library has been lying vacant for several years on the run. The Committee recommends 
that the post of the Director-General post in the National Library should not be  kept 
vacant for such a long time and steps be taken to fill it  up immediately. The Committee 
strongly recommends that urgent action  needs to be taken  for filling up the hum an 
resource requirements of the National Library . 
14. The Committee also recommends that the Executive Head of Library should be 
an eminent Library and information Science professional with strong technical 

4 
 
background. He/she may be appointed in the grade of Dire ctor General  at -least for 
three years for  taking up  the responsibility. 
 
CENTRAL SECRETARIAT LIBRARY, DELHI 
15. Central Secretariat Library (CSL), Ministry of Culture (MoC) is one of the largest 
Government Libraries in the country. CSL’s resources are an amalgamation of number of 
libraries of pre-independent India and many other old institutions such as Imperial Secretariat 
Library. Indian and Foreign Official Documents Sections are a valuable part of its c ore 
collection. It performs the function of a Secretariat Library with its collection of Government 
Reports and Gazettes.  
16. Central Secretariat Library mainly caters to the needs of all the 
Ministries/Departments of the Government of India. Non -official users such as research 
scholars, academicians, students and others can also become a member of this Library. As on 
date, total collection of the library is 8.41 lakh documents which include books, government 
publications, reports and gazettes.  
17. The Committee notes tha t Central Secretariat Library,  a premier library 
situated in the heart of the capital,  is a big attraction for politicians, bureaucrats and 
scholars. In view of its locational advantage , the Committee is of the view that CSL 
should undertake the role of advising decision makers on matters of library information 
services. The Committee also desires that CSL should play a lead role to coordinate 
with national and international agencies, associations, Non-Governmental 
Organizations ( NGOs), publishers and other stakeholders for the development of 
library services in the country  and for deriving benefit from  huge collections of 
Government reports and gazettes . 
 
 
RAJA  RAMMOHUN ROY LIBRARY FOUNDATION, KOLKATA  (RRRLF) 
(Autonomous Org.) 
 
18. Raja Rammohun Roy Library Foundation (RRRLF), was set up in May 1972 with the 
objective to promote and support the public library movement in the country, providing 
financial and technical assistance for development of Public Library System and Services 
under its schemes, inculcating reading habits among the masses with the active cooperation 
of the State/ U.T. Library Authorities and Voluntary Organizations operating in the field of 

5 
 
library services.  RRRLF has its Head Office Located in Kolkata and small zonal offices 
located in Delhi, Mumbai, Guwahati and Chennai. RRRLF promotes library movement and 
develop public library service all over the country through the implementation of two types of 
schemes – Matching and Non-Matching, to provide assistance towa rds building up of stocks 
of books and reading materials, modernization of library services, providing furnitures, 
storage items, digitization etc. 
19. Raja Ram Mohan Roy Library Foundation (RRRLF) was established in May, 1972 by 
the Ministry of Culture, G ovt. of India to spread library services all over the country in 
cooperation with State Governments, Union Territory Administration and Organizations  
working in the field. 
20. It is an autonomous organization fully financed by the Ministry of Culture, 
Government of India. It is registered under the West Bengal Societies Registration Act, 1961. 
The basic idea behind establishing the foundation was to take the library movement not only 
to small towns and villages but also to the remotest corner, in cooperati on with the state 
governments, union territory administrations and other organizations engaged in the library 
service and mass education.  
21. The Committee, therefore, recommends that central government, state 
governments and RRRLF should come forward and  take initiative for proper 
development of public library system in India. They should devise a master plan to 
revive India's public libraries to cater to needs of special groups like children , 
differently abled, elderly people and ethnic minorities and  achieve the goal of 
information for all.  
 
DELHI PUBLIC LIBRARY, DELHI (Autonomous Org.) 
 
22. The Delhi Public Library was established as a part of UNESCO project in 1950 and 
has developed into a major public library system and serves the entire metropolis. Delhi 
Public Library provides services to adult and child readers without any gender, religi on, caste 
and class discrimination, as a form of social education. It provides platform to meet the 
recreational needs of the readers to highlight their hidden talent. The library has a central 
library, 3 branches, 19 sub-branches, 1 community library, 8 r ehabilitation colony libraries, a 
Braille library, 144 mobile library service centers (including 25 Braille mobile library 
services) and 33 book reading centers in the capital Delhi. Delhi Public Library is expanding 
its services as a centre of knowledge dissemination and culture. 

6 
 
23. However Committee notes that membership of Delhi Public Library has 
witnessed decrease in recent times , one of the reasons being Covid-19 pandemic. It has 
come down to 1.5 lakh membership from what it was prior to corona perio d i. e. 1.85 
lakh. Being a model library created in 1951 in Asia with UNESCO’s technical, financial 
assistance, it should lead other libraries in country and extend all possible help  in their 
growth.  Delhi Public Library should make all out efforts to increase its membership/ 
viewership in the interest of general public. 
 
RAMPUR RAZA LIBRARY, RAMPUR, UTTAR PRADESH (Autonomous Org.)   
24. The Rampur Raza Library was founded by Nawab Faizullah  Khan in 1774. It was 
taken over by the Government of India in 1975 by an Act of Parliament. Honorable Governor 
of Uttar Pradesh is the Chairman of the Rampur Raza Library Board. The Rampur Raza 
Library has a collection of approximately 17,000 manuscripts & rare items including 150 
illustrated manuscripts with 4000 illustrations, 1,000 miniature paintings in 35 albums, 2,000 
specimens of Islamic calligraphy in 84 calligraphy albums, 300 Art objects, 1300 historical 
coins and approximately 62,000 printed books. 
 
KHUDA BAKHSH ORIENTAL PUBLIC LIBRARY, PATNA, BIHAR (Autonomous Org.) 
25. Khuda Bakhsh Oriental Public Library (KBOPL) has evolved out of a personal 
collection of Mohammad Bakhsh of Chhapra, Bihar. His son, Khuda Bakhsh enriched the 
collection further and converted it into a public library in 1891, with the then Govt. of Bengal 
as its Trustee. In December, 1969 an Act of Parliament, declared the Library as an Institution 
of National Importance and from July, 1970 it is functioning as an autonomous insti tution 
governed by a Board constituted by the Government of India with the Governor of Bihar as 
its ex-officio Chairman. 
26. KBOPL possesses about 21,000 manuscripts of rare value mainly in Arabic, Persian 
and some in Turkish, Urdu, Hindi and Sanskrit lang uages, 3,00,000 printed books (including 
a large collection of Journal of Rare values) and about 2,000 original paintings of the 
Mughal, Rajput, Oudh, Iranian and Turkish schools.  
27. The Committee noted that there was no regular Director in the library for the 
period 2014 to April 2019 and there was also no board in 2018. Board has been 
reconstituted in the year 2020. The Committee is dismayed to note that under the 
administrative control of Ministry of Culture, the said library had been running 
without a  permanent Director for a few years which must affect the functioning and 

7 
 
decision-making process adversely. The Committee recommends that Ministry of 
Culture should shed this apathetic attitude in the interest of Libraries and general 
public.
