7. The funds under CRIF are allocated for development and maintenance of National 
Highway works including Bharatmala projects, Road Transport projects, works on State roads 
including EI&ISC works, etc. Total budget of Ministry, IEBR and Pvt. Sector Investment since 
2014-15 is at Annexure -I. The details of CRIF share used for NHs, Road Transport and State 
roads including EI&ISC since 2014 -15 is at Annexure -II. The scheme -wise Outstanding 
liabilities of sanctioned projects/ Bank of Sanction (BOS) of various works of the Ministry as on 
01.04.2021 is at Annexure-III. 
8. The Committee notes that through the amendment made by F inance Act, 2018, 
more sectors viz., Ports, Shipyards, Inland Waterways, Airports, Railway track and 
Commercial Infrastructure/ Stations, Urban Public Transport, etc., in Transport Sector 
besides other Sectors (Energy, Water and Sanitation, Communication, Social and 
Commercial Infrastructure), have been included under the CRIF. The Committee feels 
that the budgetary support that CRIF now provides to all these crucial sectors will help in 
achieving all round growth of the Indian economy. The Committee furthe r notes that the 
distribution under CRIF has been made more transparent as it is to now be decided by a 

 
5 
Committee headed by Hon’ble Finance Minister as per Section 7A of the CRIF Act, 2000 
depending on the priorities of the project. 
 
CRIF State Roads 
9. The Ministry informed the Committee that it allocates funds for State Roads under the 
Central Road and Infrastructure Fund (CRIF) Scheme and Economic Importance and Inter State 
Connectivity (EI&ISC) Schemes as per the provisions of the CRIF Act, 2000 amended  by the 
Finance Act from time to time. As per the CRIF Act, 2000 and its amendment vide the Finance 
Act, 2019. 
■ Central Government is no longer responsible for:- 
● Sanctioning of schemes; State to sanction works 
● Monitoring of State road projects and expenditu re incurred thereon; for release 
of funds to States 
● Formulation of rules for State roads. 
■ Central Govt. to formulate criteria for allocation of funds for such roads. 
10. The Committee notes that as per the CRIF Act, 2000 and its amendment vide the 
Finance Act, 2019, the Central Government is no longer responsible for formulation of 
rules for State roads. The Committee feels that the Ministry should specify the guidelines 
and technical specifications that must be followed by States to construct State roads f unded 
by CRIF. The Committee recommends that a mechanism should be put in place by the 
Ministry to carry out random checks regarding the quality of such State roads. This would 
go a long way in improving the quality of State roads being constructed by using CRIF. 

 
6 
11. The Ministry further informed the Committee that the criteria for CRF State Roads was 
proposed by the MoRT&H with the approval of Hon’ble Minister (RT&H); these have been 
finalized by M/o Finance with approval of Hon’ble Finance Minister; issued on 31.01.2020 
(Annexure-IV). 
12. The Ministry apprised the Committee about the following major aspects of the criteria for 
State roads under CRIF Act, 2000:- 
○ Criteria for allocation of funds is based on 30% weightage to fuel consumption and 70% 
weightage to geographical area of the State/ UT. 10% of such allocation to be 
earmarked for road safety works.  
○ Considering the limited available budgetary resources, aspirations of the Government, 
financing of State road projects in the second phase after com pletion of the Phase -I of 
Bharatmala under CRIF shall be duly considered.     
○ Fund shall be available for clearing outstanding liability of works sanctioned by the 
MoRT&H under CRIF (including Economic Importance & Inter -State Connectivity 
(EI&ISC) Schemes). 
○ Construction of roads connecting 'economic corridors', 'connecting roads under 
Bharatmala', 'roads connecting ports' and 'roads connecting commercial hubs' shall be 
funded under CRIF. 
○ The sanction of EI&ISC works would be similar as CRIF works.  
○ Total c ost of the schemes to be approved to be limited to the bank of sanctions of 
generally three times  of the annual allocation, except for hill States and North -East 
States (where working season is limited) for which this is to be generally be four times 
of the annual allocation for the year for the State/ UT. 

 
7 
○ Land acquisition (LA) was not being permitted earlier for State road projects except for 
pre-construction activities for ring -roads or bypasses or service roads along NHs. LA is 
now also to be allow ed for development of NHs as States’/ UTs’ contributions to share 
of Land Costs. This would facilitate participation/ contribution of States in LA cost as 
envisaged under “Grand Challenge” mechanism. 
○ Projects on de-notified/ reverted back to States/ UTs on  account of construction of NH 
bypasses, potential roads for declaration as new NHs, economically important roads, 
roads connecting NHs with particular focus on safety aspects.  
○ Road safety works, construction of ROBs/ RUBs, bridges, etc. 
○ State Governments/ UTs shall forward list of projects along with the relevant details to 
this Ministry for consideration of finalizing the same.  
○ State Govts./ UTs shall accord Administrative Approval for the projects after 
finalization of list by the Ministry. 
○ State/ UT PWDs, Road Construction Department/ Corporation, etc., to accord Technical 
Approval and Financial Sanction (TA&FS).   
○ Upto 10% of excess cost over administratively approved cost allowed. 
○ MoRT&H to release funds to State Govts./ UTs in Quarterly instalments linked to 
submission of Utilization Certificates (UCs).  
○ One third of accrual for the State/ UT for the year shall be maintained as a revolving 
balance with State/ UT while releasing funds.      
○ State Governments/ UTs to further release funds to concerned executive agencies (e.g. 
PWDs, Road Construction Department/ Corporation, etc.) within 7 days of release of 
funds by Ministry. 
○ Fund provided under CRIF shall not lapse at the end of the financial year. 

 
8 
13. The Ministry furnished details about the State / U T – wise accrual and release made for 
CRIF State roads since 2014-15 including Outstanding liabilities of sanctioned projects/ Bank of 
Sanction (BOS) as on 01.04.2021 (attached at Annexure -V). The State / UT – wise allocation 
and expenditure made for EI&IS C works since 2014 -15 including BOS as on 01.04.2021 is 
attached at Annexure-VI.  
14. During the meeting of the Committee held on 16 th  December, 2021, DG(RD)&SS 
informed that the total cost of scheme which can be sanctioned under a particular State, is limited 
to Bank of Sanctions which is limited to three times of the annual accrual/allocations in plain 
areas and four times in hilly and North -Eastern Areas. He stated that the sanction process has 
been further modified and as per the amended Act, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways 
only approves the projects which are identified and submitted by the State Governments. After 
the approval, it is the responsibility of the State Government to accord administrative approvals 
and financial sanctions and to mo nitor the progress of projects. He apprised the Committee that 
based on the progress of work, State Governments submit a utilization certificate duly audited by 
the audit committee, based on which, the Ministry releases the funds to the State Governments. 
He stated that there was no lack of clarity between the States and the Centre and that delays in 
the progress of works used to be present in many States a few years back but that now most 
States are completing projects in 3 -4 years, except some North -Eastern States where projects 
take more time because of rains and other issues. He pointed out the issue of delay in submission 
of utilization certificates by the State Governments. Another problem he highlighted upon was 
that the bank of sanctions is already h igh and the Ministry does not have any funds for further 
release as the unspent balance and current accruals of State Governments have been completely 
released. 

 
9 
15. Chief Engineer, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, during his presentation 
before the Committee on 16th December, 2021, furnished the following details regarding projects 
sanctioned under CRF/CRIF since 2016-17:

10 
17. The Committee notes the State / UT – wise accrual and release made for CRIF State 
roads since 2014-15 and the State / UT – wise allocation and expenditure made for EI&ISC 
works since 2014-15 including BOS as on 01.04.2021. The Committee feels that most of the 
States are making efficient use of the CRIF funds. Since the CRIF fund i s non-lapsable in 
nature, the Committee recommends that the Ministry must take up the issue of  inordinate 
delays in submitting the utilization certificates with the State Government, at the top -most 
level. The Ministry must impress upon the State Governme nts that sincere efforts have to 
be made to ensure that the projects sanctioned under CRIF are completed on time and the 
available funds are timely utilized.  
18. The Committee takes note of the issue highlighted by the Ministry regarding Bank 
of Sanctions already being high and the Ministry not having any funds for further release 
as the unspent balance and current accruals of State Governments have been completely 
released. Considering the backlog of funds to be released under CRIF which has been 
caused by Bank of Sanctions being high, the Committee recommends that the Ministry may 
make efforts to keep the Bank of Sanctions within the prescribed limits so that the funds 
for the sanctioned projects can be released to the State Governments on time.  
19. The Committee observes a major negative impact that the Coronavirus pandemic 
has had on the number of projects sanctioned under CRIF during 2020 -21 and 2021 -22. 
The Committee hopes that the subsequent waves, if any, of the pandemic do not have a 
significant impact on the road projects across the country and that the Ministry would be 
able to sanction a greater number of works under CRIF in the coming years.  
20. On the issue of Bank of Sanctions (BOS), the Committee reiterates its 
recommendation made in para 376 of its 296 th Report on ‘Role of Highways in Nation 
Building’, which states the following:  

 
11 
 “The Committee is of the view that the existing mechanism of bank of sanctions is 
causing a visible lack of clarity between the State Government Departments concerned and the 
Ministry of Road Transport & Highways, regarding the amount that the State is yet to be 
awarded. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may look into the issue and come up 
with suitable guidelines to ensure that there is no confusion among t he State Government 
Departments and the Ministry, regarding the share of funds to be received by the State, in any 
particular year, after factoring in the Bank of Sanctions.”  
21. The Committee observes that 10% of the allocation made to States under CRIF is to 
be earmarked for road safety works. Keeping in mind that India has the highest number of 
deaths in the world on account of road accidents and the immeasurable impact that the 
same has on countless families as well as on the overall Indian economy, th e Committee 
feels that the efforts being made by the Ministry in this regard would give a big boost if a 
higher share of CRIF funds allocated to the State Governments are earmarked for 
carrying out road safety works. The Committee, therefore, recommends th at the Ministry 
may consider increasing the percentage of funds that are earmarked for road safety works 
under CRIF, from the existing 10 percent. Further, the Ministry may evolve an effective 
mechanism to oversee and monitor optimal utilization of the fun ds earmarked for road 
safety works under CRIF.  
22. During the meeting of the Committee held on the subject in Chennai on 12 th July, 2021, 
Member (Projects), NHAI apprised the Committee of various issues faced in the land acquisition 
viz., diversion of CAL A by the State Governments during general elections, pandemic, natural 
calamities, etc., absence of suitable provision in NH Act 1956 in connection with the deposit 
money before the competent court in such cases of unwilling/absentee/ untraceable land owne rs, 
land owners approaching arbitration for more compensation, enhancement of compensation by 

 
12 
the Arbitrator , protests by land owners for higher rates, alignment mismatch  leading to shift in 
actual alignment, pendency of arbitration cases for longer period of time. He suggested that State 
Governments should have dedicated Land Acquisition Department for speedy execution of road 
projects and informed that NHAI has given all powers to Regional Officers (ROs) to execute the 
projects. It was informed that for  Tamil nadu, the annual accrual of funds is Rs. 350 crores for 
the year 2021-22 and 1/3rd of the project value had been released as advance, till that time.  
23. During the meeting of the Committee held in Kumarakom on 16 th July, 2021, Secretary, 
Public Wo rks Department, State Government of Kerala opined that the State receives low 
allocation of CRIF funds because of its small area, despite having a high density road network 
because the CRIF guidelines give 70% weightage to area of the State and only 30% we ightage to 
fuel consumption in the State. He briefed the Committee about the delayed NH projects in Kerala 
and stated that the State however is receiving good support from NHAI. Representatives of the 
State Government of Kerala, informed the Committee that  about Rs. 700 crores of funds under 
CRF/CRIF are yet to be received whereas the representatives of Ministry of Road Transport & 
Highways stated that about Rs. 126 crores are yet to be disbursed to the Government of Kerala 
and that utilization certificates for the same are yet to be received.  
24. The Committee takes note of the issue highlighted by the representatives of State 
Government of Kerala regarding the criteria for allocation of CRIF funds based on 70% 
weightage to area of the State and 30% weight age to fuel consumption in the State, and 
recommends that the criteria may be reassessed to ensure that there is a logical, equitable 
distribution of CRIF funds and smaller States are not at a disadvantage in terms of the 
CRIF allocation that they receive.  The Committee feels that the existing criteria might be 
resulting into very low allocation of CRIF funds to the North -Eastern States since they are 
smaller in area and the traffic plying in those States is also on the lower side. The 

 
13 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may consider making some special changes to 
the existing criteria to permit higher allocation under CRIF to the North -Eastern States 
given their sensitive location and difficult terrain. 
25.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry and  State Governments should 
coordinate to address the issues being faced regarding the disbursal of CRIF funds to the 
State. A high -level meeting of officials of the Ministry and the State Governments should 
take place every month to resolve issues pertainin g to land acquisition, forest clearances, 
CRIF disbursal, and other problems being faced in the development of NHs in the State. 
The Committee further recommends that a comprehensive Master Plan should be 
formulated for improving road connectivity to impor tant tourism places, cultural places, 
ports etc. across the country and that CRIF funds may be utilized for implementing the 
same. The Committee recommends that the criteria for sanction of road projects under 
CRIF may be modified so as to give higher prio rity for sanctions to roads that provide 
connectivity to places of tourism and cultural significance and last -mile connectivity to 
ports. 
26. With regard to delays faced by projects under CRIF, the Committee recommends 
that the Ministry should have a syste m to identify the pending issues with State and 
Central Governments and the same should be followed up with the Chief Secretary of the 
States. CRIF funds should also be recommended for linkage of inner state roads, small 
towns to nearby NH roads and when l inkage between two states is being worked out, it 
should be ensured that both States cooperate for executing the works on time. The 
Committee further recommends that all concerned Ministries/State Departments viz., 
tourism, culture, airport, shipping, rail ways, etc. should formulate a master plan and plan 

 
14 
of action for their respective sector and convene periodical meetings to carry out the same 
in a time-bound manner. 
27.         During the meeting of the Committee held on 16 th December, 2021, a Member of the 
Committee raised the issue of poor quality of roads constructed by the State Governments under 
CRIF. He queried about the quality monitoring mechanism for the same and highlighted a road 
accident in his constituency wherein three people got killed beca use of a road that was left dug 
up. The Chairman desired that complaint should be lodged against officers and contractors 
involved and action must be taken by the Ministry after due investigation. DG (RD)&SS 
informed the Committee that the State Government s are responsible for quality monitoring of 
CRIF works and that they have to follow the specifications for road construction issued by the 
Ministry and the Indian Roads Congress. As for quality of roads of National Highways are 
concerned, Ministry of Road transport and Highways is responsible. Some Members of the 
Committee opined that the inputs of public representatives should also be sought in the 
implementation of road projects.  
28.         Some Members of the Committee raised the issue of road contracts  under CRIF being 
awarded to bids about 32 -33% lesser than the approved estimated cost for the same and 
questioned about how the quality of roads constructed by such bidders can be expected to be 
good. A Member of the Committee suggested that a benchmark c ost of road projects should be 
calculated by the Ministry and that in case of  projects being awarded to  bids lower than the 
benchmark costs, such projects must be flagged and frequent inspection visits must be made to 
check the quality of construction of s uch flagged road projects.  
29. The Committee reiterates its recommendation made in para 10 of this Report and 
states that the Ministry should urgently work upon devising a monitoring mechanism to 
ensure that the roads constructed using the CRIF fund are of  high quality.  

 
15 
30. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry may review the existing 
guidelines for awarding of tenders for road projects under CRIF or otherwise, since it is 
often found that the projects get awarded at substantially lower bids t han the amount 
projected by the Ministry/NHAI. In such cases, the concessionaire is more likely to not 
actually complete the work at all, or do it with sub -par quality. In light of this, the 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may either come out with upper and lower limits 
for bidding for road projects or establish a mechanism to strictly monitor the quality and 
progress of road projects awarded to substantially low bids. In cases where poor 
performance and sub -par quality of road projects is noticed, t he contractor must be 
suitably penalized and their past project record must be duly considered before awarding 
any road projects in the future. 

 
16 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS – AT A GLANCE 
 
Central Road and Infrastructure Fund (CRIF) 
 The Committee notes that through the amendment made by Finance Act, 2018, 
more sectors viz., Ports, Shipyards, Inland Waterways, Airports, Railway track and 
Commercial Infrastructure/ Stations, Urban Public Transport, etc., in Transport Sector 
besides other Sectors (Energy, Water and Sanitation, Communication, Social and 
Commercial Infrastructure), have been included under the CRIF. The Committee feels 
that the budgetary support that CRIF now provides to all these crucial sectors will help in 
achieving all round growth of the Indian economy. The Committee further notes that the 
distribution under CRIF has been made more transparent as it is to now be decided by  a 
Committee headed by Hon’ble Finance Minister as per Section 7A of the CRIF Act, 2000 
depending on the priorities of the project. 
(Para 8) 
CRIF State Roads 
 The Committee notes that as per the CRIF Act, 2000 and its amendment vide the 
Finance Act, 2019, the Central Government is no longer responsible for formulation of 
rules for State roads. The Committee feels that the Ministry should specify the guidelines 
and technical specifications that must be followed by States to construct State roads funded 
by CR IF. The Committee recommends that a mechanism should be put in place by the 
Ministry to carry out random checks regarding the quality of such State roads. This would 
go a long way in improving the quality of State roads being constructed by using CRIF. 
(Para 10) 
 The Committee notes the State / UT – wise accrual and release made for CRIF State 
roads since 2014-15 and the State / UT – wise allocation and expenditure made for EI&ISC 
works since 2014-15 including BOS as on 01.04.2021. The Committee feels that most of the 
States are making efficient use of the CRIF funds. Since the CRIF fund is non -lapsable in 
nature, the Committee recommends that the Ministry must take up the issue of  inordinate 
delays in submitting the utilization certificates with the State Government, at the top -most 

 
17 
 
level. The Ministry must impress upon the State Governments that sincere efforts have to 
be made to ensure that the projects sanctioned under CRIF are completed on time and the 
available funds are timely utilized. 
(Para 17) 
 The Committee takes note of the issue highlighted by the Ministry regarding Bank 
of Sanctions already being high and the Ministry not having any funds for further release 
as the unspent balance and current accruals of State Governments have been completely 
released. Considering the backlog of funds to be released under CRIF which has been 
caused by Bank of Sanctions being high, the Committee recommends that the Ministry may 
make efforts to keep the Bank of Sanctions within the prescribed limits so that the fun ds 
for the sanctioned projects can be released to the State Governments on time.  
(Para 18) 
The Committee observes a major negative impact that the Coronavirus pandemic 
has had on the number of projects sanctioned under CRIF during 2020 -21 and 2021 -22. 
The Committee hopes that the subsequent waves, if any, of the pandemic do not have a 
significant impact on the road projects across the country and that the Ministry would be 
able to sanction a greater number of works under CRIF in the coming years.  
(Para 19) 
On the issue of Bank of Sanctions (BOS), the Committee reiterates its 
recommendation made in para 376 of its 296 th Report on ‘Role of Highways in Nation 
Building’, which states the following:  
 “The Committee is of the view that the existing mechanism of  bank of sanctions is 
causing a visible lack of clarity between the State Government Departments concerned and the 
Ministry of Road Transport & Highways, regarding the amount that the State is yet to be 
awarded. The Committee recommends that the Ministry m ay look into the issue and come up 
with suitable guidelines to ensure that there is no confusion among the State Government 
Departments and the Ministry, regarding the share of funds to be received by the State, in any 
particular year, after factoring in the Bank of Sanctions.”  
(Para 20) 

 
18 
 
The Committee observes that 10% of the allocation made to States under CRIF is to 
be earmarked for road safety works. Keeping in mind that India has the highest number of 
deaths in the world on account of road accidents an d the immeasurable impact that the 
same has on countless families as well as on the overall Indian economy, the Committee 
feels that the efforts being made by the Ministry in this regard would give a big boost if a 
higher share of CRIF funds allocated to t he State Governments are earmarked for 
carrying out road safety works. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry 
may consider increasing the percentage of funds that are earmarked for road safety works 
under CRIF, from the existing 10 percent.  Further, the Ministry may evolve an effective 
mechanism to oversee and monitor optimal utilization of the funds earmarked for road 
safety works under CRIF.  
(Para 21) 
The Committee takes note of the issue highlighted by the representatives of State 
Government of Kerala regarding the criteria for allocation of CRIF funds based on 70% 
weightage to area of the State and 30% weightage to fuel consumption in the State, and 
recommends that the criteria may be reassessed to ensure that there is a logical, equitab le 
distribution of CRIF funds and smaller States are not at a disadvantage in terms of the 
CRIF allocation that they receive. The Committee feels that the existing criteria might be 
resulting into very low allocation of CRIF funds to the North -Eastern States since they are 
smaller in area and the traffic plying in those States is also on the lower side. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may consider making some special changes to 
the existing criteria to permit higher allocation under CRIF to the N orth-Eastern States 
given their sensitive location and difficult terrain. 
(Para 24) 
  The Committee recommends that the Ministry and State Governments should 
coordinate to address the issues being faced regarding the disbursal of CRIF funds to the 
State. A high -level meeting of officials of the Ministry and the State Governments should 
take place every month to resolve issues pertaining to land acquisition, forest clearances, 
CRIF disbursal, and other problems being faced in the development of NHs in the State. 

 
19 
 
The Committee further recommends that a comprehensive Master Plan should be 
formulated for improving road connectivity to important tourism places, cultural places, 
ports etc. across the country and that CRIF funds may be utilized for implementing the 
same. The Committee recommends that the criteria for sanction of road projects under 
CRIF may be modified so as to give higher priority for sanctions to roads that provide 
connectivity to places of tourism and cultural significance and last -mile connectivity to 
ports. 
(Para 25) 
 With regard to delays faced by projects under CRIF, the Committee recommends 
that the Ministry should have a system to identify the pending issues with State and 
Central Governments and the same should be followed up with the Chief Secretary of the 
States. CRIF funds should also be recommended for linkage of inner state roads, small 
towns to nearby NH roads and when linkage between two states is being worked out, it 
should be ensured that both States cooperate for executing the works on time. The 
Committee further recommends that all concerned Ministries/State Departments viz., 
tourism, culture, airport, shipping, railways, etc. should formulate a master plan and plan 
of action for their respective sector and convene periodical meetings to carry out the same  
in a time-bound manner. 
(Para 26) 
 The Committee reiterates its recommendation made in para 10 of this Report and 
states that the Ministry should urgently work upon devising a monitoring mechanism to 
ensure that the roads constructed using the CRIF fund are of high quality.  
(Para 29) 
The Committee further recommends that the Ministry may review the existing 
guidelines for awarding of tenders for road projects under CRIF or otherwise, since it is 
often found that the projects get awarded at substantially l ower bids than the amount 
projected by the Ministry/NHAI. In such cases, the concessionaire is more likely to not 
actually complete the work at all, or do it with sub -par quality. In light of this, the 

 
20 
 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may either come out with upper and lower limits 
for bidding for road projects or establish a mechanism to strictly monitor the quality and 
progress of road projects awarded to substantially low bids. In cases where poor 
performance and sub -par quality of road projects is  noticed, the contractor must be 
suitably penalized and their past project record must be duly considered before awarding 
any road projects in the future. 
(Para 30)

At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members of  the Committee and the Director 
General (Road Development) & Special Secretary, Min istry of Road Transport and Highways 
and other senior representatives of the Ministry to  the meeting, apprising them of the agenda of 
the meeting i.e.  to deliberate on ‘Review of Central Road and Infra structure Fund (CRIF) 
Works’. 
2.         In his opening remarks, the Chairman sta ted that the amendment of the Central Road 
Infrastructure Fund (CRIF) Act, 2000 through the Fi nance Act, 2018 and replacing the earlier 
Act with the CRIF Act, 2000 has been done to use th e proceeds of the road cess under CRIF to 
finance other infrastructure projects including por ts, shipyards, waterways, some portion of the 
railway infrastructure and even social infrastructu re including educational institutions, medical 
22

 
colleges etc. He asked the Director General (Road D evelopment) & Special Secretary to 
highlight the impact of the recent amendments of the CRIF Act, 2000. He queried about the bank 
of sanctions issued and amount of funds released to  the State Governments under CRIF during 
the last three years. He enquired about the rationa lity of the existing criteria for allocation of 
funds under CRIF Act, 2000, which is based on 30% w eightage to fuel consumption and 70% 
weightage to geographical area of the State/UT. He further sought information regarding the 
present mechanism with regard to allocation, accrua l and release of CRIF funds to the State/UT 
Governments and any delays that State/UT Government s might be facing in release of funds by 
the Government of India, under CRIF. 
3.         The DG (RD)&SS, Ministry of Road Transpo rt and Highways began his deposition by 
informing the Committee that the earlier CRF Act, 2 000 came into effect in the year 2000 and 
was amended through the Finance Act, 2018 and renam ed as Central Road Infrastructure Fund. 
He further stated that as per the Finance Act, 2018, CRIF is to be administered by the Ministry of 
Finance through the Department of Economic Affairs.  He further elaborated that earlier, 41.5 
percent of the cess was given for the National High ways, 10 percent for the State Roads and the 
rest for other infrastructure, however, after 1 st  April, 2018, a Committee headed by the Finance 
Minister and aided by a Committee of Secretaries, d ecided upon the distribution of the CRIF 
among the various Ministries/Organizations. He appr ised the Committee that the total cost of 
scheme which can be sanctioned under a particular S tate, is limited to Bank of Sanctions which 
is limited to three times of the annual accrual/all ocations in plain areas and four times in hilly 
and North-Eastern Areas. He stated that the sanctio n process has been further modified and as 
per the amended Act, Ministry of Road Transport and  Highways only approves the projects 
which are identified and submitted by the State Gov ernments. After the approval, it is the 
responsibility of the State Government to accord administrative approvals and financial sanctions 
and to monitor the progress of projects. He apprise d the Committee that based on the progress of 
work, State Governments submit a utilization certif icate duly audited by the audit committee, 
23

 
based on which, the Ministry releases the funds to the State Governments. He stated that there 
was no lack of clarity between the States and the C entre and that delays in the progress of works 
used to be present in many States a few years back but that now most States are completing 
projects in 3-4 years, except some North-Eastern St ates where projects take more time because 
of rains and other issues. He pointed out the issue  of delay in submission of utilization 
certificates by the State Governments. Another problem he highlighted upon was that the bank of 
sanctions is already high and the Ministry does not  have any funds for further release as the 
unspent balance and current accruals of State Governments has been completely released. 
4.         Chief Engineer, MoRTH thereafter made a power point presentation on the subject and 
briefed the Committee about the major aspects of th e CRIF Act, 2000. He apprised the 
Committee about the details of CRIF share used for NHs, Road Transport and State roads 
including Economic Importance and Inter State Conne ctivity Scheme (EI & ISC) since 2014-15 
and the scheme-wise outstanding liabilities of sanc tioned projects/ Bank of Sanction (BOS) of 
various works of Ministry as on 1 st  April, 2021. He briefed the Committee about the ma jor 
aspects of the criteria for State roads under CRIF Act, 2000. He stated that 1,627 projects under 
CRIF worth Rs. 38,141 crores are currently under pr ogress and that 1,616 projects worth Rs. 
19,666 crores have been completed during the last t hree years and current year. He informed the 
Committee that CRIF is non-lapsable and there is no  provision to withhold and earmark the fund 
to a different State. 
5.         The Chairman recommended that the Minist ry should give priority to road projects that 
provide connectivity to places of tourism, culture,  railways, civil aviation and shipping, and that 
a certain percentage of funds should be allocated towards such road projects only. 
6.         A Member of the Committee raised the iss ue of poor quality of roads constructed by the 
State Governments under CRIF. He queried about the quality monitoring mechanism for the 
same and highlighted a road accident in his constit uency wherein three people got killed because 
24

 
of a road that was left dug up. The Chairman desire d that complaint should be lodged against 
officers and contractors involved and action must b e taken by the Ministry after due 
investigation. DG (RD)&SS informed the Committee th at the State Governments are responsible 
for quality monitoring of CRIF works and that they have to follow the specifications for road 
construction issued by the Ministry and the Indian Roads Congress. As for quality of roads of 
National Highways are concerned, Ministry of Road t ransport and Highways is responsible. 
Some Members of the Committee opined that the input s of public representatives should also be 
sought in the implementation of road projects. 
7.         Some Members of the Committee raised the  issue of road contracts under CRIF being 
awarded to bids about 32-33% lesser than the approv ed estimated cost for the same and 
questioned about how the quality of roads construct ed by such bidders can be expected to be 
good. A Member of the Committee suggested that a be nchmark cost of road projects should be 
calculated by the Ministry and that in case of proj ects being awarded to bids lower than the 
benchmark costs, such projects must be flagged and frequent inspection visits must be made to 
check the quality of construction of such flagged road projects. 
8.         Members of the Committee raised various queries, some of which were replied to by the 
DG (RD)&SS and other representatives of the Ministr y. The Chairman then directed that written 
replies to the queries which remained unanswered may be sent to the Secretariat within a week. 
(The witnesses then withdrew) 
9. The Chairman, thereafter drew the attention of t he Committee to the fact that it is 
presently, inter-alia , examining the subject ‘Issues related to land acq uisition at Bagdogra 
Airport’. The Chairman stated that during its Study Visit to Kolkata on 18 th  November, 2021, the 
Committee had discussed the issues relating to the functioning of Airports in West Bengal 
wherein the issue of land transfer by the Ministry of Defence to Airports Authority of India to 
expand the Bagdogra Airport was raised. Though the State Government and Airports Authority 
of India were keen to develop/expand the said airpo rt, the key hindrance for it is the non-transfer 
25

 
of 3.5 acres of land which is currently under the p ossession of Ministry of Defence. The 
Committee directed the authorities to solve the iss ue between themselves so that the airport can 
be expanded/developed. Both the State Government of  West Bengal and Airports Authority of 
India are willing to fully compensate the Ministry of Defence for acquiring this piece of land. 
However, inter-Ministerial differences still persis t. On earlier occasions, when such disputes 
existed in the State of Goa relating to National Hi ghway projects, the Committee acted as a 
catalyst and helped to resolve the issue. With a vi ew to thrash out this issue once and for all, the 
Committee decided to call for written views/suggest ions of State Governments and hear their 
officials on the subject. Accordingly, the Committe e authorized the Chairman to obtain 
necessary orders from Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha in this regard. 
10. A verbatim record of the proceedings of the mee ting was kept.

At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members of the Committee to the first meeting 
of the reconstituted Committee and apprised them of  the agenda of the meeting, i;.e. (i) oral 
evidence of Secretary, Ministry of Tourism on the s ubjects - * * * and "Promotion of Indian

(i) Oral Evidence of Secretary, Ministry of Tourism 
2.         Thereafter, the Chairman invited the Sec retary, Ministry of Tourism to make a 
presentation on the above subjects which are instru mental in promoting tourism in the country. 
The Secretary,   Ministry of Tourism during the cou rse of his deposition made a detailed 
presentation on Tourism Infrastructure Development Schemes. While making the presentation, 
the Secretary elaborated on the Schemes of the Mini stry viz. ‘ Swadesh Darshan,’ ‘PRASHAD,’ 
‘Assistance to Central Agencies’ and ‘Adopt a Herit age.’ He informed that the ‘Swadesh 
Darshan’ Scheme aimed to develop a theme-based inte grated tourism infrastructure with 15 
thematic circuits identified for development of 76 sanctioned projects across 31 States and UTs 
with a budgetary allocation of Rs. 5526.71 Crore for the year 2021-22 and that the Ministry  
 
*Relates to other matters.  

 
24 
 
completed projects in Tehri (Uttarakhand), Khajuraho (M.P.) and Thenzawl (Mizoram) under the 
Scheme. He further stated that the PRASHAD Scheme a ims to develop Ghats, tourist Reception/ 
Facilitation Centers, Public amenities, open-air am phitheatres, museums, medicine centers, 
external infrastructure such as water supply, sewag e, drainage, electricity, roads and use of 
renewable sources. The Secretary also informed the Committee that under the PRASHAD 
Scheme, 61 sites have been identified for developme nt of tourism infrastructure and 37 projects 
have been sanctioned for an amount of Rs. 1214.19 c rore. Highlighting the challenges faced in 
execution of the tourism infrastructure projects, t he Secretary made a mention of the delay in 
land availability and statutory clearances, delayed  tendering and slow project implementation by 
State Governments. The Secretary also apprised the Committee that the Scheme ‘Assistance to 
Central Agencies' aims to develop and upgrade basic  tourism infrastructure and has 55 projects 
in pipeline with budgetary allocation of Rs. 629.06 Crore and has 19 completed projects in its lap 
till date. The Committee was further informed that under the ‘Adopt a Heritage Scheme’ which 
aimed at increasing awareness about heritage and in volved community participation as well as 
development of hard and soft interventions at the s ites, 27 MoUs (Memorandum of 
Understanding) have been signed for 27 sites.  
3.         The Chairman emphasized the need for inc reasing connectivity to tourist spots by road, 
rail, air and waterways and suggested that CSIR fun ds/ state govt. funds should be used for 
improvement of the same. He stated that the coopera tion on part of Indian embassies in 
promotion of tourism in overseas markets is almost non – existent and emphasized that in order 
to boost the GDP of our country, the overseas promo tion and publicity of Indian tourism should 
be revamped to derive maximum advantage from the to urism generating markets. He also 
suggested that a master-plan should be prepared  fo r better connectivity to all the tourists 
destinations. 

 
25 
 
4.        The Chairman also suggested that various unexplored/lesser known tourist spots may be 
added / highlighted on the Ministry’s website porta l so as to attract more tourists to different 
destinations and facilities. 
5.         Replying to the query regarding the role  played by Indian Embassies in increasing India's 
share of the global tourism market, the Secretary informed the Committee that the Ministry had a 
discussion with the Ministry of External Affairs (M EA) regarding separate listings of top ten 
countries from which India has a good tourist rush and another list of top ten countries from 
where heavy tourist rush is expected for India and that the MEA has already appointed twenty 
earmarked nodal officers in these countries to deal  with the issue of tourism. Upon the question 
of using Central Road Fund (CRF) for tourist places  with the help/ cooperation of Ministry of 
Transport, the Secretary stated that the process to  develop highways and roads out of CRF 
money was an ongoing process and some of the connec tivity projects  had already been 
undertaken by NHAI. 
6.         Members of the Committee raised various queries on need of tourism infrastructure 
development in various States; identification and d evelopment of revenue-generating domestic 
tourist destinations in States; establishing Souven ir Shops selling miniatures of historical 
monuments, development of Haats, identifying and tr aining local families willing to provide 
local homemade food and home-stay facilities in the ir abodes to the tourists; creating revenue 
potential through promotion of Seaport tourism; pro motion of cruise tourism and Monsoon 
tourism; assessment and pre-listing of privately–ow ned culturally rich buildings and taking steps 
towards their preservation; assessment of tourist o ffices abroad; making Tourist Information 
Centers accessible; lack of funds for assistance to the States in capacity building, etc.  Some of

the queries which remained unanswered may be sent to the Secretariat within a week.

markets, participating in various multilateral and bilateral forums to strengthen India as a brand 
in tourism, partnering with SAARC/ASEAN countries to promote thematic circuits etc. 
4. The Secretary, MoT informed the Committee that the efforts made by tourism offices 
abroad in organizing tourism fairs, exhibitions, 'I ncredible India' road shows, seminars, joint 
promotional campaigns and advertising campaigns in print and digital media, extending brochure 
support to foreign tour operators, events with Indi an Missions and production, distribution of 

 
29 
 
publicity material in the local languages etc. are lacklusture due to structural dogmas as they are 
working as per the conditions and situations of for eign countries. Thereafter, the officials of the 
MoT proceeded to show an audio-visual  promotional film shown abroad under the Incredible 
India brand followed by a powerpoint presentation. 
5. The Secretary, MEA then apprised the Committee that  the MEA will work towards 
cooperating with the tourism offices set up by the MoT to monitor the tourist flow, gathering 
inputs through representatives to engage in researc h and enhance tourism promotion overseas 
etc. The Committee was informed of the MEA and Indi an Mission’s efforts in conducting road 
shows, ‘Know India’ Seminars, travel-expos, coopera ting with the MoT in printing native-
language brochures for 'Incredible India Campaign,'  hiring tour operators/ travel writers for 
extensive social media outreach etc, signing MoUs o n Tourism with various countries. The 
Committee was further informed that the MEA, in las t five years, has conducted the India 
Technical and Economic Cooperation (ITEC) flagship programme in nine courses which has 
trained 256 foreign experts in tourism and is still  in progress.  The MEA also sends Indian artists 
to participate in foreign festivals and invites art ists from abroad to participate in Indian festivals  
through Indian Council for Cultural Relationship (I CCR) to enhance tourism promotion. 
Highlighting the 3Ts (Tourism, Trade and Technology ) mantra given by the Hon’ble PM for 
Indian Missions, the Secretary, MEA informed the Co mmittee that a dashboard has been 
developed to capture tourist flow in the country. 
6. The Chairman applauded the efforts made by the Indi an Missions in the field of tourism. 
He observed that good public relations and tourism development should be an important part of 
improvement of relations between countries which em bassies should work upon. He queried 
whether any spending on advertisements was being do ne on part of the Ministry and raised 
several issues like vanishing stone-age art, ancient literature etc due to lack of protection, need to 

 
30 
 
establish affordable tourism hotels around sites/mo numents and suggested that the Ambassadors 
should present monthly reports to the concerned Min istries on the efforts made/ work done on 
their part and artification of auditoriums should b e done. The Secretary MoT informed the 
Committee that no spending was done on advertisement front, by the Ministry due to the ongoing 
pandemic. The Chairman expressed deep concern over exploitation of tourists by hotels, need to 
grant deferment to hoteliers/restaurateurs in payme nt of taxes during pandemic, lack of roadmap 
for internal road development around tourist places , lack of a planned Tourism Policy etc. and 
desired to hold separate meetings in future with th e respective Chief Secretaries of the Union 
Territories as well as Ambassadors of the MEA to un derstand their views on Tourism Policy and 
promotional plans. He also queried about the status  of budget allocation with respect to the 
PRASAD Scheme.  
7. Members raised issues/ queries regarding inclusion of tourism industry in Concurrent/ 
State List, conducting gigs/ concerts to bring diff erent cultural artists to perform, promoting 
hospital/ medical/ wellness tourism, education tourism and food/ culture tourism, improving poor 
road conditions and connectivity, tackling lack of tourist hotels, properly trained tourist guides 
and basic amenities near tourist spots, lack of tou rism offices abroad, hiring marketing 
specialists/ experts to identify lacunae in tourism sector etc. 
8. The Chairman observed that it is important to analy ze the strategies and specialties of the 
top ten countries in tourism sector in order to com pare them with the Indian Tourism sector and 
know where it lags behind.  The witnesses responded  to some of the queries raised by the 
Chairman and Members of the Committee. The Chairman  informed the Committee about the 
future meeting on ‘connectivity of roads’ and direc ted the witnesses to furnish written replies to 
queries/points/issues raised by him and the Members of the Committee . 
9. The meeting adjourned at 5:08 P.M.

1. Introduction 
 
1.1 Tourism – an Engine of Economic Growth 
 
Given the potential of tourism as a vehicle for job creation, economic growth and  
development, Tourism has been recognized as an engine for economic growth. 
Globally, strong economic growth has generated millions of new travelers looking for  
exceptional travel experiences, be it business or leisure, domestic, regional or 
international, and this trend is expected to continue with sustained momentum. 
 
1.2 Incredible India Brand 
 
The Government launched ‘Incredible India’ campaign to tap into the vast tourism  
potential of the country in an organized manner. An integrated communication 
strategy aimed at promoting India as the preferred destination for the international  
traveller was formulated. The campaign highlighted various facets of Indian culture  
and history such as yog a, spirituality, festivals and monuments. The Incredible India  
campaign is one of the most successful campaigns that placed India on the world  
tourism map. 
 
1.3 Increasing International Recognition 
 
India's philosophy of 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' sees the world as one family. It gives 
India an unwavering belief in multilateralism. India’s traditions of non -violence and 
pluralism, diversity and tolerance, its yoga and Ayurveda, its Bollywood and classical  
dances, are all well known. There is an increasing international recognition of India’s 
cultural and civilizational heritage. The rise of Indian diaspora to top echelons of  
technology industry and other professions across the world has given a great 
recognition to India. 
 
1.4 India Tourism – Growing consistently but yet to realize full potential 
 
As a travel destination, few other nations can offer the diversity of products and  
experiences found in India. Before COVID -19 pandemic, International Tourist Arrivals 
in India have been consistently growing with 17. 91 million international tourist 
arrivals in 2019. India, however stands at 23rd rank in terms of  international arrivals 
and 12th rank in terms of foreign exchange earnings from tourism for year 2019. 
India is yet to realize its full potential as a tourist destination. 
1.5 Aatmanirbhar Bharat – Overseas Demand will be crucial for Growth of Tourism 
 
Challenged by COVID-19, India has come out with the resolve to become self -reliant. 
“Aatmanirbhar Bharat” is a call to become vocal for local. It rests on the five pillars of 

54  
economy, infrastructure, systems, demography and demand. India’s quest for self - 
reliance is about creating strong enterprises in India. Enterprises that can become  
global forces. Self -reliance is about generating empl oyment and empowering our  
people to come out and create solutions that can define the future of our country. 
 
A thriving tourism industry is of vital importance for India’s journey towards 5 Trillion  
Dollar Economy. With the mantra of ‘vocal for local’, India seeks to attain 
“Aatmanirbhar Bharat” by realizing its full potential as a tourism destination. 
Overseas demand for Indian tourism products will be crucial for “Aatmnirbhar 
Bharat” 
 
1.6 Need for Greater Synergy with Indian Missions for promotion of Tourism 
 
Tourism destinations, the world over, are competing with each other  to increase  
their share in the global market. It will further intensify in future when international  
travel resumes post COVID-19 pandemic. The countries will adopt aggressive 
marketing and promotional strategies in source markets. This involves generating  
widespread awareness and generating interest in their tourism destinations and 
products amongst the trade and consumers and further, converting that interest into  
actual footfalls. 
The Ministry of Tourism has 8 offices overseas viz. Beijing, Dubai, Frankfurt, London,  
New York, Paris, Singapore and Tokyo. These offices play a pro-active role in 
enhancing tourist arrivals by promoting India in the tourism generating markets 
overseas. The overseas offices undertake various promotional activities for 
positioning India as a tourism destination in major source markets vis a vis other  
competing destination. 
Indian Missions abroad have also been promoting India as tourism destination and  
post pa ndemic, a renewed  effort will be required to  position India as preferred  
tourism destination. There  is a need to  have a coordinated strategy and framework 
to synergize the efforts of Ministry of Tourism with Ministry of External Affairs and  
Indian Missions. 
1.7 Partnership with Indian Missions for Inbound Tourism 
 
In order to forge partnership with Indian Missions for Inbound Tourism and ensure  
effective implementation, a detailed framework has been evolved covering the 
vision and objectives, key strategic areas, key operational areas and governance of  
the institutional arrangement. 
2. Vision and Objectives 

55  
2.1 Vision 
 
To create a unified strategy and forge partnership  amongst Ministry of Tourism,  
Indian Missions and other relevant Stakeholders to  promote Inbound Tourism to  
India 
2.2 Objectives 
 
The key objectives of the Strategy are: 
 
(i) Position India as the most favoured tourist destination 
(ii) Create right perception about India as a tourism destination 
(iii) Promote India as a 365 days destination 
(iv) Promote specific themes, destinations and products of Indian Tourism 
(v) Strengthen India’s role in various multilateral and bilateral forums on Tourism 
 
3. Role of Indian Missions in promoting Inbound Tourism 
 
Indian Missions will take ownership to promote Inbound tourism to India in the host 
countries where India Tourism Offices are not located i.e. in countries other than  
USA, UK, Germany, Russia, Dubai, China, Singapore and Japan. Missions will assign  
dedicated Officers for promotion of tourism and designate poin ts of contact for the  
Ministry of Tourism and other tourism stakeholders. 
 
In countries where India Tourism Overseas offices are located, they would work in  
close coordination with the respective Missions to undertake various promotional  
activities. 
 
Indian Missions and India Overseas offices will execute a strategized, targeted 
approach tailored to each host country to promote Inbound tourism to India. 
 
4. Key Strategic Areas 
 
4.1 Inbound Tourism Strategy to be a holistic approach 
 
Inbound tourism strategy should not to be just a campaign, but part of a holistic  
approach to promote Inbound tourism. It is important to focus on providing a safe,  
seamless, connected and unique experience to the visitors. Bringing together 
business and government to define smart  targets will be critical to ensure that the  
entire industry can coalesce and be held accountable to ambitious targets and their  
achievement. 

56  
The digital arena has become  the new playground for  brands to promote their  
products, services a nd destinations and effective digital strategy should be in place  
to promote Inbound tourism. 
 
4.2 Country specific Strategic Plans 
 
The Ministry of Tourism in consultation with Ministry of External Affairs and other  
relevant Ministries and Industry Stakeholders will identify the top source markets  
including established as well as emerging markets. In addition, focus areas such as  
Buddhist markets will be identified. 
 
The Ministry of Tourism will accordingly prepare country specific multi-year 
strategic plans for marketing in these Key Markets, which should include 
 
(i) Needs, Requirements and Preference of travelers 
 
The Missions can help in identifying the needs and requirements of the 
travelers from these source  markets and their preferences such as  Cultural 
and Heritage, Yoga and Wellness, Adventure, Eco -tourism, Medical, MICE etc.  
Industry can also provide the feedback. 
 
(ii) Specific Initiatives and campaigns 
 
The plans may identify specific initiatives and campaigns apart from generic  
measures applicab le to all the markets. The plans may also have targets for  
specific markets. 
 
(iii) Mega familiarization tours 
 
Plans for organizing Mega familiarization tours for specific countries and 
covering specific tourism offerings such as Culture and Heritage, Yoga and  
Wellness, Medical Value travel, Adventure tourism need to be included in the  
Plans. 
 
(iv) International Roadshows 
 
Plans for Important International Roadshows should be prepared in 
consultation with Indian Missions and Industry Stakeholders for various 
markets, which will showcase the relevant Indian Tourism products and 
offerings and B2B meetings. 
 
(v) Connect with Indian Diaspora 

57  
Missions will leverage their connect with Indian Diaspora to motivate them to  
travel to various Indian Destinations. The Mission will also strategize how can  
the diaspora be leveraged to promote Indian tourism in their host countries. 
 
4.3 Annual Events to be hosted by India 
 
Plans for important events for promotion of Inbound Tourism shall be prepared in  
consultation with Indian Missions and Industry Stakeholders. Some of the key 
events are International Buddhist Conclave, India Tourism Mart, Yoga Day etc. 
 
4.4 Annual International Events where India participates 
 
Plans for Important International Travel Marts such as WTM, ITB, ATM etc., which  
help in promoting Inbound tourism shall be prepared in consultation with Indian  
Missions and Industry Stakeholders. Indian Missions shall extend their fullest 
support to Indian delegation including businesses for successful participation. 
 
4.5 Specific Strategy for Medical and Wellness Tourism 
 
Medical tourism, especially wellness tourism and AYUSH may be promoted to 
position India as a health and wellness destination. A coherent strategy to be 
developed by Ministries of Tourism, Culture, AYUSH and External Affairs with Indian  
Missions playing a proactive role in promoting Medical and Wellness Tourism in the  
identified source markets. 
 
4.6 Specific Strategy for MICE Tourism 
 
MICE Tourism (Meetings, Incentives, Conferences, Exhibitions) constitutes an 
important element of tourism and has a multiplier effect on the economy. A specific  
strategy to promote India’s MICE offerings and winning bids for international events  
need to planned. Support from the Indian Missions will be crucial for winning the 
bids for hosting the events in India. 
 
4.7 Facilitating VISA 
 
Indian Missions can facilitate VISA for travel and tour operators and other visitors  
such as medical travellers and those attending MICE events in India. Ministry of  
Home Affairs is developing e-VISA mobile application, which can be expedited. 
 
4.8 Facilitating direct connectivity 
 
The Missions can facilitate introduction of direct connectivity from source markets.  
South East Asia, Eastern Europe and South America have huge potential for 
increasing foreign tourist arrivals to India. Therefore, it is important to introduce 

58  
direct flight connectivity from these markets which have a keen interest in India and  
have the potential to contribute to tourist traffic to India.  MoCA may look into  
initiating direct flights between India and countries that are witnessing a rise in the  
number outbound international tourists. 
 
5. Key Operational Areas 
 
5.1 Planning and monitoring of tourism trends 
 
The Missions and India Tourism overseas offices in their resp ective countries will  
carry out the following activities 
(i) Create a database, for the respective country, of travel agencies, tour 
operators, independent travel planners, MICE agencies, travel & consumer 
Media and other relevant stakeholders in the travel industry 
(ii) Monitor relevant tourism trends and opportunities and prepare quarterly 
market reports that can be shared with Ministry of Tourism and the private  
sector stakeholders in the Indian inbound tourism sector 
5.2 Public Relation & Communication 
 
The Missions and India Tourism Overseas offices need to undertake public relation  
and communication relevant to tourism promotion and will carry out the following  
activities 
(i) To track and report articles related to India in the local media 
 
(ii) To ensure placement of positive news stories in trade and consumer media 
 
(iii) To ensure placement of official press releases from MOT 
 
(iv) Image building and to counteract negative publicity as and when required 
 
(v) Active presence on Social Media 
 
5.3 Relationships & Outreach 
 
The Missions and India Tourism Overseas offices will carry out the following activities 
 
(i) To build relationships with various stakeholders to create awareness about  
Indian tourism products 
(ii) To be a source of India related information for the local travel trade, media and 
other stakeholders 

59  
(iii) To engage with museums, universities, trade organizations, local clubs etc. for 
promotion of India 
(iv) To bring annual conferences of travel and hospitality associations in the 
identified markets to India 
(v) To identify eminent opinion makers, celebrities, TV teams, tour operators etc. 
who can be invited to India under the Hospitality scheme of the Ministry 
(vi) To advise in the selection of travel shows for participation 
 
5.4 Support to visiting MOT/ State/ Industry delegations 
 
The Mission to extend necessary support to assist the Ministry of Tourism in 
organizing Road Shows, events, business visits and relevant social events during the  
visit of Ministry officials and/ or cooperating Indian agencies Extend support to State 
Governments/UT Administrations for organizing Road Shows. Inbound tour 
operators travelling from India to various source markets may be provided requisite  
support. 
 
5.5 International Cooperation & Engagement with Multilateral/ Bilateral Forums 
 
Concrete action plans  for Partnerships, learning from experiences of countries that  
have developed strong tourism sectors and collaborating for mutual benefit need to  
be worked out in pursuance of the MOUs signed with different Countries in the field  
of Tourism. 
 
Active engage ment in multilateral forums like UNWTO, G -20, ASEAN, BRICS, IBSA,  
SAARC need to be pursued. Partnerships may be explored with SAARC and ASEAN  
countries to develop and promote common packages on themes that link the 
countries such as the Buddhist circuit, R amayana circuit, Himalayan circuit, Heritage  
circuit that would yield excellent dividends to all participating nations. 
 
5.6 Engagement with international industry bodies 
 
Effective engagement  in close coordination  with Indian industry in international  
industry bodies like the World Travel and Tourism Council (WTTC), Pacific Asia Travel 
Association (PATA) etc. to collaborate with the tourism players across geographies,  
market intelligence, communicate with the global industry on key issues and 
harness their expertise for the benefit of our industry. 
 
5.7 Facilitate FDI into Tourism Sector 

60  
Government of India has allowed 100% FDI in hospitality sector. India is developing  
various destinations and actively promoting investment from Private Sector 
including Public Private Partnerships. The Missions can engage with the trade/ 
industry to promote and encourage investment in tourism and hospitality sector in  
India. 
 
6. Governance and Monitoring 
 
6.1 The Ministry of Tourism will set up a digital platfor m to bring visibility to all the  
stakeholders about the activities to promote Inbound Tourism. It will have a 
dashboard on trends and track performance of Inbound tourism from various 
countries. 
 
6.2 The Ministry of Tourism will organize quarterly meetings with relevant Ministries,  
participating States and Industry Stakeholders to review the progress on various  
initiatives and activities.

REPORT  
 
The Indian Civil Aviation sector has seen an unprecedented growth in passenger traffic in 
the recent past and a corresponding increase in the  number of Airports, Aircrafts and Flight 
routes. The launch of Regional Connectivity Scheme- Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik (RCS-UDAN) 
has further propelled this growth. The growth of India’s civil aviation sector can be gauged from 
the fact that it has consistently clocked double-di git growth in last few years and India’s 
domestic passenger traffic has more than doubled fr om around 61 million in FY 2013-14 to 
around 137 million in 2019-20, a growth of over 14%  per annum. Also, the International 
passenger traffic has grown from 47 million in FY 2 013-14 to around 67 million in FY 2019-20, 
a growth of over 6% per annum. Besides, India’s dom estic air traffic made up 69 percent of total 
airline traffic in South Asia. The World Economic Forum’s Global Competitiveness Report 2018 
ranks India as 53 rd  out of 140 countries worldwide in air transport infrastructure. India is also 
catching up with other leading aviation markets in terms of market penetration. In addition, 
transportation of cargo is also set to grow at a fa st pace in the next few years to keep pace with 
the expected growth in economy of the country. Indi a’s domestic air cargo handled grew by 8% 
Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) between FY 2013- 14 and FY 2019-20, while 
international air cargo grew by 6% per annum. From more than 700 registered aircraft, the figure 
is likely to reach 1,200 in next few years and the freighter aircrafts deployed by Indian airlines 
have increased from 7 (2018) to 28 during the last three years (2021). It has been forecasted that 
India will cross over into the top 10 air freight markets in the near future. 
2. The Niti Aayog has recognised the significant contribution of the Civil Aviation Sector to 
economic development and GDP. In its policy documen t titled ‘Strategy for New India @ 75’  
has envisaged the following strategies/ objectives for the sector:- 
 Enhance the affordability of flying to enable an in crease in domestic ticket sales from  
103.75 million in 2016-17 to 300 million by 2022. 
 
 Double air cargo handled from about 3.3 million tonnes in 2017-18 to about 6.5 million 
tonnes.  
 Expand the maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) industry from USD 1.8 billion in 
2017 to USD 2.3 billion.  
 Expand airport capacity more than five times to handle one billion trips a year.  

2  
• Enhance availability and affordability of regional air connectivity and revive/upgrade 56 
unserved airports and 31 unserved helipad through t he Regional Connectivity Scheme — 
Ude Desh Ka Aam Naagrik (RCS-UDAN).  
 Ensure that airport tariffs, taxes on fuel, landing  charges, passenger services, cargo and 
other charges are determined in an efficient, fair and transparent manner.  
3. The Ministry of Civil Aviation is responsible for t he formulation of national policies and 
programmes for the development and regulation of th e Civil Aviation sector in the country. It 
also looks after the administration of the Aircraft  Act, 1934, Aircraft Rules, 1937 and various 
other legislations pertaining to the aviation sector in the country. In addition to primary functions 
of framing of policies, the Ministry provides guidance to the organizations in the implementation 
of policy guidelines, monitors and evaluates their activities and also provides their interface with 
Parliament. It also supervises implementation by th e organizations of special programmes of the 
Government, particularly those intended for the weaker sections of society.

Greenfield Project, Brownfield Project and Defence Brownfield Project  
 
17. The Committee enquired from the Ministry about the Greenfield, Brownfield and  
Defence Brownfield projects in the Civil Aviation s ector; the advantages and disadvantages 
thereof; and whether the Ministry has formulated any guidelines in this regard. The Committee is 

9  
aware that the National Highways Authority of India  (NHAI) under the Ministry of Road 
Transport and Highways (MoRTH) has formulated such a guideline as regards Greenfield and 
Brownfield projects in Highways construction. Minis try of Civil Aviation (MoCA) apprised the 
Committee that the Ministry has already notified a Greenfield Airport Policy in 2008 in reference 
to which 21 Airport Projects have received ‘In-Prin ciple’ approval of MoCA for setting up of 
greenfield airports, out of which 8 airports have a lready been operationalised. The Ministry 
further gave the following details:- 
Greenfield Airport  
 
A Greenfield airport is conventionally referred as an aviation facility being developed on  
empty land or previously undeveloped land and an ai rport whose commissioning, planning & 
construction process is carried out from the scratc h/grassroot level. As stated above, the 
Ministry has formulated a Greenfield Airport Policy , 2008 and guidelines for setting up of 
greenfield airports. The airports which are Greenfi eld in nature are given ‘In-Principle’ 
approval as per criteria, guidelines and procedures formulated in the Greenfield Airport Policy. 
Brownfield Airport  
 
A Brownfield airport is conventionally referred to as an aviation facility, which has existing 
infrastructure for development of airport such as r unway, terminal building etc. Development 
works are carried out further on these facilities a nd additional facilities required to meet the 
increased passenger load and aircraft operations are created in phased manner. 
Advantages of Greenfield Airports 
 
 Airport at Greenfield sites can be planned as per the governing guidelines for 
unrestricted development of airport and aircraft movement upto full potential.  
 Availability of Land for future expansion of Airport.  
 
Disadvantages of Greenfield Airports 
 
 Requirement of more time and money for creation of complete new infrastructure at 
airport as well as Airport connectivity.  
 Green field airports will take more time to operationalize against brownfield airport.  
 
Advantages of Brownfield Airports 

10   
 Brownfield airports already have airport infrastructure.  
 
 As airport infrastructure already exists at Brownfield airports and it only needs to be 
upgraded as per requirement, this will lead to cost effectiveness of airport.  
 Connectivity is already available to places of importance in a city, like offices,  
hospitals, institutions etc.  
Disadvantages of Brownfield Airports 
 
 Limited scope for expansion due to land locked situation.  
 
 High cost for acquisition of land for expansion and rehabilitation.  
 
18. The Ministry also informed that it has not drawn any guidelines or blueprint regarding the 
advantages and disadvantages of the Greenfield Projects over Brownfield Projects. 
19. In reply to a query as to whether a policy and outl ine with reference to Brownfield 
Project, Greenfield Project and Defence Brownfield Project has been drawn out, the Ministry 
informed that a policy on Greenfield airports is in  place since 2008. The policy outlines the 
guidelines for setting up of Greenfield Airports ac ross the country by Government or private 
entities. As per this Policy, the promoter seeking to develop an airport has to submit the proposal to 
the Central Government for consideration by the Steering Committee. Applications for setting up 
of greenfield airport are considered by the Steerin g Committee/ competent authority for grant of 
'in-principle' approval, after they have completed all necessary formalities of obtaining pre- 
feasibility study report, site clearance, clearance s from regulatory agencies, etc. The applicant 
proposing to set up an airport can make an applicat ion to the Steering Committee in the format 
available at the website of Ministry of Civil Aviat ion at www.civilaviation.gov.in . As such 
Government of India has not formulated a Policy for  development/upgradation of Brownfield 
airports in the Country. These airports are operati onal airports and their development/upgradation 
is undertaken from time to time depending on the tr affic demand and land availability etc. by the 
concerned airport operators. 
20. The committee feels that the Ministry is off mark a s regards the understanding on 
creation of white paper for policy makers, as to ho w and why Green Field Projects are the 
future of the nation. The Ministry has had a long e xperience of developing airports which 
were owned by the State Governments or by Airport Authority of India. While a long  time 
vision is always envisaged for an Airport project to grow for next few decades, however the 

11   
Committee feels that the Brown Field Projects are i mportant to enhance the footprint of 
aviation network in the country but given an option of redoing an existing airport to that of 
a Green Field project, there should be a clear and ambitious policy of the Government to 
identify locations for furtherance of New Airports.  India being a country with large 
population, the comparison of number of aircrafts p er person in India is far less than those 
of United States of America and China which have a comparable population figure and 
geographical area. 
21. Committee would like to clarify further this point with the example of the Patna 
Airport in which over thousand crores is being spen t without adding any operational 
advantage and still continuing with all the limitat ions, which existed as far operations is 
concerned, would remain there even after spending a  thousand crores. The reason why the 
Committee has been emphasising the need of having a  distinct plan of action is a case study 
of Patna and proposed Bihta Airport, which is yet t o go for a PIB clearance with an 
estimated investment of around 800 Crores. The comm ittee is fully aware that Bihta 
Airport is going to be another duplication of exist ing facility in Patna, without any 
additional commensurate advantages, as it is a Defe nce Brown Field project. Therefore, it 
requires a fresh thinking to optimally utilize publ ic resources with a view to create world 
class facilities and provide an edge in civil aviat ion infrastructure. The State of Bihar could 
have benefited immensely from a Green Field Project , if this matter was well explained by 
the Central Government to the State Government when  the Central team on its own had 
forwarded a proposal of redeveloping the Bihta Airport. 
22. The Committee notes that it would be far too clear if the Government spells out the 
advantages and how Green Field Projects would compl etely change the face of Aviation in 
this country. Taking another example of Devanahalli  Airport Bangalore, which emerged as 
a Green Field Project, while there were two Airport s existing in the city of Bangalore. One 
was Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) and other w as Yelahanka Airbase of the Air 
Force. The State Government along with the Central Government chose to ignore both 
these airports to develop an international airport and today there is quantum jump in the 
Air Traffic of Bangalore and also emerging as a Maj or International Hub in the south. 
With these examples, which the Airport Authority an d the Ministry of Civil Aviation 
already  has,  it would be  pertinent  for  the Ministry  of  Civil  Aviation  to  spell out,  why 

12   
prospects of a Green Field Project are far superior  and have distinct advantages in terms  
of economics, passengers movement, increasing passe ngers footprint and future expansion 
possibilities and growth looking at the market size in India. 
23. The Committee notes with concern that the Ministry has so far not conducted any 
study or published any blueprint regarding the adva ntages and disadvantages of  
Greenfield and Brownfield projects. The Committee u nderstands that for Highways 
construction, the NHAI under MoRTH has already draw n out such guidelines. The 
Committee expresses concern that though both Highwa ys and Airports construction are 
infrastructure projects, yet the Ministry of Civil Aviation has lagged behind in this regard. 
The Committee feels that though the MoCA has notifi ed a Greenfield Airport policy since 
2008, yet for hastening the construction of airport s, a proper blueprint or guidelines 
regarding both Greenfield and Brownfield airports i s the need of the hour and therefore 
recommends that it may be formulated at the earlies t. The Committee also expresses its 
concern that though 21 airports had received „in-pr inciple /uni201F approval of the Ministry, since 
notification of Greenfield Airport policy in 2008, yet only 8 airports have been 
operationalized. The Committee recommends that the Ministry needs to focus on the 
operationalization of the remaining airports and fe els that the formulation of a guideline,  
as noted above, will expedite the development of airports. 
24. The Committee noted that in the next two to three y ears, there would be a proposal 
for six to seven new Greenfield airports. From the recent experiences, it has been noticed 
that the Greenfield airports which were developed during the last decade have saturated on 
their existing capacities and need further expansio n and augmentation of facilities, 
however, lack of land availability is limiting the scope of expansion of Greenfield airports. 
The Committee therefore, recommends that every Gree nfield airport must be planned in 
such a way that it should meet the requirements of at least next 40 years. Necessary land  
for the airport may be acquired based on the futuri stic planning; construction; and 
development can be undertaken in the future depending on the requirements.
