Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) services  
 
29. The Committee was informed that annual turnover of Indian MRO industry was 
approximately Rs. 2300 crore pre-Covid, which amoun ts to around 15% of India’s civil MRO 
expense. The balance 85% goes to MROs in Singapore,  Malaysia, Middle East, European Union 
(EU) and United States of America (USA) etc. The de tails of MRO services being availed at 
Indian MRO and MRO abroad are at Annexure-I. The Mi nistry also informed the Committee the 
following reasons for carrying out most of the MRO services abroad:- 
 Tax anomaly with global MROs in terms of GST and various other levies and surcharges;  
 High airport charges in terms of land rentals, airport royalty etc.;  
• Lack of support from global manufacturers – many of  whom hold back key technical 
maintenance manuals from Indian MROs;  
• Lack of counter-operability with global regulators like Federal Aviation Administration 
(FAA) of USA and European Union Aviation Safety Age ncy (EASA) – this means every 
Indian MRO has to be dependent on approvals and clearances by foreign inspectors;  
• Procedural issues – problems with custom clearances  of urgent parts consignments, 
airport entry passes for experts etc;  

18   
• Absence of large corporate houses – given the lack of profitability and attractiveness of 
the sector;  
• Artificial divide between the civil and military MRO industry – both work in silos though 
the key suppliers like Boeing, Airbus, Dassault, Safran, United Technologies Corporation 
(UTC), General Electric (GE), Honeywell, etc. are common to both;  
 The lack of availability of hangar space at key international airports in India;  
 Non-availability of spare parts in the region which  leads to frequent grounding of aircraft 
for lack of spares. This is driven by a lack of OEM  support for the Indian market, though 
it is gradually changing with growth in the market and the custom duty regime which 
discourages MROs from stocking parts on behalf of customers; 
• A large part of the frequently removed parts are co vered under the Flight Hour 
Agreement (FHA) or Power by Hours (PBH) contracts o f the airlines with large MRO’s / 
OEMs;  
 There are very limited components manufacturing capabilities within India;  
 Fleet of all the carriers in India (except Air Indi a to some extent) is leased and all these 
carriers have FHA/ PBH contracts for Line Replaceab le Units (components) primarily 
with Lufthansa Technic, Turkish Technic and Air France / KLM; and  
 April, 2020 was the beginning of the pandemic globa lly, which has adversely impacted 
the airlines financially. Their financial condition  impacts the MROs directly. Besides, 
construction projects were impacted as their effici encies were reduced due to the 
lockdowns that were in place at different times during these past two years.  
30. The Committee was further informed that the Governm ent has, however, taken various 
measures to create a conducive environment for the development of aircraft Maintenance, Repair 
and Overhaul (MRO) services and has announced new M RO Guidelines on 1st September, 2021 
with a view to create a congenial atmosphere in the  country for the development of MRO 
industry for aircraft/helicopter/drones and their e ngines and other parts. The salient features of 
the guidelines are as follows:- 
 Concession fee, in any manifestation including roya lty, shall not be levieable on new/ 
renewal of existing contracts.  

19   
 Selection of agency and procedures for allotment of  land/ space under rationalized land/ 
space rental for new MRO contracts and renewal of e xisting MRO contracts, shall be 
through e-tender by AAI.  
 The renewal of the existing land leases/ space lice nse of MRO service providers/ Aircraft 
Maintenance Organizations (AMOs) shall be on the ba sis of bidding wherein Right of 
First Refusal (RoFR) shall be given to the existing  lessee/ licensee to match the first rank 
bid in terms of the selection criteria provided its  bid is within 15% of the most 
competitive bid received.  
 The quoted/ accepted lease fee shall be escalated @ 15% after every 3rd year.  
 The maximum period of contract, new or renewal, for allotment of land/ space shall be 30 
years from the date of handing over of site.  
31. Other Steps taken by Government of India to encourage MRO services are as follows:- 
 
 Goods and Services Tax (GST) on MRO has been reduce d from 18% to 5% with full 
input tax credit from 1 st April, 2020.  
 Transactions sub-contracted by foreign Original Equ ipment Manufacturers (OEMs)/ 
MROs to domestic MRO are treated as "exports" with zero-rated GST w.e.f. 1 st April, 
2020.  
 Rules have been simplified for export of leased air craft in complete or semi knocked- 
down conditions, opening up new opportunities in re delivery checks and aircraft 
component recycling.  
 Custom duty has been waived on tools, toolkits and spares imported by MROs.  
 100% Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) has been permitted via automatic route for MRO.  
 Simplified clearance processing of parts.  
 Relaxed restrictions on utilization of duty-free parts from one year to three years.  
 The Government is facilitating civil-military MRO c onvergence by fostering greater 
technical and business collaboration.  
32. The Ministry has also highlighted the following reasons as to why MRO services are 
being availed abroad and not availed from Indian MROs: 
 Lack of Infrastructure for EASA Certified Airframe MRO Services  
 OEMs not willing to Partner with Local MROs to protect their Repair Shops Abroad.  

20   
 OEMs/Bouquet Component Service Providers not willin g to sub-contract Local MRO to 
protect their own shops and they provide spares at 10-12% of their cost, to local MROs 
which makes overhaul by local MRO unviable.  
 OEMs support required to develop landing gear shops in India  
 
33. In reply to a query as regards the impact of the in centive given to the MRO industry and 
whether any assessment was done by MoCA in this reg ard, the Ministry stated that the impact of 
incentives taken by the Government to promote MRO i ndustry has led to Original Equipment 
Manufacturers (OEMs) setting up maintenance facilit ies in India. General Electric (GE) has 
established an engine/ overhaul repair facility at Nagpur. The first phase of MRO is operational 
and quick turn repairs of engines have been carried  at Nagpur engine test cell preparatory area. 
Pratt & Whitney (PW) has established a facility at Mumbai for repair of PW 1100 engines with 
the phase-I covering engine module replacement, which is already operational. 
34. The Committee notes with serious concern that out o f the total MRO services 
turnover of Rs. 15,353 crores, the annual turnover of the Indian MRO industry is just Rs. 
2,300 crores, which is just 15% of India /uni201Fs civil MRO expense. The balance 85% MRO 
services amounting to a colossal amount of Rs. 13,0 53 crores are availed from MROs based 
abroad in Singapore, Malaysia, Middle East, EU and USA etc. The massive amount of the 
MRO services availed from abroad can be gauged from  the fact that the amount is more 
than the total B.E. allocation of Rs. 10,667 crores  for 2022-23. The Committee laments the 
huge outgo of avoidable foreign exchange. It is of the opinion that Maintenance, Repair  
and Overhaul (MRO) organizations play a major role in the economy of airline operations. 
Since, 85% of these activities are carried out abro ad, there is a strong case to bring these 
MROs to India as the MRO expenditure is expected to  grow further with the growth in  
civil aviation sector. The issues which come within  the ambit of foreign suppliers can also  
be addressed by giving them incentives to operate i n this country. India with its large 
technical manpower base can easily provide the manp ower for MRO services. The reasons 
for carrying out MRO services abroad, include tax a nomaly with global MROs in terms of 
GST/ levies/ surcharges etc.; high airport charges for land rentals, airport royalty, lack of 
availability of hangar space etc. The Committee rec ommends that the Ministry should take 
up the aforesaid issues with the Ministry of Financ e and other concerned agencies and try 
to address the issues at the earliest. The issues w hich are within the ambit of the Ministry 

21   
itself viz. airport charges, hangar space etc. should be expedi tiously resolved by the 
Ministry and AAI. 
35. The Committee notes from the reply of the Ministry that one of the reasons why 
MRO services are availed abroad is that OEMs based abroad are not willing to partner 
with local MROs to protect their repair shops abroad and they provide spares at 10-12% of 
their cost, to the local MROs which makes overhaul by local MROs unviable. The 
Committee seriously expresses its concerns on this attitude of the OEMs based abroad and 
feels that the Ministry should frame guidelines mak ing it obligatory for OEMs based 
abroad and who are getting business from Indian air lines companies to set up repair shops 
in India itself. Besides, it should also be made ma ndatory for the foreign OEMs to supply 
spare parts at the same rates available abroad or m anufacture their spare parts in India in 
collaboration with local MROs.

invariably be installed. The latest ILS systems and  night landing facilities should also be

need for expansion and alterations for installation  of ILS or security/ safety apparatus, at a

Installation of HEPA Filters at Airports  
 
72. The Committee enquired from the Ministry whether it s suggestion regarding installation 
of High Efficiency Particulate Air (HEPA) filters at airports, in view of the COVID-19 about two 
years back, has been examined and whether the techn ical feasibility and report thereof has been 
obtained and if so, whether guidelines of the Ministry in this regard to various airports have been 
issued. 
73. The Ministry in its reply stated that HEPA filters are special type of filters generally 
recommended for use in Pharmaceutical Industries an d Healthcare facilities to treat exhaust air. 
HEPA filters used in Heating, Ventilation and Air C onditioning (HVAC) system can trap 
particles up to 0.3 micron with 99.97% efficiency. However, since COVID-19 particles are as 
small as 0.06 microns, installation of HEPA filter as a barrier against COVID-19 particles is not 
an effective way to fight against spread of the vir us. Further, it is not technically feasible to 
install HEPA filters at airports as for an airport HVAC system, HEPA filters will not work 
efficiently, as addition of these filters will dras tically increase the pressure drop across the filte rs 
and existing HVAC system will not have enough power  to move air through the HEPA filters 
and. It will instead put extra stress on the system  resulting into pressure drop, lower air flow and 
poor efficiency of Air Conditioning system. Moreove r, ISHARE (Indian Society of Heating, 
Refrigeration and Air Conditioning Engineers), a pr emier institute of global level in the  
exclusive field of HVAC, had issued guidelines on o perating of Air conditioning and ventilation 
system to control spread of Corona Virus Disease (C OVID)-19 in Residences, Workspaces and 
Healthcare Facilities and recommended Minimum Effic iency Reporting Values (MERV)-13 
filters and Ultra Violet Germicidal Irradiation (UV GI) system in Offices and Commercial 
buildings and HEPA filters in Healthcare facilities  for treatment of exhaust air from COVID-19 
patients. In accordance with the guidelines issued by ISHARE, AAI has provided UVGI systems 
and replaced existing filters with MERV-13 filters in the existing Air Handling Units (AHUs) 
depending upon feasibility, at its various airports and work is in progress at some of the airports. 
74. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry that HEPA filters are not effective 
against COVID-19 virus and that it is also not tech nically feasible to install such systems at 
airports. The Committee, therefore, recommends that  as per ISHARE guidelines, UVGI 
systems and MERV-13 filters may be installed at all  the airports in the country, especially 
the ones where there is international arrivals from  countries where COVID-19 cases are 

36   
still prevalent. The Committee desires to know the airport-wise status of installation of 
UVGI systems and MERV-13 filters across the country  and the action plan of the Ministry 
to combat future waves of COVID-19.

Rationalisation of Air Fares and Cancellation Charges in Domestic Sectors  
 
86. The Committee during its deliberations expressed co ncern at the fact that in domestic 
sector, private airlines are charging different air fares for same sector, route and same duration of 
flights and desired to know whether Ministry has an y guidelines regarding rationalization of 
fares. The Ministry apprised the Committee that wit h repeal of Air Corporation Act in March, 
1994, the provision of air fare approval was dispen sed with by the Government. At present, air 
fare is neither regulated nor fixed by the Government. Airlines are free to fix the reasonable tariff 
under the provision of Sub-rule (1) of Rule 135, Ai rcraft Rules, 1937, having regard to all 
relevant factors including the cost of operation, c haracteristics of service, reasonable profit and 
the generally prevailing tariff. 
87. Further, Ministry apprised that as per prevailing r egulation, all scheduled domestic 
airlines are required to display route-wise and cat egory-wise fares on their respective websites. 
The airlines remain compliant to the Sub Rule (2) o f Rule 135 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, as  
long as the fare charged by them is in line with fa re displayed on their website. Under the 
provision of Sub Rule (1) of Rule 135 of the Aircra ft Rules, 1937, every air transport 
undertaking engaged in scheduled air services requi re to establish tariff having regard to all 
relevant factors, including cost of operation, char acteristic of services, reasonable profit   and 

40   
the generally prevailing tariff. Airlines are free to charge reasonable air fares as per their 
operational viability and the airlines remain compliant to the prevailing  regulations. 
88. However, due to the unprecedented circumstances pre vailing due to COVID-19 
pandemic, fare bands with upper and lower limits we re introduced by the Government invoking 
power under Section 8(B) of the Aircraft Act, 1934 as a temporary measure. The fare bands  
serve the dual purpose of protecting the interests of the travelers as well as that of the airlines, 
and have been revised from time to time. Fare cappi ng is presently applicable on a rolling basis 
for a 15 days cycle.

a charter of the passenger’s rights, which inter-alia , defines certain rights to passengers in case   
of flight delays, flight cancellations, boarding de nied due to overbooking, flight diversions, 
cancellation charges and lost/ delayed/ damaged bag gage. To make the passenger charter 
enforceable, Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) has inter-alia amended the Civil 
Aviation Requirements (CAR), Section-3, Series M, P art-II titled "Refund of Airline Tickets to 
Passengers of Public Transport Undertakings", with the following provisions:- 
 Cancellation charges must be indicated prominently at the time of booking.  
 
 Under no circumstances, the airline or its agent shall levy cancellation charges more than 
the basic fare plus fuel surcharge.  
 The airlines shall not levy any additional charges to process the refund.  
 
90. In reply to another query of the Committee regardin g ticket fares in domestic sectors and 
reasons as to why airlines are charging extra fare for selecting the seats while booking of ticket 
and whether there should only be one price for the same flight for all seats, the  Ministry 
informed that travel by air is a contractual matter  between airline and passenger, which is 
commercial in nature. DGCA has issued Air Transport  Circular 01 of 2021 titled "Unbundle of 
services and fees by scheduled airlines". Under the  provision of said circular, service for 
preferential seating is unbundled and charged separ ately on opt-in basis. As per the information 
received from Airlines, they offer some preferentia l seats on opt-in basis. However, passengers 

41   
can always select any free seat available or would be assigned a seat, free of charge at the time of 
check-in at the airport, if they do not wish to purchase a preferred seat. 
91. As regards pricing of the tickets, the Committee no tes the reply of the Ministry that 
at present, air fare is neither regulated nor fixed  by the Government and airlines are free  
to fix the reasonable tariff under the provision of  Sub-rule (1) of Rule 135, Aircraft Rules, 
1937 having regard to all relevant factors includin g the cost of operation, characteristics of 
service, reasonable profit and the generally prevai ling tariff. Also, as regards the concern  
of the Committee regarding extra fare for seat sele ction, the Ministry has stated that travel 
by air is a contractual matter between airline and passenger, which is commercial in  
nature. The Committee is of the opinion that for Ci vil Aviation sector to grow in an open 
market, it is justifiable that the private airline operators should be given a free hand to fix 
the air fares as they are governed by competition. However, the Committee would like to 
draw the attention of the Ministry to the provision  of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, which has 
specifically mentions that the fares should be reas onable and should maintain reasonable 
profit. In the above context, the Committee feels t hat the reply of the Ministry stating that 
air travel is purely a contractual matter between t he airline and the passenger, is not at all 
justified. The Committee is of the opinion that a b alance also must be maintained between 
the commercial interests of the airlines and the in terest of the passengers. The Committee 
feels that the passengers should not be fleeced in the garb of commercialization and 
therefore recommends that the Ministry should maint ain a close watch on the fare pricing 
by the airlines to ensure that it is not exorbitant . It also recommends that at least for the 
same sector, route and duration of flight, in all t he private airlines, the Ministry should 
issue guidelines so as to ensure similar or least v ariation in fares among all airlines. The 
Committee is also of the opinion that fixing of dif ferent fares for selection of seats in the 
same flight is arbitrary and unjustifiable. Hence, Committee on the principle of equity feels 
that all the seats in a same flight should have sam e fare. The Committee also recommends 
that the Ministry should strictly enforce the DGCA Charter and ensure that under no 
circumstances, the airlines levies cancellation cha rges more than the basic fare plus fuel 
surcharge. The Committee may be informed about the mechanism adopted by the Ministry 
to ensure that the Aircraft Rules, 1937 and DGCA Ch arter is being followed in letter and 
spirit by all private airlines.

The committee feels that the Ministry is off mark a s regards the understanding on creation 
of white paper for policy makers, as to how and why  Green Field Projects are the future of 
the nation. The Ministry has had a long experience of developing airports which were 
owned by the State Governments or by Airport Authority of India. While a long time vision 
is always envisaged for an Airport project to grow for next few decades, however the 
Committee feels that the Brown Field Projects are i mportant to enhance the footprint of 
aviation network in the country but given an option of redoing an existing airport to that of 
a Green Field project, there should be a clear and ambitious policy of the Government to 
identify locations for furtherance of New Airports.  India being a country with large 
population, the comparison of number of aircrafts p er person in India is far less than those 
of United States of America and China which have a comparable population figure and 
geographical area. 
(Para 20) 
 
Committee would like to clarify further this point with the example of the Patna Airport in 
which over thousand crores is being spent without a dding any operational advantage and 
still continuing with all the limitations, which existed as far operations is concerned,  would 

55   
remain there even after spending a thousand crores.  The reason why the Committee has 
been emphasising the need of having a distinct plan  of action is a case study of Patna and 
proposed Bihta Airport, which is yet to go for a PI B clearance with an estimated 
investment of around 800 Crores. The committee is f ully aware that Bihta Airport is going 
to be another duplication of existing facility in P atna, without any additional  
commensurate advantages, as it is a Defence Brown F ield project. Therefore, it requires a 
fresh thinking to optimally utilize public resource s with a view to create world class 
facilities and provide an edge in civil aviation in frastructure. The State of Bihar could have 
benefited immensely from a Green Field Project, if this matter was well explained by the 
Central Government to the State Government when the  Central team on its own had 
forwarded a proposal of redeveloping the Bihta Airport. 
(Para 21) 
 
The Committee notes that it would be far too clear if the Government spells out the 
advantages and how Green Field Projects would compl etely change the face of Aviation in 
this country. Taking another example of Devanahalli  Airport Bangalore, which emerged as 
a Green Field Project, while there were two Airport s existing in the city of Bangalore. One 
was Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) and other w as Yelahanka Airbase of the Air

these airports to develop an international airport and today there is quantum jump in the 
Air Traffic of Bangalore and also emerging as a Maj or International Hub in the south. 
With these examples, which the Airport Authority an d the Ministry of Civil Aviation 
already has, it would be pertinent for the Ministry  of Civil Aviation to spell out, why

of economics, passengers movement, increasing passe ngers footprint and future expansion 
possibilities and growth looking at the market size in India.

The Committee notes with concern that the Ministry has so far not conducted any study or 
published any blueprint regarding the advantages an d disadvantages of Greenfield and

allow domestic airlines to fly over defence airfiel ds in consultation with the Ministry. 
Hence, the Ministry should take up this issue expeditiously with the MoD. 
(Para 28) 
 
Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) services  
 
The Committee notes with serious concern that out o f the total MRO services turnover of 
Rs. 15,353 crores, the annual turnover of the India n MRO industry is just Rs. 2,300 crores, 
which is just 15% of India /uni201Fs civil MRO expense. The balance 85% MRO services 
amounting to a colossal amount of Rs. 13,053 crores  are availed from MROs based abroad 
in Singapore, Malaysia, Middle East, EU and USA etc . The massive amount of the MRO 
services availed from abroad can be gauged from the  fact that the amount is more than the 
total B.E. allocation of Rs. 10,667 crores for 2022 -23. The Committee laments the huge 
outgo of avoidable foreign exchange. It is of the o pinion that Maintenance, Repair and 
Overhaul (MRO) organizations play a major role in t he economy of airline operations. 
Since, 85% of these activities are carried out abro ad, there is a strong case to bring these 
MROs to India as the MRO expenditure is expected to  grow further with the growth in  
civil aviation sector. The issues which come within  the ambit of foreign suppliers can also 
be addressed by giving them incentives to operate i n this country. India with its large 

58   
technical manpower base can easily provide the manp ower for MRO services. The reasons 
for carrying out MRO services abroad, include tax a nomaly with global MROs in terms of 
GST/ levies/ surcharges etc.; high airport charges for land rentals, airport royalty, lack of 
availability of hangar space etc. The Committee rec ommends that the Ministry should take 
up the aforesaid issues with the Ministry of Financ e and other concerned agencies and try 
to address the issues at the earliest. The issues w hich are within the ambit of the Ministry 
itself viz. airport charges, hangar space etc. should be expedi tiously resolved by the 
Ministry and AAI. 
(Para 34) 
 
The Committee notes from the reply of the Ministry that one of the reasons why MRO 
services are availed abroad is that OEMs based abroad are not willing to partner with local 
MROs to protect their repair shops abroad and they provide spares at 10-12% of their  
cost, to the local MROs which makes overhaul by loc al MROs unviable. The Committee 
seriously expresses its concerns on this attitude o f the OEMs based abroad and feels that  
the Ministry should frame guidelines making it obli gatory for OEMs based abroad and  
who are getting business from Indian airlines compa nies to set up repair shops in India 
itself. Besides, it should also be made mandatory f or the foreign OEMs to supply spare 
parts at the same rates available abroad or manufac ture their spare parts in India in 
collaboration with local MROs. 
(Para 35) 
 
Airports Authority of India  
 
The Committee hopes that the construction of airpor ts at Mopa in Goa, Navi Mumbai in 
Maharashtra and expansion of Delhi, Bangalore, Hyde rabad airports and the construction 
which has already been delayed due to COVID-19 lock downs, would be expedited and 
completed as per the revised schedule. The Committe e notes that the concessionaires are 
required to take over the commercial operations wit hin 180 days of signing of agreements. 
The Committee desires to know whether commercial op erations has been taken over by 
concessionaires at Mangaluru, Lucknow and Ahmedabad  airports as 180 days had lapsed. 
For the proposed airports at Guwahati, Jaipur and T hiruvananthapuram, the Committee 
would like to know the status of COD and whether they are likely to take over operations 

59   
by the targeted date. The Committee also desires to know whether the AAI imposes penalty 
on concessionaires in case of a default as regards delay in COD.

The Committee is also of the view that security and  safety measures, presently available at 
the airports are generally not upto standards, due to which there are frequent security 
lapses. The ILS systems are also lacking at airport s, which makes night landing  and 
landing during rainy seasons risky. The Committee, therefore, recommends that at all 
under construction airports, security and safety eq uipment of world-class level should 
invariably be installed. The latest ILS systems and  night landing facilities should also be 
incorporated at the planning stage of airports, so that the flights can operate smoothly even 
in bad weather conditions, reducing the need for diversion of flights. The Committee is also 
of the view that planning for airport construction should be futuristic, so that there is no 
need for expansion and alterations for installation  of ILS or security/ safety apparatus, at a 
later stage, which inconveniences the passengers an d also disturbs the flight operations at 
airports. 
(Para 39)

accorded priority. The Committee is of the opinion that the airport is of prime significance, 
as it will increase faster connectivity and access to the remote North-Eastern region. The

resolved, to ensure that the Hollongi airport is operationalized at the earliest.

Jaipur Airport 
 
The Committee notes that for the Jaipur Airport, th e concerned concessionaire is obligated 
to develop and expand the airport though AAI is not required to make any investment. The 

60

Requirement of Air Traffic Controllers (ATCOs)  
 
The Committee notes with serious concern that there  is a huge backlog of 708 vacancies in

created in 2013, 2014 and 2015 only. Since the year  2017, there has been no post creation at

taken with DPE only recently. The Committee is of t he opinion that the demand for  
ATCOs will rise exponentially with the growth of th e aviation sector in the country and

well in advance and inducted ATCOs continuously ove r the years. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that procedural issues regard ing manpower requirements of 
ATCOs should be addressed immediately to ensure ope rationalization of new airports that

Flying Training Organisations (FTOs)  

61   
The Committee notes that there would be a growing r equirement of around 1000 pilots 
every year in the near future. The Committee also n otes that a liberalized FTO policy has

entities who want to start an FTO. The Committee su pports the new initiatives of the

therefore gear up for the requirement of FTOs and s et up FTOs in a time bound manner. 
The Committee also notes that the Ministry has take n up the issue of reduction of GST on

regard. The Committee also recommends that keeping in view of the Atmanirbhar Bharat, 
sufficient Flight Training Organisations (FTOs) may  be established in various parts of the 
country to ensure that our boys and girls are not g oing to foreign countries to get pilot 
training.

The Committee notes the acute shortage of skilled manpower and proper training institutes

opportunities for the youth. The Committee observes  that other than the highly specialized 
jobs like commercial pilots and aircraft engineers,  there are non-technical jobs like 
airhostess, flight attendants, flight pursers, cabi n crew, ground/ cargo handling staff, 
administrative/ sales staff, where there can be a l ot of job creations. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that proper training institut es at low cost, may be setup all across 
the country to provide requisite training in the af oresaid airlines services, so that the youth 
of the country may be gainfully employed. 
(Para 56) 
 
Handling of Air Cargo  
 
The Committee notes with serious concern that over the last five years, the bulk of the Air 
Cargo has been handled by the International freighters and the Indian freighters have 

62   
handled less than 40% of the total share. The AAICL AS, a company wholly dedicated to 
development of air cargo, logistics and allied serv ices, was set up, as late as 2016, which

freighters. The Committee feels that the Indian air  cargo sector has immense potential, 
which is seen from the fact that strong resilience has been shown by the sector, even during 
the COVID-19 pandemic. The Committee notes the init iatives of the Ministry and 
recommends that all out efforts should be made to i ncrease the share of the Indian cargo 
freighters in the near future, so that the outgo of  foreign exchange can be reduced. The 
growth in this sector will also create new avenues of employment and aid the country /uni201Fs 
economic growth.

Eastern Region is primarily based on horticulture, agriculture and tea cultivation, which 
can prosper only if proper markets are created for the sale of these products. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the existing Dibrugarh airport which is a major 
airport in the North-Eastern Region, may be develop ed as a standard airport for transport 
of horticulture, agriculture and tea products to all the regions of the country.

Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS)-UDAN (Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik)

sufficient to meet the requirements of the UDAN Sch eme in accordance with the status of

make the UDAN Scheme a success and realize the drea m of the common man to avail of 
affordable civil aviation. 
(Para 65) 
 
Delays in operation of some RCS Airports  

63   
The Committee notes that the Government deserves ap preciation for operationalizing the 
long delayed RCS projects. The Committee also notes  that the reasons for the delay in

The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry that HEPA filters are not effective against 
COVID-19 virus and that it is also not technically feasible to install such systems at

systems and MERV-13 filters may be installed at all  the airports in the country, especially

The Committee expresses its serious concern at the fact that despite charging passengers, 
PBB or aerobridge facilities are not being used by private airlines to reduce operational

apathetic and unreasonable attitude of the private airlines and strongly recommends that 

64   
its circular on the aforesaid subject may be strict ly enforced. The Committee also

recommends that in the case of cancellation or dela y of flights, a provision should be 
compulsorily made by airlines to provide a waiting hall/ VIP lounge for the passengers and 
food, water and snacks should also be served to the m and the expenses for the same should 
be borne by the concerned airlines. The Committee also directs the Ministry to do a ground 
survey of all the airports and check whether the DG CA guidelines in this regard are being 
followed. 
(Para 78) 
 
High prices of Food and Beverages at the Airports 
 
The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry but o bserves that food/ beverage prices are 
very expensive at all airport food outlets. Tea, co ffee and refreshments may be available at

that the Ministry/ AAI should ensure that its Circu lar on food prices is being strictly 
followed at all the airports and packaged food is not sold at higher than MRP. 
(Para 80) 
 
Water and Snacks for Passengers in Airlines 
 
The Committee feels that atleast a policy may be co nsidered for providing a small

Accessibility features at airports for disabled passengers  

65   
The Committee applauds the sensitivity and care sho wn towards the needs of the  
differently abled persons and also appreciates that  79 out of 87 AAI airports are already

Rationalisation of Air Fares and Cancellation Charges in Domestic Sectors  
 
As regards pricing of the tickets, the Committee no tes the reply of the Ministry that at 
present, air fare is neither regulated nor fixed by  the Government and airlines are free to 
fix the reasonable tariff under the provision of Su b-rule (1) of Rule 135, Aircraft Rules, 
1937 having regard to all relevant factors includin g the cost of operation, characteristics of 
service, reasonable profit and the generally prevai ling tariff. Also, as regards the concern  
of the Committee regarding extra fare for seat sele ction, the Ministry has stated that travel 
by air is a contractual matter between airline and passenger, which is commercial in  
nature. The Committee is of the opinion that for Ci vil Aviation sector to grow in an open 
market, it is justifiable that the private airline operators should be given a free hand to fix 
the air fares as they are governed by competition. However, the Committee would like to 
draw the attention of the Ministry to the provision  of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, which has 
specifically mentions that the fares should be reas onable and should maintain reasonable 
profit. In the above context, the Committee feels t hat the reply of the Ministry stating that 
air travel is purely a contractual matter between t he airline and the passenger, is not at all 
justified. The Committee is of the opinion that a b alance also must be maintained between 
the commercial interests of the airlines and the in terest of the passengers. The Committee 
feels that the passengers should not be fleeced in the garb of commercialization and 
therefore recommends that the Ministry should maint ain a close watch on the fare pricing 
by the airlines to ensure that it is not exorbitant . It also recommends that at least for the 
same sector, route and duration of flight, in all t he private airlines, the Ministry should 
issue guidelines so as to ensure similar or least v ariation in fares among all airlines. The 
Committee is also of the opinion that fixing of dif ferent fares for selection of seats in the 

66   
same flight is arbitrary and unjustifiable. Hence, Committee on the principle of equity feels 
that all the seats in a same flight should have sam e fare. The Committee also recommends 
that the Ministry should strictly enforce the DGCA Charter and ensure that under no 
circumstances, the airlines levies cancellation cha rges more than the basic fare plus fuel 
surcharge. The Committee may be informed about the mechanism adopted by the Ministry 
to ensure that the Aircraft Rules, 1937 and DGCA Ch arter is being followed in letter and 
spirit by all private airlines. 
(Para 91) 
 
Seaplane Policy  
 
The Committee expresses serious concern that the se aplane policy is still not in place and is 
still being finalized in consultation with stakehol ders. The Committee also laments the fact 
that the first seaplane that was operationalized, w as stopped due to technical reasons. It 
expresses concern at the lack of seriousness of the  Ministry, as regards Seaplane policy.  
The Committee has repeatedly pointed out the need f or Seaplane policy in view of the fact 
that our country is endowed with rivers and lakes. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that a feasibility study may be conducted in the No rth-Eastern Region for operation of

stresses on the expeditious finalization of Seaplan e policy. It also recommends that proper 
planning should be done before start of the operati ons, so that the operations are not 
halted.

The Committee is of the opinion that adequate conne ctivity of airports with roads and

reach their destinations, from the airports, in a s mooth and safe manner. Further, the 
Committee is also of the firm opinion that Ministry  should collaborate with the State 
Governments and other stakeholders to ensure that land is allocated within a specific   time 

67   
frame for ensuring adequate road and rail connectiv ity to the airports. The Government

connectivity. 
(Para 97) 
 
Considering the importance of the issue, the Committee had earlier taken up the issue in its 
297 th Report on the subject „Functioning of Airports Auth ority of India /uni201F. The Ministry in 
its action taken notes on the aforesaid Report info rmed that the project of National Master 
Plan incorporating the Airports, Roadways, Railways , Shipping, Gas pipe lines, Power

Chairperson, AAI to Chief Secretaries of various State Governments to align and relate the 
City Master Plans also with the Airport Master Plans. 
(Para 98) 
In view of the above reply, the Committee in its 30 8 th Action Taken Report on the 
Recommendations/ Observations contained in its Two Hundred and Ninety Seventh Report 
on the subject „Functioning of Airports Authority of India /uni201F, had noted the proactive action 
taken by the Ministry, to ensure connectivity, and that a letter had been sent by

(Para 99) 

68   
Helicopter operations in the country  
 
The Committee is of the opinion that transportation  of both passengers and cargo by 
helicopter holds a great potential in our country, especially in hilly areas, where it is

been set for the process. The Committee also apprec iates the new initiative „Heli-Disha /uni201F 
wherein administrative guidance would be provided f or civil helicopter operations. The 
Committee hopes that this will facilitate and help in the growth of helicopter operations in

Promotion of Drone Industry  
 
The Committee is of the firm opinion that drones of fer significant benefits to almost all 
sectors of the economy. Drones can create employmen t potential for the youth and can aid 
the economic growth of the country in a big way, if  it is given a proper policy direction.

country is primarily an agricultural country, use of drones in agriculture can help  increase 

69   
the agricultural productivity of any crop. The Comm ittee commends the enactment of

Development of Aero Sports  
The Committee notes that a mere token allocation of  Rs. one crore has been made for the

great potential for Aero Sports. It can act as a bo ost for adventure tourism in the country,

Leveraging Tourism through Airports  
 
The Committee feels that airports act as a first ga te of entry for both the domestic and

the airports leave a lasting impact on the mind of a tourist and also create interest in them

recommends that besides offering tourist destinations suggested by Ministry of Tourism for

70  
sculpture displays. The Committee recommends that p romotional signages for promoting 
tourism can be explored through commercial concessi onaires. The AAI can explore the

to the international tourists, which will help in promotion of tourism in the country. 
(Para 115) 
 
Evacuation of Stranded Indians in Ukraine  
 
The Committee notes that the Government has embarke d upon a massive operation 
namely, „Operation Ganga /uni201F, to evacuate stranded Indian nationals, especially , students, 
from the war torn region of Ukraine. Some private a irlines and Indian Air Force are 
engaged in this effort, through special flights. Th e Committee understands that the 
Government of India is also exploring options for e vacuating the stranded nationals 
through corridor/ cross border roads to neighbourin g countries and thereafter bringing 
them back to the country by air. The Committee appl auds this well-coordinated 
humanitarian efforts of the Ministries of Civil Avi ation; Defence; and External Affairs and

arrangements for their transport to their native places.

Culture plays an important and pivotal role in the development agenda of any nation. 
It represents a set of shared attitudes, values, go als and practices. Culture and creativity 
manifest themselves in almost all economic, social and other activities. India is a vast and 
diverse country with a rich cultural heritage that has been widely appreciated all over the 
world. 
 
2. The mandate of the Ministry of Culture revolves aro und preservation and 
conservation of our cultural heritage and promotion  of all forms of art and culture, both 
tangible and intangible. The functional spectrum of  this Ministry is wide, ranging from 
generating cultural awareness at grassroots level t o promoting cultural exchanges at 
international level. 
 
3. Broadly, the Ministry is working on protection, dev elopment and promotion of all 
types of Heritage and Culture namely, tangible Heri tage, Intangible Heritage and Knowledge 
Heritage. In addition, the Ministry also harbours t he responsibility of Gandhian Heritage and 
Commemoration of important historical events and centenaries of great personalities. 
 
4. Major programmes/activities relating to promotion, dissemination, preservation and 
conservation of the cultural heritage of the countr y are being implemented through a network 
of two attached offices, six subordinate offices an d 28 Autonomous organisations by the 
Ministry. It also implements schemes for promotion and dissemination of Art and Culture 
under umbrella(s) namely; Centenaries and Anniversa ries Schemes; Kala Sanskriti Vikas 
Yojana, National Mission on Cultural Mapping and Ro admap, Development of Museum, 
Development of Libraries and Archives and Global En gagement and International 
cooperation which also includes two Missions namely : National Mission on Libraries and 
National Gandhi Heritage site Mission. It has no Centrally Sponsored Schemes. 
 
5. On the salient features of the Budget of 2022-23 , the Ministry in its written reply has 
informed that the budgetary allocation for 2022-23 is about 11.95% more than the budgetary 
provisions at BE 2021-22. As per re-classification of expenditure under accounting heads 
approved by Ministry of Finance, the Ministry has p repared the entire expenditure in the 
following three major categories:

3357.45 crore in BE 2022-23 as compared to the proj ection of Rs 3843.68 crore in BE 
2021-22 by the Ministry. The Committee observes tha t Culture is integral to the 
development of the country because it promotes econ omic growth providing 
employment to a large section of population and spu rs other economic sectors thereby, 
contributing to the GDP of the country as also play s an important role in uniting the 
country. Further it is instrumental in sustenance o f our rich and diverse cultural 
heritage. Since the Ministry of Culture has the one rous responsibility of the 
preservation, development and promotion of the coun try's tangible and intangible 
heritage, the Committee is convinced that the BE allocation of 3009.05 crore for 2022-23 
is not commensurate with the fund requirements of t he Ministry. It  may  impact the 
vital activities of promotion and preservation of o ur cultural heritage. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry should be p rovided with the projected 
financial outlay at RE 2022-23 stage so that the Mi nistry can achieve its targets/plans  
for preservation and conservation of our cultural h eritage and promotion of art and 
culture. 
 
10. In a reply to the Committee, the Ministry has state d that approved outlay for the 
Ministry for 2021-22 has been Rs. 2687.99 crores, r educed further to Rs. 2665.00 crores at 
RE stage. Against the approved outlay, the Ministry  has incurred an expenditure of Rs. 
1842.05 crores by 31 January 2022. Reasons for less  expenditure given by the Ministry are 
COVID pandemic and restrictions on tours and travels in the period. 
 
11. The Committee observes that the Ministry should ide ntify a core set of priorities 
so that the budgeted allocations are not divided wi th a very thin spread in numerous 

5  
areas and become less impactful. The Committee acco rdingly recommends the Ministry 
to review its priorities and concentrate on schemes /programmes which are absolutely 
essential so that scarce resources could be optimal ly utilized for achieving the desired 
results in focused areas.

13. The Archaeological Survey of India was set up in 1861 and is an attached office of the 
Ministry . Its main functions are preservation, con servation and development of protected 
monuments and sites including World Heritage Monume nts and antiquities, exploration and 
excavation of ancient sites, specialized study of i nscriptions and Indian architecture, 
maintenance of Archaeological site Museums, operati on of the Antiquities and Art Treasures 
Act, and research and Training in different areas o f Archaeology. It has 3693 monuments 
(including World Heritage Monuments) comprising pre -historic stone-age sites, temples, 
mosques, churches and forts. A National Mission for  Monuments and Antiquities has also 
been operationalised in ASI. 

6  
14. Out of the Ministry's proposed budget for 2022-23 , ASI has been allocated 35% of  
the total   outlay of   the   Ministry of Culture i. e. Rs. 1052.98 crore under Revenue and    Rs. 
27.36 Crores under Capital , a total of Rs. 1080.34 Crores 
 
 
15. The Committee is pleased to note that the budgetary  allocation of ASI has been 
increased from RE 2021-22 allocation of Rs. 915.43 crores to Rs. 1080.34 crores in BE 
2022-23. The Committee observes that India is a cou ntry with obvious constraints in 
resources. Hence in order to obtain the best possib le outcomes, it is imperative that 
allocation of resources is prioritized across compe ting ends and the available funds are 
deployed in a more efficient and productive manner.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry should make efforts to  make optimum utilisation of 
funds available in an efficient manner so that cons ervation, development and 
maintenance of the protected monuments of ASI are c arried out and the best results are 
achieved. With the gradual removal of COVID-19 rest rictions more and more tourism 
activities are going to increase. ASI should make f resh endeavours to make use of this 
opportunity to generate more revenue through e-tick eting and other means available to 
it. 
 
16. The Committee notes that in the wake of the Coronav irus pandemic, ASI 
monuments and sites received lesser footfall in 201 9-20 and 2020-21. The Committee 
would like to observe that as the spread of Corona Virus is likely to see a decrease in 
2022-23, ASI should chalk out plans for acceleratin g ongoing programmes for 
conservation and preservation of monuments. The Com mittee hopes that 2022-23 
augurs well for ASI and also the tourists visiting the monuments. The Committee hopes 
that more and more tourists are likely to visit mon uments and this would help in 
generating more revenue during this year and touris ts with logistic support are 
facilitated. 
 
17. The Committee further recommends that since influx of tourists provides 
livelihood to significant sections of the populatio n, there is ample scope for growth and 
employment generation in this sector as Covid restr ictions are being relaxed. The 
Ministry should harness the huge potential of cultural heritage for this purpose. 

7  
18. In its Two Hundred Eighty Ninth (289 th ) Report, the Committee recommended

VACANCIES IN VARIOUS ORGANIZATIONS OF THE MINISTRY  
 
34. Replying to a query whether any review has been done in the recent past regarding the 
personnel requirements of ASI for proper developmen t and preservation of centrally  
protected monuments, the Ministry in its written re ply has stated that a review has been done 
regarding the personnel requirement of ASI for prop er development and preservation of 
Centrally protected monuments. As a result, 758 pos ts have been created in 2021. Nearly 400 
of the newly created posts belong to the conservati on cadre responsible for upkeep/ 
preservation of Monuments. 
 
35. The Ministry in its written reply has furnished the  details of the vacancies and 
the steps taken to fill them in ASI (placed at Anne xure-I) and other organizations 
(Annexure-II) of the Ministry. The Committee feels that the vacancy details reflect a 
very pathetic state of affairs in all the organizat ions of the Ministry. In the Archaeology 
Cadre of ASI, against the total sanctioned strength  of 420, the vacant positions are 166, 
similarly in the Conservation Cadre, against the to tal strength of 918 there is a 
mammoth vacancy of 452 positions. The situation is not any better in other Cadres of 
ASI or other organisations of the Ministry. The Com mittee thus finds it difficult to 
understand how the Ministry can ensure the efficien cy of its organizations and manage 
to meet the present human resource needs of the res pective organisations, leave alone 
there being any scope for new initiatives by the or ganisations. The Committee strongly 
recommends that the Ministry may set up a foolproof mechanism in place to ensure that 
the staffing requirements of all its organizations are met at all times, so as to enable 
them to carry out their mandate in letter and spirit. 
 
36. The Committee is anguished to note the large scale vacancies in all the 
organizations of the Ministry for years together an d shocked to find that in some cadres 
the vacancies are more than 50% of the sanctioned s trength. It fails to understand how 
the Ministry will achieve the task of conserving th e culture and heritage of such a vast 
country with less than 50% of the sanctioned strength. 
 
37. The Committee notes with concern that a large numbe r of vacancies in  
important organizations like ASI, National Archives , Anthropological Survey of India 
etc.       are vacant for a considerable period of time. The Committee, therefore, strongly 

12   
comments that concerted efforts be taken to fill up  the vacancies at a fast pace to 
improve the organisational functioning. It is obser ved that due to not filling up the 
vacancies regularly the organizations are facing deemed abolition of several posts which 
have many other ramifications. The Committee feels that most of the organizations in 
the Ministry require specialized qualifications and  the students/candidates who study 
these subjects do not have many other opportunities  and if the posts are not filled 
timely, many qualified and talented candidates woul d be age barred, thus causing loss  
to the Government by spending in their education an d not availing the benefits of their 
knowledge/expertise as well as career of the candid ates. Similarly delayed promotions 
also play a negative role in the morale of the offi cials. The Committee is, therefore, of  
the considered opinion that all the vacancies to be  filled by promotions must be filled, at 
the earliest within a span of six months and the Di rect Recruitment vacancies be filled 
up within a year. The Committee also recommends tha t the organisations should 
identify the anticipated vacancies of Direct Recrui tment and request UPSC/SSC in 
advance to initiate action to fill up the vacancies  which will enable the organisations to 
serve better for the purpose for which they have been established.

47. Replying to a query about the roadblocks being face d by the National Monuments

country, the Ministry in its written reply has stat ed that as per Section 20E(1) of the Ancient

(INTACH), or such other expert Heritage bodies as m ay be notified by the Central 
Government, shall prepare Heritage bye-laws in resp ect of each protected monument and 
protected area. Vide Gazette notification no. 1671 dated 30.08.2012, the Regional Directors  
of ASI have been notified as Competent Authorities for the purpose of preparation of HBLs  
as per section 20E of the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites Remains Act, 1958. 
 
48. As regards the actions to expedite the Heritage Bye  Laws for all the protected

in the process of being notified for Heritage Consu ltations and Preparation of 
Heritage Bye -Laws. 
 
(ii) Preparation of Heritage bye–Laws: As mentioned abov e, 30 more heritage 
bodies located all over the country have recently b een approved by the HCM for the 
purpose of Section 20E of the AMASR Act, 1958. Thes e are in the process of being 
notified. It has been decided that the draft herita ge bye-laws will henceforth be 
prepared by these notified heritage bodies and the role of Regional Directors of ASI 
will be of vetting such HBLs and then forwarding th em to the NMA. Draft Request

(iii) Heritage Consultation: The preparation of draft her itage bye-laws will

of HBLs has been delegated to the Heritage Bodies, a separate Heritage consultation

in order to promote and strengthen Indian culture a broad by sanctioning grant-in-aid  
to Indo-foreign friendship cultural societies for achieving the desired results. 
(Para 52) 
 
 
The Committee notes that as against the BE 2021-22 allocation of Rs 9.90 crores, the RE 
allocation has been increased to Rs. 10.50 crores i n RE 21-22. But the  actual 
expenditure till 31.01.2022 is only Rs 5.11 crores,  i.e., less than 50%. The Committee 
desired to be apprised of the reasons for less than  50% utilisation under this head and 
the basis on which the budget allocation is being i ncreased. The Committee also  
requests that the Ministry should also ensure that the balance 50% of funds are spent 
fully. The Ministry also must ensure that in future , funds are spent evenly throughout 
the year. 
(Para 53) 
 
 
NATIONAL MISSION FOR PRESERVATION OF MANUSCRIPTS 
The Committee notes that Rs. 3.28 crores was alloca ted in B.E. 2021-22 but it is 
surprised to note that there is no allocation in R. E. 2021-22 and BE 2022-23. The 
Committee fails to understand the reasons for the s ame. The Committee recommends 
that proper allocation be made in future for such a n important area so that a national 
resource base for manuscripts can be preserved and created. 
(Para 55) 
 
 
NATIONAL MISSION ON CULTURAL MAPPING AND ROADMAP 
The Committee is pleased to note that an allocation  of Rs. 19.13 crore on account of 
National Mission on Cultural Mapping and Roadmap ha s been made in BE 2022-23. 
This will go a long way in achieving its aims. The Committee hopes the fund allocated 
for the same will be utilised in the most prudent, planned and beneficial manner and 
would like to be apprised of the actual spendings under this head in the last few years. 
(Para 57) 

37   
SUPPORT TO ACADEMIES, MUSEUMS, LIBRARIES, BUDDHIST TIBETAN 
INSTITUTIONS AND MEMORIALS 
The Committee notes that the BE 2022-23 allocation to these Akademies, Museums, 
Libraries, BTI and Memorials is more or less the sa me as in BE 21-22 with slight 
increase/ slight decrease. But the actual expenditu re in 21-22 till 31.1.22 in respect of 
Akademies, Libraries and BTI Memorials is quite low  as compared to BE allocation. It 
is especially very low in case of Akademies while t he RE allocation for 2021-22 is Rs. 8 
crores higher than BE allocation, the actual expenditure is only Rs. 239.45 (till   31.1.22) 
i.e. only 68.5% of the RE allocation. The Committee  notes that even when the actual 
expenditure in these and some other cases are low, the allocations have been increased 
significantly in RE. 
(Para 60) 
 
 
The Committee hopes and urges the Ministry of Culture to ensure that allocations are 
fully spent and not surrendered at the last moment. 
(Para 61) 
 
 
ARTISTS PENSION SCHEME AND WELFARE FUND 
The Committee, therefore, strongly reiterates that the pension amount needs to be 
reviewed without further delay and it should be mad e respectable for a person who has 
contributed to the society and country in continuing the various art forms. 
(Para 63) 
 
 
It is very saddening that instead of intensifying t he efforts in recognizing the artists in 
the 75 th year of Independence, the Ministry of Culture is re ducing the number of 
beneficiaries of this scheme since 2018-19, when it  reached the highest level of 4120 
beneficiaries. The Ministry has informed that due t o COVID-19, the beneficiaries have 
not been able to submit the desired documents, henc e the disbursements have been 
delayed. 
(Para 65) 
 
 
The Committee is not satisfied with the reason adva nced by the Ministry and 
recommends that the Ministry should be rather proac tive in such difficult  
circumstances  in  providing  financial  and  medical  support  to  artists  who  might  be 

38   
struggling for their survival. The Ministry should take help from its Zonal Cultural 
Centers or the bankers of the pensioners, besides r eaching to the beneficiaries directly 
for providing them with the financial support. 
(Para 66) 
 
 
SCHEME FOR THE AWARD OF SENIOR/JUNIOR FELLOWSHIPS T O 
OUTSTANDING PERSONS IN THE FIELDS OF CULTURE 
The Committee is shocked to find the inordinate del ay in release of payments to the 
junior and senior fellows under the scheme. It is p ained to know that despite strong 
recommendations made on the subject the Ministry is  not able to release the pending 
fellowships to all the fellows of the scheme in the last one year. 
(Para 69) 
 
 
As these fellows are basically full time researcher s in the field of art and music, the 
Committee feels that they should be supported by th e Ministry in their endeavor to 
preserve and continue our cultural heritage in a be tter and respectable manner. The 
Committee therefore recommends that in view of the rising inflation the fellowship 
amount should also be reviewed from Rs. 10,000 and Rs. 20,000 per month, respectively, 
to Junior and Senior fellows, which was fixed a long time back. 
(Para 70) 
 
 
The Committee also feels that centralizing the disb ursement of the fellowship has also 
affected the timely disbursement of the fellowship.  It should be disbursed by the CCRT 
as was done a few years back. The Committee also re commends that the Research 
papers of their scheme should be sent to art colleg es/schools on rotation basis so that 
they are utilized by future generations. 
(Para 71) 
 
 
CULTURAL FUNCTION AND PRODUCTION GRANT (CFPG) AND R EPERTORY 
GRANT 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should p repare a mechanism to 
individually intimate about the sanction of the gra nt to the organisations through their 
emails and requirement of any document should also be communicated. A nodal  officer 

39   
should be nominated to coordinate with these organisations to resolve any query on 
documentation. 
(Para 74) 
 
 
The Committee reiterates its recommendation made in  para 64 of this Report that since 
the beneficiaries of this scheme are the people inv olved in preserving the intangible 
cultural heritage of the country while devoting the ir life to the art forms and 
propagating it further, they should be honored in a respectable manner. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should review the amou nt of CFPG  and  Repertory 
Grant as well as keep increasing the number of gran tees, so that more and more people 
in the country, especially from rural background, h ave the opportunity to perform and 
enrich our culture, while earning a respectable liv elihood by showcasing their artistic 
skills. 
(Para 75) 
 
 
INCLUSION OF MONUMENTS IN THE LIST OF CENTRALLY PRO TECTED 
MOVEMENTS 
The  Committee  reiterates  the  recommendation  it  made  in  its   289 
th    Report      that 
important historical monuments and sites such as Ra ma Temple at Peddathumbalem 
Village, Adoni Taluka, Kethavaram Rock arts, and Behim caves in Kurnool be included 
in the list of Centrally Protected Monuments in Con sultation with State Governments. 
The Committee further recommends that the Ministry should expedite the process of 
identifying the important historical sites/monument s for requiring protection on 
priority, adding to the list of the 1.84 lakh Built  Heritage and Sites (BHS) that have 
already been documented by National Mission of Monu ment and Antiquities (NMMA) 
in the last 15 years. 
(Para 76) 
 
 
The Committee further recommends that the list of s tolen properties of the 
monuments/historical sites also be prepared and the  cases filed in these respect should 
be vigorously pursued, if it has not been filed the n the Ministry should take steps to file 
cases for stolen properties and recover them. 
(Para 78) 

40   
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should p ursue the matter of exploration 
of Ram Setu in the right earnest with priority inst ead of waiting for the proposal from 
the National Institute of Oceanography for exploration. The Committee also wants to be 
updated about the progress in the matter as well as  the project of ASI on underwater 
exploration in Dwarka. 
(Para 80) 
 
 
UTILISATION OF FUNDS COLLECTED FOR LIBRARIES BY STA TE 
GOVERNMENT 
The  Committee  reiterates  its  recommendation  made  in  para  42  of  its 310 
th  Report, 
which is as follows: 
'The State Governments may be guided to frame rules/ recommendations in the Act 
in a manner that money collected for the purpose is  utilized properly and spent only 
for the libraries. It should not go to the other St ate accounts and be used for other 
purposes. ' 
(Para 82) 
 
 
AZADI KA AMRIT MAHOTSAV 
The Committee appreciates the celebration and comme moration of the 75 years of 
progressive India and its glorious history. The use  of low cost initiatives and social  
media with a view to involve one and all is an exce llent approach towards this 
celebration of AKAM, which will maximize the outrea ch of the programme among the 
general public without straining the limited budget ary resources available with the 
Ministry. The Committee recommends that the Ministr y may ensure high levels of 
coordination with other Ministries and help them co me up with innovative ways to 
celebrate the AKAM. Efforts may also be made to rop e in State Government 
Departments to ensure even higher outreach of the celebrations. 
(Para 84) 
 
 
VISION OF THE MINISTRY FOR INDIA@2047 
The Committee is of the considered view that the Vi sion 2047 of the Ministry is very 
encouraging, however to achieve those, the Ministry  needs to intensify its efforts from 
the beginning itself. In this direction, the Minist ry needs to optimize the utilization of 
funds and plan more proposals with demand for more funds at the RE stage. 

41   
(Para 86) 
 
 
The Committee appreciates the long-term vision of t he Ministry of Culture to move 
towards a holistic model of cultural governance tha t goes beyond the Ministry  itself. 
The Committee feels that a significant part of the cultural heritage of the country is 
intangible, and as such, promotion and preservation  of the same for years to come can 
only be made possible when the policies of the Mini stry work in tandem with  the 
policies of other Central Ministries , State Govern ment Departments, Local Bodies, 
Societies and NGOs, International Organizations etc . The Committee therefore 
recommends that the Ministry may start working on b ringing this envisioned holistic 
model of cultural governance to reality, in a gradu al manner, since doing so would not 
only promote and preserve our cultural heritage, but also increase the cultural influence 
of the country and further its tourism prospects as well. 
(Para 88) 
 
 
MISCELLANEOUS 
Co-ordination with State Governments 
The Committee reiterates the recommendations made in para 116 of its 289 
th Report on 
Demands for Grants of the Ministry, which is as follows: 
‘The Committee feels that many of the State Governme nts often do not look after 
their protected monuments. The apathy of the State Governments towards the 
cultural heritage falling under their jurisdiction,  sometimes causes irreparable 
damage to the same. The Committee desires the Minis try to look into cases of 
neglect of historical monuments and sites by the St ate Governments, take it up with 
the concerned State Department, provide technical a ssistance to them and if  
needed, consider taking over the responsibility of development and upkeep of select 
State-protected monuments in cases of extreme neglect. ’ 
(Para 89) 
 
 
Conservation of Regional Cultures, Languages, Traditions, Art and Dance forms 
The Committee is concerned to note that although In dia is home to a plethora of rich 
and distinct regional cultures, languages, traditions, art and dance forms, many of these 
are getting lost under modern influence, without be ing recorded or preserved. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry should take all possible steps to protect and 

42   
preserve the intangible culture, languages, dialect s, traditions, art and dance forms of 
regional/local communities and tribes, including th ose in North-Eastern Areas  and 
other parts of the country, so that the unique rich ness of these cultures can be passed 
onto future generations. 
(Para 90)

The Indian Shipping Sector, with about 212 ports (1 2 Major and 200 Minor ports)  
along its 7,517 km coastline, has strengthened subs tantially in the last two decades. Over the 
years, the development of other aspects of shipping , such as containerization, multi-modal 
transport services, advancement of marine engineeri ng technology etc. has enabled  
infrastructural improvement in the Indian shipping industry. Roads, rails, airports and seaports 
together with the optimum storage capacity to move large shipments have placed the industry in 
a very advantageous position. The Ministry of Ports , Shipping & Waterways has been entrusted 
with the responsibility of formulation and implemen tation of various policies and programmes  
on development of Major & Minor Ports and harbours,  maritime safety, training & skill 
development, human resource, finance etc. Approximately 95% of the country /uni201Fs trade by volume 
and 68% by value, is moved through maritime transport.

19. During the meeting of the Committee held on 18 th February, 2022 on Demands for Grants (2022-

following information regarding the comparative per formance of Major and Non- Major Ports in

20. The Committee observes that the cargo handling capa city of Major Ports in the country 
has increased by about 79 percent between the years  2014-15 and 2020-21  (ignoring the 
incomplete data for the year 2021-22 since it is ye t to be finalized), which is an annualized 
growth rate of about 10.2 percent. As compared to t his, the gross cargo  handling capacity 
of Non-Major Ports has increased by only about 52 p ercent, with an annualized growth 
rate of just 7.2 percent. In terms of Traffic handl ed, however, Non- Major Ports registered 
a growth of about 30 percent ( ∼∼ ∼∼6.7 percent annualized) between the years 2015-16 a nd 
2019-20 (excluding the Covid affected year 2020-21 and ongoing year 2021-22) whereas 
Major Ports in the country only managed a minor inc rease of about 16 percent ( ∼∼ ∼∼3.8 
percent annualized) during the same period. This da ta points to the fact that while Major 
Ports across the country have managed to increase t heir capacity at a satisfactory pace, 
which is higher than that of Non-Major Ports, the s tatistics pertaining to traffic handled at 
ports across the country do not portray a robust picture for the Major Ports in the country. 
While Non-Major Ports have managed to increase the volume of traffic handled at nearly 
the same pace at which their capacity is increasing, Major Ports paint a contrasting picture 
with annual growth in traffic handled at a mere 3.8  percent as against the capacity growth 
rate of about 10.2 percent. The Committee, therefor e, recommends the Ministry to review 
the possible reasons behind the comparative stagnan cy in the volume growth of traffic 
handled at Major Ports in the country. The Ministry  may also come up with an effective 
plan of action to further improve the growth rate o f cargo handling capacity of Non-Major 
Ports in the country. The Committee desires to be a pprised of the action taken by the 
Ministry in this regard.

21. The Ministry has drafted a National Perspective Pla n (NPP) under Sagarmala, which identifies 
opportunities for reducing overall logistics costs to improve economic efficiency and increase 
export competitiveness. All identified projects hav e been divided into pillars and categories 
based on the scopes of the implementing agency invo lved. Ministry has identified connectivity 
between port and domestic production & consumption centers through rail, road, pipeline, 
MMLP under the pillar of port connectivity, consisting of 208 projects in total worth   /Rupee 
1.36 Lakh Crores undertaken by various implementati on agencies. Out of these 208 projects, 56 
projects worth /Rupee 19,489 Crores have been completed and 69 projects worth /Rupee 84,410 Crores 
have been awarded and are currently under implement ation. Out of the 44 projects under 
Sagarmala under various stages of development, deta ils regarding projects under various stages 
of development and funds sanctioned/ released for them is given at Annexure-A. 
22. The Sagarmala programme is the flagship programme o f the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and 
Waterways to promote port-led development in the co untry through harnessing India /uni201Fs 7,500 km 
long coastline, 14,500 km of potentially navigable waterways and strategic location on key 
international maritime trade routes. As per the con cept approved by the Cabinet, implementation 
of projects earmarked under Sagarmala Programme sha ll be done by the Central Line Ministries, 
State Government / State Maritime Boards and SPVs w hich may be set up at the State- level or 
port-level. The Ministry generally takes up residua l projects from time to time which have high 
social impact or low Internal Rate of Return. The M inistry has been allocated funds of Rs. 
359.98 Crore under Revenue Section for development and implementation of projects viz. port 
infrastructure projects, coastal berth projects, ro ad & rail projects, fishery harbours, floating 
jetties, skill development projects, Coastal commun ity development, International standard  
cruise terminal and unique and innovative projects such as Ro-Pax ferry services, National 
Maritime Heritage Museums. No funds have been alloc ated under Capital Section for equity 
investment in Sagarmala Development Company Limited (SDCL). 
23. The Committee observes that out of the 44 Sagarmala  projects under various stages of 
development, no funds have been released for as man y as 31 projects, which  points to the

infrastructure and capacity augmentation are of utm ost importance. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may analyze the diffic ulties being faced in the execution of 
these projects and take necessary remedial action t o tackle the same so as to complete the 
projects on time without cost escalation and enable India to upgrade its port infrastructure

RESPONSE TO OIL SPILL HAZARDS 
45. Upon the Committee /uni201Fs query on oil spill hazards, the Ministry apprised  that a National Oil Spill 
Disaster Contingency Plan (NOSDCP) has been in plac e in order to prevent oil spill generated 
impacts on marine species and ecosystem. The NOSDCP  works with different stakeholders such 
as Ports, State Governments. The Indian Coast Guard  has been declared as National  
Coordinating Agency for coordination of oil spill r esponse action. Under NOSDCP, spills 
occurring within Notified Port areas are dealt by i ndividual ports, and in turn MoPSW is taking 
action to strengthen oil spill response capability of ports in the country. In this regard, the 
Ministry had already executed a scheme of 50% finan cial assistance for procurement of Tier-1 
Oil Spill Response Equipment to Oil handling Major Ports & Non -Major Ports which continued 
till December 2020. Most of the Oil handling ports are equipped with Tier -I Oil Spill Response 
Facility. 
46. Subsequently, the Ministry has come out with the co ncept of developing 5 Regional Oil  
Response Centers (ROSRC) along the coastline coveri ng all major and non-major ports. 
ROSRCs shall provide enhanced capability and bring domain expertise and professional 
competence required to deal with oil spills in shor test possible time and minimizing the Overall 
Impact on ecosystem. The Ministry also provided the following information: 
 
a) Annex 1 of the International Convention for the Pre vention of Pollution from Ships 
(MARPOL) convention to which India is party to, deals with Prevention of Pollution by Oil. The 
aforesaid convention besides mandating the construction and operational requirement for ships to 
prevent pollution by oil, also specifies the requir ements for emergency response in case of oil 
spill. Indian ships are surveyed at periodic interv als to ensure compliance with the requirement  
of the MARPOL Convention. 
 
b) Part XI-A of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, and M erchant Shipping (Prevention of 
Pollution by Oil from Ships) Rules, 2010, deals with aspects related to prevention of oil pollution 
by ships. 
 
c) In addition, to discourage operation of sub-standar d vessels in Indian water, Flag State 
Inspections (FSI) and Port State Control (PSC) Insp ections of ships in Indian ports are carried  
out to ensure compliance of ships with applicable regulation for prevention of pollution by oil. 

27   
d) Merchant Shipping (Regulations of Entry of Ships in to Ports, Anchorages and Offshore 
Facilities) Rules, 2012 has provisions that require  older vessels to conform to standards of 
members of the Association of International Classif ication Societies, so that possibility of oil- 
spill from such vessel is minimized. 
 
e) National response mechanism to deal with oil spill incidents has been prepared (NOS-DCP). 
In addition, to deal with compensation matters in c ase of an oil-spill from certain types of oil, 
India has become a party to the International Civil  Liability Convention (CLC-92) and the 
International Fund Convention (known as 1992 Fund). 
 
47. The Committee appreciates that a specialized agency  viz., National Oil Spill Disaster 
Contingency Plan (NOSDCP) has been established to p revent oil spill, which coordinates 
with ports, state governments and the Indian Coast Guard and that the Ministry is 
implementing sufficient measures to prevent oil spi ll hazards and their impact on marine 
species. The Committee desires to know the financia l allocation provided to NASDCP and
